documents.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders remain a leading cause of injury and lost workdays in manufacturing, yet ergonomic assessment on the shopfloor is still largely periodic, manual and subjective. This paper presents Ergo Analyzer, a contactless, camera-based system that converts ordinary video into real-time, actionable ergonomic insight. The framework detects workers in the video stream, estimates seventeen body keypoints using a real-time pose estimation model, computes joint angles and body alignment, and compares them against ergonomic thresholds. A machine learning classifier then assigns a color-coded risk level and a numerical score from zero to one hundred, together with body region sub-scores for the back, shoulders, wrists and legs. A recommendation engine converts the result into task-specific corrective feedback such as adjusting posture, raising the work surface or taking micro-breaks. A prototype built with Python and OpenCV and exercised in simulated shopfloor conditions assigned distinct risk levels to good posture, improper lifting and excessive bending, and, in a live qualitative demonstration, the risk score fell from 72 to 32 after the recommended posture was adopted. We describe the architecture, scoring method, implementation and limitations, and outline a validation plan and roadmap toward alerts, mobile applications and wearable integration

Purpose: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) due to manual material handling (MMH) are an important and widely documented occupational health burden that is common in construction, manufacturing and heavy industrial sectors worldwide. This review of assessment tools examines sensor-based monitoring and intervention outcomes in manual material handling (MMH) in construction. Design/Methodology/Approach: Through a systematic search method compliant with PRISMA 2020, we examine the peer-reviewed literature published from 2010 to 2023 as contained in six electronic bibliographic databases, namely, Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, in five domains regarding wearable and mechatronics-based monitoring interventions for work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) which are the prevalence of WMSDs in the workplace, assessment instruments for measuring physical exposure to biomechanical risk factors, effectiveness of interventions, and Axiomatic Design which helps design and structure the above-mentioned interventions. Of the 1,847 records initially retrieved, 51 studies fully met the eligibility criteria after duplicate removal and sequential screening. Research Limitation: Five interrelated research gaps are identified: integrated multi-tool assessment frameworks for construction MMH, cost-appropriate sensor instrumentation, formal design methodology application, longitudinal intervention validation, and India-specific ergonomic guidelines. Findings: The low back (median prevalence 76%), neck (60%) and shoulder (55%) were the anatomical sites with the most consistent injuries across industry. The Rapid Entire Body Assessment was the most commonly used assessment tool, appearing in nearly seven in ten included studies, and scores for construction-related tasks were uniformly between 8 and 13 in the high-risk to very-high-risk action categories. The wearable sensor systems estimated the L5/S1 spinal compression force with error within ±8.3% of laboratory optoelectronic reference systems. This indicates sufficient fidelity for deployment in the field; however, the estimated cost of validated commercial systems is USD 15,000-100,000 which limits access for small and medium enterprises. The most effective risk reduction was achieved with a combination of engineering and administrative ergonomic control interventions, as indicated by declines of 41–55% in REBA scores. Furthermore, the results indicated a 38–49% reduction in the prevalence of WMSD symptoms across 31 intervention studies included in the systematic review. Practical Implication: A five-phase mechatronics-Axiomatic Design framework is proposed to address all five gaps within a single coherent research architecture. Social Implication: The findings support mandatory site-level ergonomic assessment and low-cost interventions to reduce chronic musculoskeletal pain among construction workers, particularly in the informal sector. Originality/Value: To the authors' knowledge, this is the first systematic review to integrate assessment-tool performance, wearable sensor monitoring, intervention effectiveness, and Axiomatic Design in a single synthesis for construction MMH, and the first to propose a five-phase mechatronics-Axiomatic Design framework tailored to Indian construction.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Nine verification reports can represent nine independent observations or nine copies of one. This technical working paper measures how much fresh evidence a recursive learner receives, how much survives five training updates, and when trusting faulty source identifiers increases predictive error. Across 20 paired simulation trials, correct source identification retained a predictive advantage of 11.95 percentage points of baseline risk after five updates. Exact enumeration gives break-even case-corruption rates of 29.5% to 50.2% under two specified fault mechanisms. The eight-page paper includes three figures and reproducible Python experiments. I proudly acknowledge the role of human–AI collaboration in developing this work. Working with ChatGPT (OpenAI) has helped me expand my strategic thinking, examine competing explanations, and connect my proposals to relevant scientific and technical research. My experience, objectives, and judgment guide the work, and I retain responsibility for its claims and conclusions. I regard transparent, rigorous collaboration with AI as a constructive method for advancing ideas that may benefit humanity.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to support sleep and mental health care, yet its role in disability care remains insufficiently synthesised. This narrative review examines the ethical and practical challenges associated with AI applications for sleep and mental health in disability care, with attention to both people with disability and disability support workers. Current applications include wearable and sensor-based sleep monitoring, mood tracking systems, conversational agents, predictive models, and workforce-facing decision-support tools. These technologies may improve early detection, continuous monitoring, personalised support, and care coordination. However, the literature identifies substantial barriers to safe and equitable implementation. Practical challenges include poor accessibility, limited inclusive usability, workflow disruption, variable digital literacy, weak external validation, and concerns about reliability across diverse disability groups. Ethical concerns include privacy and data governance, meaningful informed consent, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, intrusive surveillance, and the risk of dehumanising care. The evidence base is also limited by overreliance on general mental health AI literature, minimal focus on disability support workers, a lack of longitudinal and implementation research, and insufficient co-design with people with disability. Overall, AI may offer meaningful benefits in disability care, but responsible implementation requires disability-specific evidence, inclusive design, strong governance, human oversight, and sustained commitment to person-centred and rights-based care.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly significant in global ageing studies, particularly in the contexts of Chinese cultures, where ageing populations and shrinking care workforces pose pressing challenges. While AI offers benefits like reducing care burdens and improving quality of life, researchers face ethical challenges due to rapid AI advancements and inadequate regulations. This chapter examines ethical considerations in qualitative ageing research using AI as an interventional tool, focusing on older people’s lived experiences. Unlike traditional qualitative studies, this type of research involves reduced human control and multiple stakeholders, including older adults, family members, professionals, and AI as an agentic entity. This raises concerns about human-centric values, cultural norms (e.g., filial piety, collective conformity), and risks to social justice. Using case studies from the Chinese mainland and Taiwan, we explore ethical challenges across research design, data collection, analysis, and dissemination. Guided by a six-element ethical framework that embraces beneficence, respect, voluntariness, integrity, accountability, and independence, this approach balances dynamics among key players. It also emphasises narrative ethics, ensuring older adults’ stories are heard and represented, while addressing power imbalances where AI or researchers might overshadow their voices. By integrating these principles, the chapter provides a transferable ethical framework for qualitative ageing research on AI interventions in Chinese and other cultural contexts.

documents.abstract: Technical report, code, benchmark items and run artifacts for EUROPA Alignment, an open multilingual AI-safety benchmark that applies 16 original safety scenarios to each of the 36 languages prioritized by OpenEuroLLM (576 items), with paired harmful/benign contrasts, critical-dimension score gates and a pinned independent LLM judge. The report evaluates four SFT and DPO checkpoints of a 9B OpenEuroLLM model. The PDF is in paper/europa-alignment.pdf.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Radiation Therapy (RT) scheduling requires coordination of clinical constraints and operational objectives. Large language models (LLMs) may provide a natural‐language interface for generating candidate schedules. Purpose To evaluate the feasibility of using an existing LLM to generate RT patient schedules under clinical and operational constraints through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. Methods A one‐year, three‐linear‐accelerator (LINAC) simulation included 1400 new patients across 12 treatment categories modeled after clinical practice. Structured prompts supplied ChatGPT with patient data, the current schedule state, clinical rules, and scenario‐specific objectives. Performance was evaluated across scenarios addressing weekly treatment‐time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap‐constrained temporal relaxation, and infeasible request handling. LLM‐generated schedules were benchmarked against heuristic and CP‐SAT schedules under two objective settings. A six‐week retrospective comparison evaluated 2043 appointments against a clinical schedule. Results The LLM‐generated schedules satisfied the predefined feasibility rules in all evaluated scenarios. Across scenarios, 98.6%–98.8% of evaluated fractions remained within the preferred treatment‐time window. Adding a LINAC‐continuity objective reduced the LINAC switch rate from 52.4 2.6% to 9.4 0.6%, and gap‐constrained temporal relaxation reduced daily gap to 47.1 8.5 min and Friday gap to 89.2 18.4 min while maintaining low overtime. In infeasible request tests, the framework identified predefined constraint violations and returned interpretable corrective suggestions. The optimization benchmarks also generated feasible schedules, but their results showed strong objective‐weight trade‐offs. In the retrospective comparison, all computational approaches scheduled the workload without overtime; the LLM strategies reduced mean gap by 50.8%–77.1% and increased time consistency from 86.7% to 99.5%–99.9%. Conclusion Structured LLM‐assisted scheduling was feasible in the simulation and retrospective clinical comparison, producing candidate schedules under predefined constraints. The findings support further investigation of LLMs as flexible, human‐in‐the‐loop decision‐support tools for translating clinical priorities into feasible candidate schedules.

documents.abstract: While deep neural networks provide state-of-the-art solutions to a wide range of programming language tasks, their effectiveness in dealing with foundational program analysis tasks remains under explored. In this article, we present an empirical study that evaluates four prominent models of code (i.e., CuBERT, CodeBERT, GGNN, and Graph Sandwiches), plus four popular large language models (i.e., GPT3.5 , GPT-4o mini , Qwen2.5-Coder , and DeepSeek Coder ), in two such foundational tasks: (1) alias prediction, in which models predict whether two pointers must alias, may alias, or must not alias; and (2) equivalence prediction, in which models predict whether or not two programs are semantically equivalent. At the core of this study is CodeSem , a dataset built upon the source code of real-world flagship software (e.g., Linux Kernel, GCC, MySQL) and manually validated for the two prediction tasks. Results show that all models are accurate in both prediction tasks. We also conduct a comprehensive, in-depth analysis of the results of all models in both tasks, concluding that deep learning models are generally capable of performing foundational tasks in program analysis, even though in specific cases their weaknesses are also evident. Our code and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/CodeSemDataset/CodeSem .

Activity chairs are rehabilitation-grade ergonomic chairs with features such as braking systems and seat elevation. They are designed for individuals with limited standing tolerance or balance. Currently, there is limited research examining outcomes of their use. Our study used a mixed-methods, single-subject design to investigate the subjective and objective impact of activity chairs on activity engagement among adults with standing difficulties. Five people aged 21-65 with disabilities and/or chronic conditions participated, including two women, two men, and an agender individual. Performance measures (i.e., activity duration, fatigue, pain) were reported by participants in daily activity logs for five days prior to and five days after receipt of the chair. Pre-post semi-structured interviews were conducted. Activity chairs were used for dishwashing, cooking, and studying. Quantitative data included satisfaction rating with Wheelchair Outcome Measure (WhOM) and task demand rating with NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). Qualitative data were analysed using inductive content analysis. Quantitative data were assessed using descriptive, visual, and 2-Standard Deviation (2SD) methods. Compared to baseline, three participants had increased satisfaction and reduced pain and/or fatigue using the chair. One participant had equal satisfaction and fatigue; another participant had decreased satisfaction and increased pain. Four participants had decreased total NASA-TLX score, indicating reduced task demand. Qualitatively, most participants were satisfied with seat elevation features but dissatisfied with mobility and navigation. Activity chairs may facilitate engagement in seated activities for short durations when limitations relate to musculoskeletal fatigue and pain. The device’s compatibility with individual user’s abilities and context warrants careful consideration. documents.abstract: Concurrent defects in rotating components produce overlapping vibration components, complicating the recognition of defect combinations absent from training. We formulate this task as compositional multi-label learning and propose a compositional evidence-grounded framework (CEG-LLM). The model uses a frozen large language model as a sequence encoder, with trainable low-rank adapters and four sigmoid defect outputs. Continuous waveform tokens and nominal characteristic-order descriptors represent the signal, while a four-node composition graph conditions label-wise attention. Spectral alignment and compositional regularization guide training, and a fixed template links predictions to structured signal records. On one dataset collected from a rotating component at 1500 rpm, CEG-LLM achieves an observed-state macro-F1 of 0.941. Corresponding values are 0.922 for a one-dimensional vision Transformer (ViT), 0.912 for a signal-to-text language encoder, and 0.900 for a convolutional neural network (CNN). Mean exact match across six withheld defect pairs is 0.767, and macro-F1 at −3 dB is 0.819. A top-token versus random-mask deletion contrast of 0.207 indicates sensitivity to the selected representation under that intervention. These results assess recognition of unseen defect combinations and representation sensitivity within the evaluated operating condition.

documents.abstract: Adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) are being studied for tissue repair because they can affect immune and vascular cells. Their effects, however, depend on the product, tissue, cell state, and outcome being measured. This review examines how ASCs interact with macrophages, endothelial cells, and other stromal cells. We separate direct experiments from observations in human or animal tissues and from relationships inferred by computational analysis. In mouse studies, ASC-derived interleukin-1 receptor antagonist has been linked to changes in macrophage phenotype. ASC preconditioning has also increased cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) secretion. These molecular changes alone do not show that macrophages resolved inflammation. Other studies report vascular responses and better wound repair after treatment with ASC-derived factors or extracellular vesicles. They have not established which molecular pathways cause clinical benefit in ASC-treated human wounds. Spatial analysis may help identify candidate immune–vascular niches, and graph-based artificial intelligence may test whether their cell organization adds information beyond cell numbers and clinical variables. These proposed niches remain research hypotheses, not established features of ASC-treated human wounds. Clinical translation will require a defined ASC product, measurable changes in wound-cell function, adequate tissue perfusion, durable closure, and reproducible safety.

Benchmarks of inverter-based power grids that use machine learning (ML), large language models (LLMs), and learning-based inverter control can be misleading when fluent responses are operationally infeasible, judge-based scores are biased, or forecast-accuracy metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) do not reflect reserve and dispatch consequences. This study introduces VERITAS-GridBench, an operationally grounded benchmark in which decision-support outputs are evaluated against simulator/optimizer-based "Executable Truth" using explicit feasibility and constraint-violation measures. The framework combines tool verification, rule-based checks, and calibrated multi-judge semantic assessment through Triangulated Scoring, while also incorporating reproducibility, contamination control, domain-shift testing, and a Forecast-to-Operations (F2O) pathway. The experiments compare judge-only, multi-judge, and triangulated evaluation for power-system decision support and compare representative statistical, machine-learning, sequence, convolutional, and transformer forecasting models after their forecasts are propagated to reserve and dispatch calculations. The results show that judge-only scoring can reward fluent but infeasible actions, whereas tool-verified triangulation markedly increases feasibility and reduces unsafe wins and constraint violations. The forecasting results further show that lower MAE does not necessarily imply lower operational cost or risk. These findings support end-to-end evaluation in which model quality is judged by both predictive performance and physically executable grid outcomes.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical tasks has introduced powerful tools for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning, yet the opacity of many deep learning systems has limited their acceptance in clinical environments where trust, accountability, and interpretability are essential. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses these concerns by revealing the reasoning behind AI-driven decisions. This systematic review examines XAI methods applied to medical tasks, focusing on how explanations are generated and delivered through visual, textual, counterfactual, example-based, and multimodal formats. Drawing on a structured search of six databases covering literature published between 2020 and March 2026, we analyzed 309 studies, categorizing state-of-the-art techniques by their underlying algorithms, explanation formats, and clinical applicability. Visual explanations such as saliency maps and Grad-CAM predominate in medical imaging, whereas textual, counterfactual, example-based, and multimodal methods are increasingly applied to clinical prediction, decision support, and automated report generation. We further examine benchmark datasets, evaluation practices, and empirical studies assessing explanation quality, interpretability, and user trust, and highlight ethical considerations including fairness, bias, and transparency in deployment. By synthesizing recent advances and identifying gaps, this review aims to support the development of more interpretable, trustworthy, and human-centered AI systems for healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the main issues patients’ experience while managing their chronic illness by using a large language model (LLM), an artificial intelligence system trained to process human-like text to examine qualitative interview data. This LLM-assisted approach allows for more efficient and nuanced identification of central themes, complementing traditional qualitative approaches. Thirty participants with various chronic conditions were interviewed, and the transcripts were analyzed using an LLM to identify key themes. A correlation analysis was conducted to select weakly correlated themes, indicating limited overlap between themes within the final set, for in-depth exploration. Content domains were then created by grouping related themes based on predefined criteria. The LLM assigned intensity scores for all 46 themes. Variation was observed in how themes were expressed within this exploratory sample of older adults with multimorbidity. Correlation analysis identified patterns of co-occurrence, from which six content domains were created. These domains represent model-derived groupings rather than validated constructs. This study outlines a structured approach for AI-assisted qualitative analysis. LLM-generated scores reflect model interpretation rather than direct patient-reported burden and should be interpreted descriptively. Further validation, including comparison with human coding, is needed before clinical use.

Abstract This study examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) students demonstrate and develop Critical AI Literacy (CAIL) in generative AI-assisted essay revision. Drawing on the APSE model, which conceptualizes CAIL across four dimensions (awareness, positionality, interaction strategies, and evaluation), we conducted a longitudinal case study of three focal students across four writing tasks throughout a semester. Data sources included student-AI interaction logs, think-aloud protocols, stimulated recall interviews, and both initial and revised essay drafts. Qualitative analyses were conducted to trace patterns and changes in students’ CAIL. Findings show that all three students demonstrated CAIL across the four dimensions, although critical evaluation and critical positionality emerged as the most salient dimensions. Students selectively integrated AI feedback based on rhetorical fit, linguistic appropriateness, and factual accuracy, demonstrating various levels of agency. Over time, two students became increasingly selective and context-sensitive in their engagement with AI, whereas the third demonstrated strategic engagement from the outset but showed substantial task-to-task variation in feedback uptake. Overall, the students’ trajectories were heterogeneous and task-dependent rather than uniformly progressive. These patterns challenge linear models of AI literacy and highlight its situated nature in EFL writing contexts. Pedagogically, the study calls for differentiated instruction that fosters evaluative judgment and self-representation alongside prompt design. The findings contribute to a growing body of research advocating for more nuanced, learner-centered approaches to AI integration in foreign language writing.

Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content (AIGC) introduces dynamic reference perspectives that enrich traditional fine-art education. To explore this potential, we conducted a formative inquiry and an exploratory in-class workshop with 8 art-education professionals and 30 primary students to compare two AI-supported observation modes: Generative 2D and Generative Spatial (3D) Observation. Drawing on expert assessments of student drawings and qualitative accounts of their creative experiences, our findings reveal distinct differences in how 2D and 3D generative tools shape students’ observational behaviors and creative processes. The study offers preliminary, design-oriented considerations for integrating these distinct generative tools into art classrooms while preserving active, hands-on drawing practices.

Cloud technologies are increasingly becoming transformational to the business enterprise with the issues of flexibility, scalability and data-driven decisions. A combination of cloud solutions and Enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems is now an important idea to organizations that seek to enhance operational efficiency, workflows and real-time insight into business. In this paper, the integration of cloud technologies into Oracle ERP examined with the deployment models, the service frame and the enabling technology/tools like REST and SOAP APIs, Oracle Integration Cloud and pre-built adapters considered. Observed industry practice indicates that cloud-based Oracle ERP makes collaboration, automation, cost optimization, enhanced security and compatibility with emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), low-code/no-code platforms, IoT and blockchain simpler. The review of the current practices sheds some light on the most widespread spheres of implementation issues, such as data migration, customization, and system implementation, as well as usability difficulties, integration issues, and problems. It provides some ideas concerning the approaches that might be considered to guarantee effective adoption. As this paper argues, cloud ERP implementations and integration, together with case studies in organizations, reveal the potential of cloud-powered ERP systems as strategic enablers of digital transformation, business resiliency and long-term innovation. Additionally, future trends have been of interest in the study of AI-based predictive analytics, self-adaptive ERP, and cross-industry comparative modeling to optimize cloud ERP adoption and enhance competitive edge in businesses.

Abstract Occupational exposure to biological hazards is an important occupational health concern among healthcare workers, particularly nurses and midwives who frequently perform procedures involving blood, body fluids, and sharp instruments. However, evidence on the broader range of biological hazard exposures among nurses and midwives in public hospitals of Bale and East Bale Zones is limited. Therefore, this study aimed to assess the prevalence of exposure to biological hazards and associated factors among nurses and midwives working in public hospitals of Bale and East Bale Zones, Southeast Ethiopia. An institution-based cross-sectional study design was conducted involving 407 Nurses and Midwives working in public hospitals of Bale zones. Participants were selected using simple random sampling. Data were collected using the Kobo Android application and analysed using SPSS statistics version 27. Binary logistic regression analysis was performed to identify variables associated with biological hazard exposure. Adjusted odds ratio (AOR) with a 95% confidence interval were used to assess associations, and statistical significance was declared at p < 0.05. Overall, 68.6% (95% CI: 63.6–73.0) of nurses and midwives reported at least one occupational exposure to a biological hazard during their professional lifetime career. Recapping needles after use (AOR = 2.08, 95% CI: 1.16–3.74), lack of training on infection prevention (AOR = 2.78, 95% CI: 1.61–4.79), working > 40 h per week (AOR = 4.57, 95% CI: 2.41–8.67), lack of safety guideline at working unit (AOR = 3.80, 95% CI: 1.91–7.58) and having work experience of less than five year (AOR = 2.21, 95% CI: 1.16–4.24) were significantly associated with exposure to biological hazards. The findings of this study revealed the high prevalence of exposure to biological hazards among nurses and midwives in the study area compared to previous studies conducted in the country. Therefore, providing training on infection prevention, establishing clear safety guidelines, and effectively managing working hours are crucial steps for enhancing occupational safety and improving healthcare outcomes.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examined basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration in relation to multidimensional academic engagement among junior high school learners in the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program and sought to inform a guidance intervention. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational design, it surveyed all 91 ARAL learners at Zosimo A. Gulle Memorial National High School, Talibon, Bohol, during Academic Year 2025–2026 through complete enumeration. Adapted psychological-needs and student-engagement questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson product–moment correlation. Learners reported high psychological need satisfaction (M = 4.08), with relatedness strongest, alongside high need frustration (M = 3.56), driven principally by autonomy frustration (M = 4.14). Overall academic engagement was high (M = 3.52), although emotional engagement (M = 3.27) was moderate relative to behavioral (M = 3.67) and cognitive engagement (M = 3.61). Neither need satisfaction (r = 0.168, p = 0.111) nor frustration (r = 0.103, p = 0.333) showed a statistically significant relationship with overall engagement. Thus, reported participation and learning strategies coexisted with perceived pressure and limited emotional enthusiasm, without establishing causal explanations. The study recommends implementing and evaluating a data-driven guidance and counseling plan emphasizing learner choice, supportive tutoring, peer interaction, and psychosocial monitoring. Findings are limited by a single-school cohort, adapted self-report measures, and correlational design. This localized evidence supports sustainable, learner-centered academic recovery and guidance planning aligned with SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

Road traffic crashes (RTCs) remain a leading cause of death and disability globally. In Oman, although the number of road traffic deaths has declined over the past decade, road traffic injuries (RTIs) continue to be an important public health concern. This study aimed to identify factors associated with injury severity among individuals recorded in police RTC reports in Oman between 2018 and 2024. A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using data from the Royal Oman Police (ROP) national RTC database (1 January 2018 to 31 December 2024). The unit of analysis was the individual recorded in an RTC report, and the outcome was injury severity, categorised as none/mild, moderate, or severe/fatal. Multinomial logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) for sociodemographic, road-user, vehicle and crash characteristics; a sensitivity model additionally adjusted for governorate, year, day of the week and time of day. Of 30,307 individuals, 12,405 (40.9%) had none/mild, 12,616 (41.6%) moderate and 5,286 (17.4%) severe/fatal injuries (11.9% died). Most were male (80.9%), aged 25–39 years (43.5%) and Omani (72.9%). For severe/fatal versus none/mild injury, odds were higher for motorcycle/bicycle riders than public transport occupants (AOR = 7.40, 95% CI: 5.50–9.95) and for males than females (AOR = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.32–1.65), and lower for Omani versus non-Omani individuals (AOR = 0.79), employed versus non-employed individuals (AOR = 0.69) and those aged <25 versus ≥40 years (AOR = 0.61). Pedestrians had the highest odds, but uninjured passengers and pedestrians were not recorded, so these estimates should be interpreted cautiously. Compared with external factors, risky driving was associated with severe/fatal injury (AOR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.02–1.48), and human factors with moderate injury only (AOR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.01–1.38). In the sensitivity model, night-time crashes (00:00–05:59 vs. 06:00–11:59; AOR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.15–1.46) and Al Wusta Governorate (vs. Muscat; AOR = 1.92, 95% CI: 1.58–2.33) had higher odds of severe/fatal injury. Injury severity among individuals recorded in RTC reports in Oman was associated with road-user type, vehicle type, reported crash cause, sex, age, nationality, employment, governorate, year and time of day. Pedestrians, motorcyclists and cyclists, males, older and non-Omani individuals are priority groups for prevention. Protecting vulnerable road users, strengthening licensing and enforcement, and improving emergency response could reduce severe RTIs in Oman.

Abstract The adoption of AI-based code assistants like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot is increasingly popular among software developers, aiming to enhance coding efficiency and automate routine tasks. Nevertheless, there is limited empirical data on how these tools affect software quality attributes. For instance, while productivity may improve from a resource standpoint, code quality remains largely unchanged. This research explores how AI-supported development tools influence the sustainability of Scrum-based projects, i.e., software code quality and developer productivity. It employs a mixed-method approach, including a systematic review of 24 studies and 11 semi-structured interviews with experienced industry software developers. The results show that AI tools can contribute to various aspects of software quality, such as higher code consistency, greater maintainability, and improved defect detection and testing. The characteristics of automated code generation and code suggestions, as well as the generation of test cases through AI, were found to reduce development time and cognitive load and to encourage higher-quality outputs. Nevertheless, issues of reliability, security, and accuracy of code produced by AI, especially in complex development cases, still need to be addressed, and human supervision and validation must be ongoing, e.g., AI generates code which is hard to maintain, or AI produces code so fast and so much in quantity that humans do not have enough motivation and interest. The research also mentions that AI-assisted development assists sustainable software engineering by maximising resource usage, minimising reuse, and enhancing long-term code quality. This study offers a contribution to the further study of the role of AI in current software engineering and useful insights on the implementation of AI tools in quality-oriented software development by empirically correlating AI tool adoption with software quality results. Future research should focus on quantitatively assessing the effects of AI tools on software quality, using standardised measures such as defect rates, code quality scores, and test coverage. It would also be informative to conduct comparative research on various AI tools in different development settings.

Abstract Marine seismic interference, produced by external vessels, is a common type of noise in marine seismic data. This noise manifests as hyperbolic or linear characteristics in the shot domain, with its spectral range overlapping with that of the desired signal. Many traditional denoising methods have been proposed for the attenuation of seismic interference based on its incoherence in other domains. However, these methods may face challenges such as the degradation of desired signals. In recent years, geophysicists have begun exploring the development and applications of foundation models, which are large-scale pretrained models designed to learn general representations from data, within the geophysical domain. In this study, we introduce a foundation-model aided deep-learning (FAD) workflow for marine seismic interference attenuation. Our method utilizes a vision foundation model, the Segment Anything Model (SAM), for noise data extraction and employs the score-based diffusion model for data augmentation. Diffusion models represent state-of-the-art generative models capable of producing a multitude of data samples by learning the data distribution. The interference noise used for training is extracted before the onset of first arrivals using the SAM-based method, and the score-based diffusion model is utilized to generate diverse noise data. Subsequently, a ResUNet combined with efficient attention modules is trained to suppress interference noise. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we compare it with a state-of-the-art τ-p transform-based seismic interference attenuation method and the traditional f-k approach, and analyze the impact of different output strategies, data augmentation, and network architectures on the denoising results. Experimental results demonstrate that our method offers competitive performance in noise suppression, computation time, and preservation of desired signals. These results highlight the potential of FAD approaches in advancing geophysical data processing.

Background FAIR-Lupus explores the Normalized Excess-Risk Contribution (NERC), a descriptive mathematical index comparing selected prevalence-weighted association scores in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). It does not estimate causal attribution or attributable disease fractions. Methods A newly specified analysis replaced the submitted results. Two fixed synthetic cohorts of 100,000 subjects represented female SLE susceptibility and established SLE. We propagated multiplier uncertainty through 10,000 Monte Carlo draws and examined determinant exclusions, correlations preserving exposure frequencies, an illustrative interaction, and EBV prevalence scenarios. All exposure prevalences and the four flare risk multipliers were illustrative. No observed outcomes were analysed. Results Incident-scenario median NERC was 50.3% for family history and 34.7% for Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) seropositivity; their rank-one frequencies were 75.31% and 24.66%. Flare-scenario medians were 35.6% for stress, 26.7% for respiratory infection, 21.5% for occupational ultraviolet exposure, and 14.8% for PM 2 . 5 . Excluding family history increased EBV median NERC to 70.8%. Correlation alone produced no change when marginal exposure counts were fixed. Varying EBV prevalence from 70% to 98% changed its median share from 28.1% to 35.4%. Conclusions NERC percentages depend on the selected determinants, exposure prevalences and multipliers; they are not proportions of disease attributable to those determinants. FAIR-Lupus is a methodological exploration without empirical validation and cannot support clinical, occupational-health or individualized causal decisions.

Public institutions increasingly procure AI systems whose design they cannot inspect or change. In higher education, proprietary Early Warning Systems (EWS) leave colleges with few options beyond adjusting model outputs to address inequity. This raises a CSCW question: how is fairness work coordinated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students with unequal power to change these systems? Using student records from a public college in Ontario, Canada, we evaluate six post-hoc fairness interventions on a research EWS under simulated procurement constraints. We compare fairness, accuracy, and demographic disparities, introducing error-type profiling to trace how interventions redistribute false positives and false negatives. Interventions redistributed disparities without consistently reducing them. Two implementations favoured already-advantaged groups because they used group size to define disadvantage; small, marginalized groups remained poorly served. These findings show how procurement constraints and implementation choices shape the possibilities for fairness work. We call the resulting condition fairness theatre : dashboard metrics converge while groups’ error burdens persist or worsen.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Reliable fault diagnosis of rotating machinery, particularly ball bearings, is critical to ensuring operational safety and minimizing downtime. While acoustic signals provide rich diagnostic information, Artificial Intelligence (AI) models often suffer from overly optimistic metrics due to data leakage during preprocessing and splitting stages. This study presents a robust fault diagnosis framework with minimized leakage risk, using a multi-condition acoustic dataset. To completely eliminate leakage, a strict evaluation pipeline is implemented: (i) window-wise normalization is applied to each raw signal window prior to the Fast Continuous Wavelet Transform (fCWT) to prevent information sharing between windows, and (ii) data partitioning is strictly managed via Group Shuffle Split (GSS) and Stratified Group K-Fold (SGKF) cross-validation, ensuring that signals from the same recording do not span across training and test splits. Time–frequency features extracted directly from fCWT coefficients are processed using Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), which serves a dual purpose as an embedded feature selection mechanism and the core classifier. The framework achieves realistic and generalizable performance under distinct operational speeds (800, 1000, and 1200 RPM) and load conditions (0%, 15%, and 30%), yielding an F-score of 99.81% under GSS and a mean F-score of 99.35% across SGKF cross-validation, providing a trustworthy benchmark for health monitoring.

As Industry 4.0 is coming, Manufacturers need to evaluate suppliers with limited staff and incomplete information. Smaller suppliers may be particularly difficult to assess: their records are less standardized, and limited access to finance can obscure their capacity to fulfil orders. This paper examines whether Financial Large Language Models (FinLLMs), including FinGPT and BloombergGPT, can assist Supplier Relationship Management (SRM). It synthesizes research on quality-management workloads, supplier credit assessment, document processing, and supplier discovery, and considers the applications and limitations of the two models as representative cases. The review identifies four possible uses: extracting risk signals from text, combining textual and relational data for credit assessment, reading engineering documents, and finding suppliers through graph-based search. It also identifies limits in process-specific knowledge, numerical reasoning, confidence calibration, and the currency and coverage of training data. To clarify who should act on model outputs, the paper proposes a "boss-employee" framework organized around task division, decision authority, and calibration through human review. The framework treats AI as support for procurement staff rather than a substitute for their final judgement. It remains conceptual and requires testing in manufacturing settings.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In December 2020, an international panel of 25 experts from 14 countries met online for two days to assess developments in the construction sector and to draft road maps for vocational education and training (VET) up to 2035. The workshop was held as part of the European Vocational Skills Week 2020. Its results were saved as whiteboard exports. This report documents the procedure, the panel and the results. It is based on a complete transcription of all exports, which is included as an appendix. The findings show that the panel used developments in the sector mainly as a starting point to discuss how, where and for whom learning should be organized. Recurring elements are a single access point to training, the recognition of short learning units across Europe, reliable funding and the value of skills for clients and workers. Although the workshop did not set up a group for the dimension „Individual“, the full coding assigns 25 of the 235 original contributions to that dimension, while the category for teachers and trainers as the subject of a contribution remains empty. A retrospective from 2026 compares the results with later developments. Several needs named by the panel have since been taken up in European policy. Generative artificial intelligence, however, does not appear on any board, and the coding of the corpus confirms this: none of the 235 original contributions names analytical or generative AI explicitly, while eight name automation, robotics or data without any method and are therefore technological connection points rather than references to AI. The report closes with the limitations of the documentation and links to related work.

Foundation models provide reusable representations, promptable interfaces and volumetric priors for medical image segmentation. Translating these capabilities into reliable performance at a new hospital requires attention to imaging variation, task definitions and the information available for adaptation. This critical narrative review focuses on organ and lesion segmentation in computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. It examines three connected questions: how transferable segmentation capabilities are formed, how adaptation mechanisms address differences between centers, and which external results support practical model selection. Pretraining objectives, dense prediction interfaces, support examples and spatial modeling are compared as complementary sources of capability. Transfer strategies are then organized by access to target images, training and validation labels, and case-specific interaction, with separate consideration of parameter, representation and input optimization at test time. Evidence from center-held-out studies, external disease cohorts and human annotation experiments shows that appropriate initialization, task adaptation and interaction can yield useful gains. Their interpretation depends on the comparator, the information supplied and the unit of evaluation. Accuracy, difficult cases, prompting requirements and the cost of the complete workflow therefore need to be considered together. An information-conditional framework links changes between centers to capability requirements, available resources, adaptation mechanisms and external benefit. This framework supports study design, model comparison and annotation resource allocation for deployment at new centers.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges whether submitted academic work can serve as credible evidence of individual learning. This study examined GenAI use, critical AI practices, active teaching and assessment strategies, and self-reported verifiable-learning capabilities in higher education. A convergent post-intervention mixed-methods design involved 94 undergraduates from five cohorts, three disciplinary contexts, and two academic stages at a public university in Ecuador. Critical AI use (M = 4.06/5, SD = 0.60) and verifiable-learning capabilities (M = 3.96/5, SD = 0.60) were high and strongly associated (Spearman’s ρ = 0.641, p < 0.001), whereas GenAI-use frequency was unrelated to either construct. Final-semester students reported higher critical AI use (Holm-adjusted p = 0.004; Cliff’s δ = 0.441), but all were enrolled in Information Technology Regulations; academic stage and discipline were therefore structurally confounded. Revision, applied projects, demonstrations, authentic problems, feedback, and practical workshops received the highest ratings. Qualitative findings emphasised practice, verification, and responsible AI use, while students supported multi-source assessment and explicit rules for permitted AI use. The findings support human-centred assessment designs that prioritise critical governance of AI and credible demonstration of individual learning.

Artificial intelligence (AI) models for keratoconus frequently report near-perfect discrimination, with pooled sensitivity and specificity approaching 98% when manifest keratoconus is separated from normal corneas. These figures are increasingly invoked to answer a different, more consequential question: whether an apparently non-ectatic cornea can safely undergo refractive surgery. We argue this is a task mismatch rather than a performance shortfall. Three targets are routinely conflated-manifest keratoconus, subclinical phenotype and future post-refractive ectasia-with the evidence strongest for the target furthest from the clinical question and weakest for the one closest. Underlying this is a single methodological issue: the absence of a robust reference standard, or ground truth, appropriate to the surgical decision. These estimates also derive largely from enriched case-control datasets, with subclinical-keratoconus case proportions of roughly 25% against an estimated 1% clinical prevalence. Applied to 1000 candidates at 1% prevalence, the pooled estimates correspond to approximately one missed subclinical case (0.6-1.6) and 45 false-positive referrals (25-80), both ranges derived from the reported confidence bounds-modelled diagnostic outcomes, not postoperative ectasia risk. We propose that ectasia-risk AI be evaluated as decision support for surgical eligibility, along a decision-anchored evidence chain spanning clinical validity, calibration and threshold-specific error, transportability, decision utility and post-deployment surveillance-complementing, rather than replacing, TRIPOD+AI, PROBAST+AI, STARD-AI, DECIDE-AI and FUTURE-AI. For refractive surgery, trust should not be inferred from a high area under the curve; it should be earned through evidence that follows the decision from target definition to real-world surveillance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Quality of life (QoL) has emerged as an important indicator of well-being among medical students, particularly in demanding educational environments. Medical education is a highly demanding environment that exposes students to sustained academic and psychological stress, affecting their daily life and mental health. In addition, and due to the conflict, Syrian medical students are exposed to additional economic and psychosocial stressors, all of which necessitated us to evaluate students’ QoL after the end of the Syrian conflict. In this paper, we aimed to evaluate QoL across all its domains and to identify factors associated with variations in students’ well-being. A cross-sectional study was conducted on undergraduate (medical, dental, and pharmacy) students across public and private universities in Syria. Data were collected between November and December 2025 using a self-administered, validated Arabic questionnaire (WHOQOL-BREF). Sociodemographic, academic, lifestyle, and health-related variables were also collected. Descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlation analyses, and multivariate linear regression models were performed using SPSS. Results were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05, with 95% confidence intervals. A total of 1,110 students were included in the analysis. Participants reported the highest QoL scores in the Physical Health domain and the lowest scores in the Environment domain. The overall level of perceived stress was moderate to high. Across all QoL domains, the analysis consistently linked mental disorders and higher perceived stress to lower QoL. Unlike academic difficulties and family pressure, physical activity was robustly associated with better QoL. However, financial difficulties showed the strongest negative association with the Environment domain. Interestingly, gender was a significant associated factorsolely for Social Relationships, favoring female students. This study concluded that key associated factorsof reduced well-being included mental health issues, financial difficulties, and low physical activity, whereas intrinsic motivation and active lifestyles were associated with better outcomes. Our findings emphasize the need to implement immediate policies aimed at enhancing student well-being, especially in conflict-affected countries like Syria. Addressing these issues is crucial for improving students’ QoL and fostering academic and professional resilience. Further research should adopt longitudinal designs to monitor changes in QoL over time and explore causal correlations. Not applicaple

Background: Musculoskeletal disorders account for over 30% of work-related health harm in New Zealand (WorkSafe NZ). For forty years the response has rested on observational assessment (RULA, REBA, the NIOSH equation, and WorkSafe’s NZMAC, NZRAPP and NZART), applied with a clipboard, a printed score sheet and a trained assessor: expert-dependent, slow, and hard to repeat. Objective: To develop an online video-based ergonomic assessment system that analyses workplace tasks from a single standard video, and to establish how closely its outputs agree with laboratory reference methods.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Current applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in architectural design education emphasize open-ended ideation and image production, offering limited support for architectural synthesis. This paper proposes a hybrid analogue-AI framework for integrating Generative AI (GenAI) into the architectural design studio, employing GenAI across three stages — problem framing, solution generation, and informed refinement within which the design space repeatedly expands and contracts. Building on Author´s (2025a) AI-assisted workflow and Author’s (2025b) decomposition of the design process into cognitively matched steps, this framework positions GenAI as a support to design reasoning without replacing analogue representation, human agency, or architectural judgement. We argue that constraining GenAI inputs with prior analogue work may support reproducibility, informed creativity and design control, contributing to outcomes that are both original and constructible while addressing recurring AI dependency on open-ended prompting and stylistic iteration.

In the past, human factors (HF) in infrastructure projects was often applied later through design reviews and standards-based checks after important design decisions had been made. As transport systems become more complex, HF practice is moving toward earlier, more immersive, and more evidence-based testing of designs before infrastructure is built. This presentation describes the development of a HF Lab Implementation Plan for a large transport infrastructure project. The plan was developed through document review, workshops, analysis of users and key activities, and a targeted literature review. HF lab methods and tools were assessed using a rating framework covering both the robustness of evidence for measuring design against success outcomes and whether each method was fit-for-purpose for the project and Human Centred Design (HCD) topic area.
Machine learning and artificial intelligence are increasingly becoming integral components of contemporary bioengineering and biomedical research [...]
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Human Factors has long employed the use of prototype modelling as part of design assessment principles. From using real aircraft to demonstrate evacuation behaviours, to producing mock-ups of car chassis to determine maintenance access points, physical models have been used to demonstrate the limitations of design to designers and policy makers. However, large full-scale models are expensive to build, and often rely on a pre-existing design, which means that they are often met with change resistance from engineers who have progressed through multiple design stages with a mental model that has now been physically built. Here I will introduce the work undertaken using digital human modelling as part of engineering design in the rail industry

Background: The American Joint Replacement Research-Collaborative (AJRR-C) is a National Institutes of Health-funded P30 Core Center for Clinical Research and seeks to accelerate practice-changing arthroplasty research by leveraging the American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) and shared multicenter research infrastructure. The AJRR-C convened 2 complementary meetings to establish a scalable coordinated pathway from the identification of high-priority clinical questions to the initiation of prospective studies. Methods: In July 2025, leaders from The Hip Society, The Knee Society, the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons, the AJRR, the Orthopaedic Research and Education Foundation, and the broader research community identified and prioritized clinical research questions regarding infection, perioperative management, new technologies, surgical techniques, implants, and quality. In April 2026, orthopaedic surgeons, methodologists, and artificial intelligence experts reconvened to evaluate contemporary approaches for addressing these priorities. Results: A central theme of the meetings was the importance of utilizing a fit-for-purpose approach in which study design is tailored to the clinical question, available data, and potential sources of bias. Clinical questions with clear equipoise and feasible interventions may warrant randomization, whereas questions involving rare outcomes, rapidly evolving technologies, surgeon preferences, or long-term surveillance may be better addressed with observational studies. Participants emphasized the need for a robust, sustainable network for arthroplasty clinical trials that provides the shared infrastructure necessary for coordinated site engagement, standardized data definitions, reliable longitudinal follow-up, and AJRR linkage across multicenter trials. Two new AJRR-nested randomized trials arose from the priority-topics meeting, and their development demonstrates the potential of the AJRR-C consensus model to translate research priorities into practice-changing evidence generation. Conclusions: The AJRR-C established a coordinated pathway from the prioritization of research to the implementation of multicenter studies to address high-priority arthroplasty research questions. Sustaining this model requires continued collaboration among orthopaedic societies, investigators, methodologists, and the AJRR, as well as reliable funding mechanisms.

Abstract The project DatProForge (Data-driven Process Modelling of Drop Forging Processes to Increase Productivity Using Adaptive Tool Design Methodology), conducted within the first funding period of SPP 2422 has established the foundations for an end-to-end digital process chain combining experimentally acquired process data, automated finite element (FE) simulations, radar-based condition monitoring, and data-driven and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The resulting methodology provides the basis for developing an intelligent assistant system for process design and optimisation. The intelligent assistant system employs machine learning (ML) and XAI methods to identify defect risks, determine their key influencing factors in a transparent manner, and generate recommendations for process optimisation and adaptive tool design. Using a hot bulk forging process on a servo screw forging press as a representative use case, the paper demonstrates how research results on sensor systems, radar signal processing, stochastic simulation, underfill prediction, vent-channel optimisation, and data-pipeline modelling can be integrated into a unified assistance system. Particular attention is given to the joint analysis of simulation results and experimentally acquired process data to identify relevant process and machine-related effects and to account for associated uncertainties. The resulting simulation-to-reality transfer approach enables the FE models to be successively refined by incorporating these effects, thereby progressively improving their agreement with the real forging process. Combined with interpretable data-driven models, this approach provides a foundation for robust, data-driven decision-making in process optimisation and adaptive tool design.

Landfill operations present a unique and high-risk environment for Whole Body Vibration (WBV). Heavy plant operators—particularly those manoeuvring compactors, excavators across waste—are frequently exposed to high levels of vibration. These are particularly prominent in the side-to-side plane due to the inherent instability of uneven waste surfaces and repetitive operational patterns. This presentation explores the lessons learned over time from a multi-year program dedicated to understanding and mitigating WBV risk, aligning with the conference theme of learning from the past to lead in the present. The evolution of our approach reflects a transition from reactive compliance to proactive, data-driven health management. Initially, risk was viewed through a narrow lens of equipment age and occurrences of injury but exposure assessments revealed that technical specifications alone were insufficient predictors of operator exposure. Through consistent assessments, three critical aspects emerged: the mechanical condition of the seating systems, specific operator training, and the systematic management of health outcomes through early intervention. The outcome from these interventions led to slow change in vibration levels and a downward trend in reported musculoskeletal discomfort such as back pain. Key findings highlight that even new machinery can fail to protect operators if seat suspension is not used correctly or operation of the machines exceeds the capability this engineering control can provide. This session outlines the roadmap we followed in applying the hierarchy of controls to an "invisible" hazard. The takeaway is clear: to ensure we protect the future of worker health, we must move beyond assessments as a snapshot in time and embrace an approach that integrates engineering controls with empowered workers through training along with ongoing health surveillance. By treating all hazards as dynamic rather than static, we can significantly elevate the standard of long-term occupational health.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose: The objective of this study is to analyse the potential of remittance-dependent households in Feni district to transform into sustainable entrepreneurs through artificial intelligence (AI) and human-centred support. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopted a mixed-methods approach, using surveys and key informant interviews (KII). Findings: The study shows that remittances are mainly used for consumption and productive investment is limited. AI-based digital finance, market intelligence and business planning tools are helpful in decision-making and entrepreneurship development. However, human support is essential for building trust and behavioural change. Therefore, an integrated model of AI and human support is most effective. Original/Value of the Paper: This study provides guidance for policymakers and development practitioners and contributes to the achievement of SDGs 1, 8 and 10. Keywords: Remittance Utilisation, Artificial Intelligence, AI, Entrepreneurship Development, Migrant Household Citation: Hoque, M. S. (2027): From Remittance Dependence to AI-Supported Entrepreneurship Development: A Roadmap for Sustainable Livelihoods in Feni District, Bangladesh. World Journal of Science, Technology and Sustainable Development (WJSTSD), Vol. 22, No. 1, pp. 35-xx.

Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine-learning models, is increasingly applied to complex forensic chemical, material, and biological evidence. High reported performance does not itself demonstrate generalization to new forensic material. We conducted a systematic methodological review of 446 reports and 1,005 eligible evaluation regimes, examining independence of final evaluation, physical and biological parent grouping, information leakage, external or shifted testing, and transportability. Following source-based methodological assessment and human adjudication, source-supported leakage was classified in 284/446 reports (63.7%); 36/446 (8.1%) showed strong potential concern, 85/446 (19.1%) had uncertain boundaries, and 41/446 (9.2%) had no identified leakage concern. External or shifted evaluation was reported in 278/446 reports (62.3%), although only 94/278 (33.8%) had an evaluation satisfying five strict criteria for transportability of an unchanged pipeline. At regime level, 135/521 external or shifted evaluations (25.9%) satisfied these criteria. Source-supported leakage occurred in 195/308 Biological reports (63.3%) and 87/133 Chemical/Material reports (65.4%): prevalence ratio 1.033 (95% CI 0.889–1.200). The primary comparison did not identify a significant difference across these domains. Casework claims should therefore be evaluated against the independence of the relevant forensic unit, the complete development–test boundary, the shift actually examined, any target-data adaptation, and the applicable performance denominator.

Introduction Remote-work labels describe an advertised work arrangement, but whether they accompany different advertised requirements remains unclear. Drawing on signaling theory and work design research, we examine two layers of advertised demand: platform-native functional categories and O*NET-anchored work-style language. Methods The primary analysis uses 550 digital-marketing advertisements from one public LinkedIn dataset, including 220 with an explicit remote-work flag and 330 without a recorded flag. An expanded sample of 1,394 advertisements includes the primary sample and assesses sensitivity to the occupational boundary. Overlap-weighted regression adjusts for role family, seniority, employment type, and description length, with standard errors clustered by employer identifier. The seven-element Work-Style Demand Index (WSDI) measures the breadth of matched work-style signals, rather than their intensity or employees' traits. Results The adjusted WSDI remote-flag contrast was –0.018 (95% CI –0.047 to 0.012); the five-element adaptive/growth subindex (AWDI) contrast was -0.008 (95% CI –0.043 to 0.026). Functional breadth differed by +0.058 categories (95% CI –0.091 to 0.206). These estimates provide no clear evidence of an association and do not establish equivalence. The descriptive networks each retained 10 work-style edges, with six shared edges. A rule-based context check found most matches outside identified benefits/equal-opportunity text, but did not establish construct validity. Discussion The study offers a transparent way to examine how work-arrangement information co-occurs with advertised demands. It distinguishes employer-side text signals from applicants' interpretations and employees' experiences.

This article is devoted to the analysis of theoretical approaches to understand the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in the political sphere as presented in Russian research of 2023–2026. Based on a comparative analysis of these studies, the paper proposes a systematization of approaches regarding AI role: as a technological tool for optimizing political processes, a source of new risks, and an emerging quasi-subject of political communica-tions. It is demonstrated that these approaches are not mutually exclusive but rather reflect different facets of the same phenomenon. The research identifies a key contradiction between the active integration of AI into public administration and maintaining methodological limitations concerned with agency ambiguity, liability blurring, and trust deficit. The author makes the following conclusion: at the current stage, AI remains an auxil-iary tool lacking full-fledged political agency.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Presentation given at the Basel Biometric Society Annual Meeting 2026: Quantitative drug development in the age of AI. Abstract: Use of Generative AI is very common in many domains of specialized expertise, including biostatistics. However, applying GenAI to produce high-quality results in a specialized field - particularly within the high-stakes, regulated environment of the pharmaceutical industry - is far from straightforward. In this presentation, I will discuss practical approaches for using GenAI and agentic tools effectively. Different use cases bring distinct gains and risks. At one end, GenAI can be remarkably effective at strengthening the technical foundations of a project - adding checks, linting, formatting, automated tests, and version control - at low risk and cost. At the other end, when we ask AI to solve complex problems within a specialized domain, meaningful human oversight becomes considerably more difficult. Strong human-in-the-loop controls demand a systematic, deliberate approach across the full workflow - from planning to execution - together with the ability to observe and interpret an agent's actions, judge the reliability of its output, and apply the right technical capabilities, including appropriate skills, tools, agents, and agent harnesses. Developing both the technical skills to use GenAI and a clear understanding of use-case scenarios and their associated risks is essential. Doing so allows us to treat AI as a capable tool and thought partner rather than an opaque black box, and to generate results for which we can confidently take accountability.
