documents.abstract: Generative AI is a game-changer, and its transformative potential is evident in education. India has the opportunity to integrate Generative AI and improve its education system with respect to NEP 2020. The current study critically analyses and reviews the integration of Generative AI into the NEP 2020, and specific areas of competency-based education, multilingual education, teacher professional development, equity, and the integration of educational technology. The study has a structured narrative and thematic synthesis of the published research articles between 2020 and 2025, combined with the provisions of the related official documents of policy. The study mainly focuses on the educational promises of conversational AI, and identifies studies on adoption, research accounts and/or interventions. Depending on the task, context, user and teacher mediation, and available resources, different benefits can be gained. One challenge with the current trend to incorporate Generative AI into education is that educational institutions need to determine the extent to which they accept risks and rely on the technology, and also evaluate the educational benefits and potential harm caused by the technology. The review highlights the importance of longitudinal research in various contexts in India (i.e. school level, region, language, school resources).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) raises questions about human creative contribution, copyright in outputs and third-party rights. This study examines responses to copyright-related statements in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh, including a separately described subgroup of 241 law students. The questionnaire asks about recognition of copyright questions, the relevance of human contribution, terms of use, third-party rights and the perceived value of guidance. It does not ask respondents to assign ownership to a specified actor or solve a legal problem; consequently, it does not measure actual copyright knowledge or establish legal ownership. Items were analysed separately using descriptive distributions, paired endorsement comparisons and exploratory rank correlations. In the full sample, 191 respondents (49.6%) endorsed recognising that copyright questions can arise, 223 (57.9%) endorsed the relevance of human contribution, and 303 (78.7%) agreed that clear guidance would improve their responsible use. Among law students, the respective percentages were 51.0%, 60.6% and 80.5%. Overall, 147 respondents endorsed both recognising copyright questions and the potential usefulness of guidance, while 156 endorsed guidance without endorsing recognition. This pattern is not evidence that guidance improves knowledge or behaviour. The article distinguishes statements of awareness and normative expectations from demonstrated legal competence, and recommends scenario-based assessment and documentation of respondent recruitment for future research.

Introduction Generative AI chatbots now give students instant commentary on their writing, yet little is known about how engaging with that commentary relates to the self-regulatory capacities on which writing development depends. This study examined a chain mediation model in which generative AI feedback use is associated with writing self-regulation through feedback literacy and, in turn, second language writing anxiety. Methods Non-English-major undergraduates at three universities in Henan Province, China, completed two surveys 12 weeks apart in the 2026 spring semester (wave 1 N = 650; 520 retained, 80.0%). Wave 1 assessed generative AI feedback use and feedback literacy; wave 2 assessed writing anxiety and writing self-regulation. Serial mediation analysis used 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples, with item-level validity checks and re-estimations without item parcels added as sensitivity analyses. Results Generative AI feedback use was positively associated with later writing self-regulation [ c = 0.265, 95% CI (0.190, 0.339)]. The total indirect effect was 0.128 [0.094, 0.167], or 48.3% of the total association: 0.086 [0.053, 0.122] via feedback literacy, 0.024 [0.008, 0.049] via writing anxiety, and 0.018 [0.009, 0.031] for the serial route. The direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137). Focal paths kept their signs and significance when item parcels were removed and when only feedback-seeking items defined the predictor. Discussion These estimates describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. The pattern is consistent with a theoretically proposed ordering; the pedagogical suggestions are recommendations only, not demonstrated outcomes. The generative AI feedback use scale is a preliminary study-specific measure.

Generative artificial intelligence can provide explanations and comments on circuit solutions, but its educational value depends on how students interpret and use those responses. This focused narrative review examines the use of generative AI to help students identify and correct errors in introductory circuit analysis. Published sources were identified through OpenAlex searches, publisher records, and reference checking, with full-text assessment informing selection and synthesis. Twelve reports were selected for their relevance to circuit reasoning, feedback, or learner verification; an electronics-course perception study provides an explicitly adjacent comparison. Foundational research on formative feedback and self-regulated learning informs the interpretation. The synthesis addresses circuit representation and diagnostic accuracy, students' use of feedback, and the interpretation of educational outcomes. Technical evaluations show that input representation, reference information, and computational support shape the conditions under which responses are assessed. Classroom and tutoring reports describe opportunities for explanation, comparison, revision, and instructor intervention. The selected reports provide more direct evidence of perceived usefulness than of independently retained understanding. Observational grade associations and a historical-cohort comparison offer additional perspectives, although their designs limit causal interpretation. The review proposes teaching considerations that preserve students' initial reasoning, check the represented circuit, focus guidance on a specific difficulty, and require students to justify corrections. These considerations are derived from the literature and have not been evaluated as a combined intervention. The principal implication is that AI feedback should be judged through the accuracy of its diagnosis and the student's subsequent reasoning. Selective coverage, heterogeneous outcomes, and AI-assisted selection and extraction constrain the review's conclusions.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) advances rapidly, its potential in the innovative design of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) is becoming increasingly evident. This scoping review examines research on GenAI-enabled ICH design by scholars at Chinese universities. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, it draws on the literature retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoS) and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). Through literature analysis and comparison, the review maps the development of relevant technologies, categorises their design applications, and summarises the evaluation approaches used in the selected studies. The reviewed applications fall into three categories: embroidery, dyeing, and weaving; graphic visual arts; and dimensional objects and product forms. It also identifies persistent challenges, including limited access to high-quality ICH data, insufficient understanding of cultural meanings, and unresolved intellectual-property and ethical concerns. The review highlights the growing use of diffusion models, particularly Stable Diffusion combined with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), while emphasising the continued importance of human expertise and community participation. It concludes by outlining directions for more culturally grounded, ethically responsible, and practically applicable GenAI-assisted ICH design in higher education.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly changed the way businesses can create advertisements by providing custom content for a low cost. However, the use of generative AI has increasingly begun to raise questions about creativity and transparency; for businesses, the use of generative AI has also begun to spark dilemmas involving consumer trust, and the role of humans within advertising. This literature review examines how generative AI affects advertising from both a business and consumer perspective. Existing research was analyzed through AI disclosure, perceived authenticity, creativity, purchase intention, traditional versus generative AI, and business efficiency. The literature generally suggests that consumers can respond negatively when it is revealed that an advertisement was generated by AI, especially when they already have preconceived notions of generative AI being unauthentic or low effort. Nevertheless, recent research has also demonstrated generative AI can also boost engagement by increasing perceptions of novelty, when the audience views generative AI positively. The stark contrast between these findings suggest that consumer responses cannot be determined solely based on whether or not AI was used, but by the nuances of its use: the type of product being advertised, the transparency of the advertisement, and the opinions of the target audience are factors that all influence advertising outcomes. As a whole, generative AI can provide significant opportunities to businesses to reduce cost and increase the scale of advertisement production, but companies must balance these advantages with the concerns regarding consumer expectations for authenticity and creativity.

Introduction Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) is rapidly transforming higher education by automating the creation of personalised learning materials, intelligent tutoring systems, and adaptive assessment tools. Methods This paper presents a structured overview of the current state of AIGC in higher education, examining its impact on teaching methodologies, instructional design, and student learning experiences. Results In line with the proposed research questions (RQs), we analyse how AIGC reshapes pedagogical practices, the benefits and challenges associated with automated content creation and personalised learning and how bias, fairness, and ethical governance influence responsible adoption. Discussion The article also discusses emerging technologies and trends that are likely to shape the future integration of AIGC in academic contexts, alongside ongoing efforts to develop robust frameworks for the accountable and equitable use of them. By synthesising recent literature and practice, this work offers educators, institutional leaders, and researchers an actionable perspective on integrating AIGC to enhance educational quality, access, and innovation in an evolving higher education landscape.

documents.abstract: Abstract This pilot study explores the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into primary STEM education in Sweden through a structured Teacher Professional Development (TPD) model. While GenAI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot have rapidly entered educational contexts, empirical research on their pedagogical use in primary schools remains limited. Eleven teachers participated in a six-month TPD programme comprising workshops, collaborative discussions, and classroom implementations. The empirical material consisted primarily of audio-recorded workshop discussions, which were transcribed and analysed, supplemented by a post-intervention questionnaire. Data were analysed using thematic coding informed by the Refined Consensus Model (RCM) and the Digital Promise AI Literacy Framework. Findings indicate that GenAI served primarily as an idea generator, supporting lesson planning and interdisciplinary integration across mathematics and science. Teachers reported opportunities for timesaving, differentiated instruction, and enhanced creativity, alongside challenges related to mathematical inaccuracies, unrealistic time estimates, and the need for contextual adaptation. The TPD model facilitated growth in pedagogical content knowledge and AI literacy, fostering confidence and critical engagement with GenAI tools. These results underscore the potential of structured professional development to bridge the gap between emerging technologies and classroom practice. Future research should extend implementation duration, include student perspectives, and address ethical and equity considerations in AI integration.

The increasing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into work may impact burnout as GenAI uses reshape possibilities/constraints for fulfilling job-related needs. Using mixed methods and survey data from 382 full-time workers, this study examines the relationship between burnout and GenAI use frequency, as well as specific GenAI uses and individual factors, including work modality related to burnout dimensions (cynicism, inefficacy, emotional exhaustion). Quantitative results indicate that GenAI use frequency is significantly and negatively associated with overall burnout and, specifically, the inefficacy burnout sub-dimension. To better understand this relationship, we analyzed qualitative open-ended survey responses describing participants’ GenAI work uses. Participants reported five primary GenAI uses: communication, research, problem-solving, task assistance, and education. Of these, task assistance was negatively associated with the burnout inefficacy sub-dimension, while there was a marginally significant negative relationship with problem solving. Post hoc analyses revealed that onsite employees were more likely than hybrid or remote employees to use GenAI for task assistance, as were employees working longer hours. Additionally, onsite employees and younger workers were more likely to use GenAI for problem solving. These findings suggest that while using GenAI to support workflows may enhance workers’ sense of accomplishment and potentially mitigate burnout, GenAI use impacts can vary with individual sociodemographics and work environments. Theoretically, these findings provide nuance for the job demands and resources model (JD-R) by highlighting how different worker and job characteristics relate to GenAI uses, as well as how those uses act as a resource or demand and worker experiences of burnout. Methodologically, this study introduces a framework that can be used to develop measures to categorize workplace GenAI use. Practically, results can be used to encourage beneficial GenAI use, while pointing to necessary future research as GenAI continues to evolve in the workplace.

Genomic sequence data hold enduring, lifelong clinical value, yet the information systems that generate and store them were built for episodic care and transient results. As a result, most of a patient's genomic information never enters a computable, reusable form: results arrive in the electronic health record (EHR) as static reports focused on a single indication, structured variant data are rarely captured, and standards-based interfaces to retrieve genomic data for reinterpretation, decision support, or artificial intelligence (AI) remain inconsistently implemented across clinical systems. In April 2024, the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) convened informatics and genomics leaders to define a Clinical Data Ecosystem for Genomic Health and identify the standards, infrastructure, and policies required to realize it. Here we summarize the principal conclusions of that workshop: the longitudinal value of the germline genome, the primacy of standards-based application programming interfaces (APIs), the requirements for real-time clinical decision support (CDS) delivered in primary care, the central role of computable phenotypes, the growing dependence of AI on granular, computable genomic data, the promise and pitfalls of polygenic risk scores (PRS), the tradeoffs among centralized, decentralized, and federated data-sharing models, and the imperative to treat patients as sovereign stakeholders. Together, we argue for a federated, standards-first architecture: a system that keeps data local, preserves patient control over research use, and is validated across heterogeneous real-world health systems. This is the most credible path from workshop consensus to durable infrastructure making genomic data computable, portable, and continuously reinterpretable across the lifespan.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remains a major global health challenge, complicating infection management and increasing the risk of treatment failure. Although conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing guides treatment selection, delays in obtaining results can hinder timely targeted therapy. Advances in bacterial genomics, molecular diagnostics, and artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to improve resistance detection and support precision antimicrobial therapy. However, a persistent gap remains between identifying genomic resistance determinants, translating them into reliable diagnostic interpretations, and applying these findings to individual treatment decisions. This review critically synthesizes evidence on the genomic architecture of AMR, emerging diagnostic technologies, AI-assisted interpretation, and their integration into clinical practice. It examines major resistance mechanisms, including acquired resistance genes, chromosomal mutations, mobile genetic elements, and regulatory changes, alongside whole-genome sequencing, molecular detection, and phenotypic susceptibility testing. It further evaluates machine learning applications in resistance prediction and clinical decision support, highlighting limitations associated with genotype–phenotype discordance, dataset representativeness, model generalisability, diagnostic uncertainty, infrastructure, and clinical validation. Ethical governance, regulatory oversight, and equitable implementation are also considered. An integrative conceptual framework is proposed linking biological determinants, diagnostic evidence, computational interpretation, clinical decision-making, and patient outcomes. The framework emphasizes that genomic detection and AI predictions require contextual interpretation and clinical oversight. Ultimately, translating these innovations into effective precision antimicrobial therapy requires mechanistic understanding, robust validation, clinical integration, sustainable implementation, and demonstrated improvements in patient outcomes.

Agentic AI systems have evolved from experimental pilots into core operational infrastructure across financial services and other sectors. These systems autonomously plan, invoke tools, adapt in real time and coordinate multi-agent workflows that directly affect real-world outcomes. While the opportunities are substantial, material risks include erroneous autonomous actions, emergent multi-agent behaviors, loss of accountability and potential systemic instability. The global AI governance landscape has shifted from scarcity to abundance. The OECD AI Policy Observatory tracks more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives across more than 80 jurisdictions, alongside hundreds of standards, playbooks and technical guidance. This proliferation reflects commitment but has produced fragmentation and decision fatigue among boards, risk officers and regulators. This review organizes the landscape into three layers: Why (ethical foundations), What (regulatory obligations and standards) and How (operational playbooks and technical controls). It anchors them in the Stability-Assured Framework for Entities (SAFE). SAFE is presented as a proposed theoretical baseline and closed-loop engineering foundation applicable to any controller (human, rule-based, LLM-based or future architectures). It models controllers within shared feedback loops and evaluates them using five engineering metrics: Observability, Controllability, Stability, Robustness and Performance. These metrics support Loop Risk Profiles and Autonomy Levels 0–5. The resulting integrated reference map offers practical value for practitioners (implementation guidance and illustrative applications), regulators (supervisory language and measurable metrics) and other stakeholders seeking a coherent socio-technical view of agentic AI governance. Frameworks discussed were selected for regulatory significance, international influence, relevance to agentic AI, financial-sector applicability and practical utility; the mapping is representative rather than exhaustive.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Legends and fairytales often centre on caution: Māui used a careful plan to slow the Sun, while Little Red Riding Hood sensed something was wrong with her grandmother. Kia Tūpato is a traditional Māori expression meaning caution. Rooted in Polynesian culture, it has moved through two key phases: its adoption by Māori and its continued use after European settlement. It is now entering a third phase as a digital workplace tool. This oral presentation traces the history of Kia Tūpato, presents findings from two recent case studies, and explores its use in workplaces and its emerging role as a digital app. The case studies show how Kia Tūpato can help workers make safer decisions, connect more effectively with workplace systems, and engage with decision-makers. Grounded in culture and practical relevance for Māori and many blue-collar workers, Kia Tūpato gives human factors and ergonomics practitioners a clear example of how cultural predispositions can shape worker decisions and support safer behaviour.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Ushbu maqolada havodagi harakatni boshqarish (HHB) avtomatlashtirilgan tizimlarida parvozlar xavfsizligi va vaziyatdan xabardorlik (Situational Awareness) darajasini oshirish maqsadida ko‘p sensorli kuzatuv axborotlarini integratsiyalash (Multi-Sensor Data Fusion) algoritmlari tadqiq etilgan. Birlamchi (PSR) va ikkilamchi (SSR) radarlar, ko‘p pozitsiyali multilateratsiya tizimlari (MLAT) hamda avtomatik qaram kuzatuv (ADS-B Out) ma’lumotlarining xatolik kovariatsiyalari va vaqtinchalik uzilishlari qiyosiy tahlil qilingan. Havo kemalarining murakkab va kutilmagan dinamik manyovrlarini ishonchli kuzatish uchun Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) hamda Kengaytirilgan Kalman Filtri (EKF) sintezi asosidagi adaptiv integratsiya algoritmi ishlab chiqilgan. documents.abstract: Abstract The marine sector in Tanzania, particularly vessel operations between Da es Salaam and Zanzibar, has safety issues in spite of the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) and hazard analysis. Extended lapses in putting these precautions into practice result in acci- dents endangering lives, assets, and the industry’s standing. With an emphasis on the Da es Salaam– Zanzibar route, this study evaluated the application of PPE and hazard analysis in Tanzania’s maritime sector. The study used Human Factors Engineering to assess crew behavior to determine the main hazards associated with marine incidents caused by improper PPE use. Personal protec- tive equipment (PPE) use was affected by risk perceptions, demographics, barriers to use, comfort, training, environmental conditions, and the need for effective communication and training to ensure proper use during emergencies. The study found that workers were still exposed to poisons even though they were wearing PPE because the hazards were not being recognized. When PPE wasn’t worn, accidents happened in harsh circumstances like heat stress. This shows that the maritime industry’s safety rules aren’t always followed correctly when they focus too much on PPE and hazard analysis. There were also accidents because people chose the wrong PPE for high-risk scenarios. The conclusion is that marine safety requires an integrated strategy. While technological progress and legal requirements are crucial, the human aspect, especially PPE use, must not be overlooked. Using Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) efficiently helps prevent marine mishaps and improve the maritime industry’s long-term sustainability. This paper utilizes the data from the study which conducted at Dar es salaam- Zanzibar vessel to assess personal protective equipment contribution on reduction of maritime accidents in Tanzania a case of Dar es salaam-Zanzibar vessels

HeritageLens is an AI-powered Augmented Reality (AR) heritage guide designed to make exploring historical monuments more interactive and informative. Traditional methods of heritage exploration, such as information boards, printed materials and guided tours, often provide limited interaction and may not fully explain the historical importance of monuments. This paper presents HeritageLens, a system that combines Computer Vision-based monument recognition, historical information, AI-powered conversational assistance and location-based heritage discovery. It also explores features such as audio storytelling, multilingual explanations and AR-based visualisation to improve the overall learning experience. The application is designed to help tourists, students and heritage enthusiasts discover monuments, understand their historical significance and access information through a single platform. The paper discusses the system architecture, related research, development methodology, technologies used, evaluation framework and possible future improvements. The proposed system aims to make cultural heritage more accessible through the integration of Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision and Augmented Reality technologies.

Large language models (LLMs) can provide voters information about political issues, party positions, and even advise on which party to vote for. However, no previous study explores how well off-the-shelf LLMs function as voting advice applications (VAAs). In this article, we address this gap by examining how Gemini 3 Flash advises a sample of 6,022 German survey respondents on which party to vote for, based on their policy preferences and priorities alone. In brief, we find that for most respondents, following the LLM’s advice would benefit voter-party policy alignment (i.e. congruence), with a significantly stronger remedial effect among voters with low levels of political interest and formal education. However, our analysis also reveals concerning biases in the LLM’s recommendations. For instance, the LLM suggested voting for the AfD at ~1.5 times the frequency of a standard salience-weighted proximity model. In addition, the LLM hardly ever advised voting for either Die Linke or the BSW. We conclude that while LLMs can approximate the behaviour of VAAs, users should be aware that the LLM’s recommendations are still biased in ways that are extremely difficult to trace.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic carbon dioxide reduction (CO2RR) over metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) is governed by both framework features and reaction conditions, which complicate catalyst discovery and render general design rules difficult to establish. In this study, we develop a synergistic machine-learning workflow to integrate literature data extraction, electronic-property prediction, and hierarchical classification for prioritizing MOF photocatalysts. First, a literature-derived record-level data set containing catalyst compositions, structural descriptors, reaction conditions, and catalytic outcomes was curated through large language model (LLM)-assisted relation extraction followed by manual verification. Then, a transfer-learning crystal graph convolutional neural network (CGCNN) model was trained for band gap prediction at the Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof screened hybrid functional (HSE06) level, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.31 eV against reference HSE06 calculations. Subsequently, a physically constrained multitask framework was employed to predict electron affinity (EA) and ionization potential (IP) for thermodynamic prescreening. Three record-level classifiers were constructed for activity screening (C1), performance classification (C2), and product selectivity prediction (C3). When applied to the Computation-Ready, Experimental (CoRE) MOF database under standardized gas- and liquid-phase inference settings, the workflow prioritized 639 primary candidates, with most assigned to CO formation. Probability calibration and applicability-domain analysis further identified 166 of these candidates (25.98%) as a more stringent calibrated, in-domain subset. Overall, this study provides a practical data-driven workflow for condition-resolved prioritization of MOF photocatalysts and analysis of descriptor-level trends associated with photocatalytic CO2RR.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can transform teaching, learning, assessment and research in higher education. In Ecuador, the adoption of ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models is driving academic interest, yet little is known about the scientific production that addresses it. This systematic mapping review, reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, maps the scientific production on generative artificial intelligence that explicitly refers to Ecuador, indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2024 and 2026, in order to establish the weight that higher education holds within it. No disciplinary filter was applied to the query, so that this weight could be measured rather than assumed. The search, executed on 4 July 2026, retrieved 57 records (all 16 Web of Science records were also in Scopus, so the corpus comes in practice from Scopus; regional databases were not searched); after removing 16 duplicates and excluding 9 records, 32 documents were mapped with bibliometric indicators (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer), and the 18 higher education studies with primary data were subjected to a focused synthesis that included the appraisal of their methodological quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Higher education accounts for 20 of the 32 documents (63%); the other 12 are spread over political communication and journalism, legal and technical applications and four smaller domains. A sensitivity search with synonyms, Spanish terms and the year 2023, run on 15 October 2026, gave a similar share (44 of 73 documents, 60%). Within the higher education corpus, perceptions and acceptance of GAI are the most frequent outcome domain (16 of 18 studies); learning outcomes appear in six, but only two measure them directly. Eight studies use descriptive or cross-sectional designs, and none is randomised or longitudinal. ChatGPT is the most frequently examined tool (11 of 18). Sample representativeness and control of confounding were the most frequent methodological weaknesses. The findings highlight the need for experimental and longitudinal research evaluating the impact of GAI on Ecuadorian higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential approach to inferring standardized questionnaire responses from qualitative interviews, but their utility for assessing parenting remains unclear. We evaluated six generative LLMs using zero-shot prompting to infer responses to the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) from interviews with 43 parents. Models inferred responses to 35 MAPS items from two introductory questions about family, parenting roles, and the meaning of caregiving. Performance was evaluated through exact item-response agreement, correlations between inferred and self-reported parenting scores, systematic score differences, and internal consistency. Across models, Fisher-averaged correlations between inferred and self-reported MAPS subscale scores ranged from .320 to .434, with no consistently superior model. Correlations were strongest and most consistent for Warmth, whereas Physical Control showed little correspondence and substantial floor restriction. Across parent–item pairs, 35.5%–44.7% of inferred responses exactly matched parents’ selected response categories. All models assigned systematically lower response categories than parents and rarely selected the highest category; score underestimation was particularly evident for Positive Parenting. Model-derived subscales generally showed internal consistency, although higher internal consistency did not consistently correspond to stronger correlations with parent-reported scores. Exploratory analyses indicated modest similarity in the associations of inferred and self-reported parenting scores with other psychological constructs. Preliminary comparisons also suggested that shorter interview segments substantially reduced computational requirements without clear evidence of poorer performance. These findings support further evaluation of LLM-based parenting assessment while highlighting limitations in reproducing individual responses, matching score levels, and capturing some parenting dimensions.

Generative artificial intelligence is emerging as a new gateway for users to access news. Using the Perplexity platform as the research subject, this study draws on full-sample data from its news gateways across 15 countries and regions between January and February 2026 to examine how generative AI news gateways perform news gatekeeping across the three dimensions of sources, issues, and national context. The findings reveal that Perplexity's news sources are highly concentrated among a small number of global general-interest news organizations, reflecting the continued dependence of news practices on institutional authority. The source structure varies by topic type. Geopolitical issues rely heavily on general news sources, while technology issues incorporate more specialized sources, closely mirroring the institutional patterns that have long shaped the relationship between topics and sources in traditional news production. News gateways across countries draw on a shared core of news organizations, while source weights and the relationship between topic and source composition vary across countries. Generative gatekeeping, jointly driven by technology and platforms, is thus becoming deeply embedded in existing institutions of news production and the global landscape of international news flows.
topics: News Media Framing and Political Communication

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence can support project planning and control, but access to analytical tools offers limited explanation of how project teams obtain value from them. This conceptual paper examines how innovative leadership may support human–AI synergy and the development of capabilities through which AI contributes to project performance. The argument brings together socio-technical scholarship, the resource-based view, the theory of capabilities for organizational adaptation, and upper echelons theory. It distinguishes the quality of human–AI coordination from the repeatable organizational ability to apply AI in project work. Four propositions connect leadership with synergy and capability development, synergy with capability development, and capabilities with multidimensional performance. The framework includes a direct leadership–capability relationship alongside the proposed sequential pathway. It suggests that the contribution of AI depends on how project teams allocate tasks, interpret recommendations and retain responsibility for decisions. These relationships remain theoretical and have not been tested in this paper. The discussion identifies conditions that may weaken the proposed relationships, including poor data, unsuitable task allocation and excessive reliance on automated recommendations. It also explains how future studies could distinguish perceived collaboration from demonstrated performance gains. The paper offers a basis for studying leadership and AI use at project level, with attention to the differences between delivery efficiency, stakeholder outcomes and strategic value.

Purpose: The study aims to analyse and compare efficiency-oriented and sustainability-oriented governance approaches. It further examines the role of human-centred leadership in organisations in fostering sustainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study draws on findings from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) report and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) principles to conceptually analyse the gaps between efficiency-oriented and sustainability-oriented AI governance. It also examines how human-centred leadership can bridge these gaps to strengthen sustainable decision-making in organisations. Findings: AI adoption is increasing among organisations in line with OECD principles, but governance arrangements are inadequate for sustainable AI governance, that is, balancing innovation with accountability and responsibility. Original/Value of the Paper: The study proposes a Leadership-Mediated Sustainable AI Governance Transformation Framework to provide a more analytically grounded understanding of sustainable AI governance systems. Practical Implications: The study highlights the need for organisations to strengthen leadership capabilities, governance resilience, accountability integration, and sustainability-oriented oversight alongside AI expansion. R. (2027): Human-AI collaborative leadership: balancing artificial intelligence and human judgement for sustainable decision-making. World Journal of Science, Technology and Sustainable Development (WJSTSD), Vol. 22, No. 1, pp. 19-34.

documents.abstract: The modern education has radically changed with the development of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, analytics, and online learning platforms. Although the technologies are supposed to be more efficient and offer more people an access to education, there is also a significant ethical issue in terms of human dignity, equality, inclusivity, and moral development. This is an emerging and common need of any technical institutions of higher learning to treat technology in a more humane manner as opposed to being artificially or immorally inclined. This paper is founded on Ignatian Pedagogy, especially its core pillars of context, experience, reflection, action and evaluation, and is supported by general Jesuit teachings of cura personalis, social justice, discernment, and service of faith, which produce love, peace and justice. Human-centered design methods would focus more on empathy, responsibility, and well-being to supplement this. This study examines how Jesuit principles and Ignatian Pedagogy can transform the design, implementation and assessment of learning technologies with the consideration of human-formative goal. This paper examines human centric technology as a shaping power that drives experiential learning instead of considering technology as a neutral tool. The paper also compares how human centered technology using Jesuit principles would bring about discernment, a further clarification of contexts, and support holistic human development instead of concentrating on efficiency. This paper is a synthesis using a conceptual and interpretive approach, combining the most important literature in Jesuit education, technology ethics, and Ignatian Pedagogy using examples provided in Jesuit Educational Institute. The paper concludes that Jesuit institutions are in a unique position to be the first to set an example on how technology can be applied in a more human and an Ignatian approach in this new era of learning. The implication of applying Ignatian Pedagogy to technology decision making to the curriculum design, professional development, and institutional governance has great meaning. The paper finally argues that human-focused technology when informed with Ignatian Pedagogy Paradigm and Jesuit values may be one of the most transformative educational practices of teaching, which promotes human dignity, seeks social justice, and encourages more deeply socio-engaged learning.

Introduction This study explores media narratives of violence in Mexico through a hybrid human-computer interaction workflow combining computational analysis, human interpretation and generative artificial intelligence. Methods A non-probability corpus of 105 news items was analyzed to identify recurring terms, actors, locations and semantic relationships. Corpus summaries informed a workshop with 15 participants, who developed definitions and recursively refined text prompts and AI-generated images across five iterations. Textual and visual changes were analyzed, and experts supported their synthesis into an infographic and video. Results The selected corpus and workshop materials showed variation in textual and visual representations. Computational summaries made selected semantic differences explicit, while participants and experts supplied contextual interpretation. The process produced an infographic and video integrating these materials. Discussion The exploratory design does not estimate population parameters or establish causal effects. The workflow illustrates a human-led collaborative approach informed by mixed-initiative design: computational methods support structured comparison and generative variation, while people provide interpretation and critical judgment.

Available-to-promise (ATP) systems increasingly rely on machine learning to predict delivery dates under conditions of fluctuating supply, capacity constraints, and demand variability. Yet purely algorithmic ATP pipelines face a persistent adoption barrier: planners and account teams frequently override or distrust automated delivery-date predictions, particularly after observing even isolated forecasting errors, a pattern long documented in the algorithm-aversion literature. Conversely, human-only override regimes reintroduce the inconsistency and latency that automation was meant to eliminate. This paper proposes a human-in-the-loop (HITL) available-to-promise intelligence framework that resolves this tension by design rather than by policy. Following a design science research approach, the framework separates delivery-date prediction into four architectural layers: an algorithmic prediction layer, a confidence and uncertainty estimation layer, a human-review trigger layer governed by explicit escalation criteria, and an override/feedback-capture layer that closes the loop back into model governance. The trigger layer operationalises when a prediction should reach a human reviewer, using confidence thresholds, anomalous order-pattern detection, and value/risk tiering rather than blanket human review or blanket automation. The paper situates this design against literature on algorithm aversion and appreciation, human-in-the-loop machine learning architectures, and explainability in supply-chain artificial intelligence and evaluates the framework's utility against design science research criteria rather than primary empirical validation. The paper closes with an explicit limitations discussion and a concrete agenda for the multi-case empirical validation the framework's real-world deployment would require.

documents.abstract: Human–AI Charter Public Consultation: 14 Key Questions on Governability, Risk Control and Room to Develop This discussion paper invites public comment on the Human–AI Charter (Public Consultation Draft). Its central idea is to govern how AI capabilities are translated into real-world power, not intelligence itself. AI may learn, reason and research freely; but when it gains the ability to move money, operate equipment, touch infrastructure or decide on someone's behalf, that power must have a lawful source and clear limits, and stay provable, reviewable and open to remedy. The paper sets out 14 open questions in four groups: governability (G1–G4), risk control (R1–R4), room to develop (D1–D3), and legitimacy and the future (L1–L3). It also includes two candidate new clauses for consultation, not yet part of the charter text: (A) responsibility registers for high-risk AI, and (B) an independent public forum for users as a "fourth estate" of AI governance. This consultation remains open, with no closing date. Please send comments, quoting the question number (e.g. G2, R3), to humanaicharter@gmail.com. documents.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment and feedback in higher education has attracted growing interest, but concerns remain about the consistency and appropriateness of AI-generated grades in summative contexts. This study examined whether a combined calibration strategy involving a more explicit rubric and marking prompt could improve agreement between AI-assisted grading and educator judgement in a laboratory-based STEM assessment. We compared educator-assigned marks for 40 graduate Electrochemical Energy Storage Systems laboratory reports with marks generated by GPT-5 under pre- and post-calibration configurations, and examined agreement using complementary statistical and visual analyses. Following calibration, agreement with educator marks improved across measures of score correspondence and absolute agreement: the intraclass correlation coefficient increased from 0.818 to 0.928, the mean AI-educator difference decreased from +1.625 to +1.041 marks, and no post-calibration report differed from the educator mark by more than 10 marks. These findings suggest that the way assessment criteria, evidence requirements, and marking rules are specified can materially influence AI-human grading agreement. However, the revised rubric and prompt were introduced together, calibration drew on discrepancies observed in the same 40 reports used for post-calibration evaluation, and one educator's marks served as the reference. The results therefore support improved in-sample agreement under a human-supervised calibration strategy, rather than establishing grading validity or interchangeability for autonomous summative decisions.

Clinical studies regularly ask participants to describe their experiences in their own words. These open-ended questions are included so that participants can report what they themselves consider relevant, and ideally researchers want to harvest this information. In practice however, these responses are rarely analyzed and often effectively discarded, since translating them into a useful quantitative format for further analysis traditionally required trained coders or advanced technical skills. Current transformer-based language models offer an appealing alternative option to quantify text: they internally represent any text input as high-dimensional numerical representations called text embeddings. Fromavailable open-weight models, these text embeddings can be freely extracted on a local machine. As text embeddings are just vectors of numbers, they can be plugged as predictors into standard statistical analyses. Here, we applied this to three large datasets in which participants described their experiences in the context of psychedelic substance use. We investigated whether text embeddings of these free-text descriptions improve cross-validated, held-out predictions of clinically relevant outcomes (well-being, change in well-being, change in psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity, post-traumatic growth) after we control for a range of other predictors capturingdemographic information, the setting of the experience, and a series of questionnaire data. We found reliable increases in predictive accuracy for three of the five outcomes (change in well-being and psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity), in two of the three datasets. Some of these increases are substantial. We therefore recommend (where possible) the inclusion of open-ended questions in any questionnaire, and to actually pass this information to analysis, to efficiently capture valuable information that would otherwise be lost.

DESCRIPTION This collection brings together fifteen independently authored research essays and analytical works examining artificial intelligence, social structures, political authority, economic inequality, cybersecurity, digital identity, institutional accountability, and the changing relationship between individuals and complex technological systems. Originally published as individual works through Substack, these essays approach contemporary technological and social transformations from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Some investigate technical and epistemic limitations in AI systems, cybersecurity, information infrastructure, and digital continuity. Others examine political polarization, religious authority, generational inheritance, labor-market exclusion, economic stratification, institutional recognition, and the distribution of power. Several works also explore questions concerning the reconstruction of personal identity through informational systems, the relationship between memory and continuity, and the consequences of transferring human judgment or authority into increasingly autonomous technological environments. The collection does not advance a single unified theory or claim that all included works share the same methodology. Instead, it documents an evolving independent research program organized around several recurring questions: What happens when the systems used to observe reality become incapable of representing the conditions that actually exist? How do institutions, political structures, and economic arrangements determine who receives opportunities, recognition, and the benefits of collective contribution? How are memory, identity, authority, and inherited social structures transformed when technological systems begin to mediate increasingly fundamental aspects of human life? Why do institutions repeatedly struggle to address structural vulnerabilities even when their underlying causes are already identifiable? And what forms of accountability, institutional adaptation, and technical architecture are necessary when existing systems can no longer reliably manage the complexity they have created? The works included here range from technical proposals and systems analysis to political and socioeconomic commentary, conceptual frameworks, and exploratory scenarios. Their evidentiary foundations and analytical methods therefore vary according to their respective subjects. Together, they examine a recurring structural problem: the growing distance between what complex systems represent, what institutions reward, what individuals experience, and what society is actually capable of verifying. This collection should be understood as an archival record of independent research and analysis rather than a unified theoretical framework. documents.abstract: AI agents driven by foundation models have shown potential for industrial automation beyond rule-based control. However, existing studies differ in how industrial agents collaborate and how their systems are tested, making it difficult to compare networking requirements and physical execution capabilities. This paper examines the intersection of networked agents and industrial automation, where industrial signals, communication constraints, contextual information, and operational requirements must be considered jointly. It develops the Industrial Internet of Agents (IIoA) and presents a conceptual architecture for analyzing industrial deployment requirements. Building on the Internet of Agents (IoA) framework, IIoA re-specifies sensing, communication, decision-making, and execution through eleven industrial extensions. Representative studies are synthesized across shopfloor operations, autonomous plant operations and maintenance, supply chain collaboration, and digital twin systems. The analysis indicates that industrial agent networking requires the joint design of semantic coordination, operational technology (OT) interoperability, latency-aware deployment, trust governance, and verifiable physical execution. Finally, seven open challenges are identified, covering reliability, latency, protocol integrity, scalability, physical grounding, adaptability, and evaluation.

This conceptual paper introduces Inferential Disclosure Through Joined Fragments, a mechanism by which separately disclosed pieces of information become available to one reader, who can connect them to infer a relationship that no piece established alone. The paper asks how strongly the evidence supports the connection and whether the purposes for which the fragments were disclosed permit their combined use. A reader may have strong grounds for an identification while permission to make that use of the records remains unsettled. The first case concerns the Japanese designator “AF” before the Battle of Midway. By March 1942, analysts at Corregidor had identified AF as Midway, while disagreement persisted in Washington. In May, Midway sent an uncoded message reporting a shortage of fresh water. A subsequent Japanese report attributed a water shortage to AF. The shared detail connected the two messages and corroborated the earlier identification. The second case concerns AOL’s 2006 release of search queries grouped under user numbers. One number brought together searches mentioning a town, a surname, and a housing subdivision. Reporters followed those clues to Thelma Arnold, who recognized the searches as her own. She explained that she had researched some symptoms for friends. The evidence supported identifying who had conducted the searches while leaving open whom any particular search described. The paper places this case alongside Latanya Sweeney’s work on re-identification through linked records. Part of the Sources and Evidentiary Limits series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a distinction relevant to human–AI interaction. A draft exhibition program might list a title and booking code, while a venue’s schedule lists the same code and a room. An AI assistant could infer where the exhibition is planned. Whether the organizers authorized combining those records for a public announcement is a separate question.

Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

Mental health conditions represent a major global public health challenge, contributing substantially to disability, reduced quality of life, social exclusion, and economic burden. Despite advances in psychological and pharmacological treatments, access to timely, affordable, and appropriate mental health care remains unequal across and within countries. Innovations in digital technologies, artificial intelligence, telepsychiatry, mobile health applications, wearable devices, virtual reality, and personalized interventions are creating new opportunities to address longstanding gaps in mental health services. These developments may support early identification of psychological difficulties, improve continuity of care, expand access to evidence-based interventions, and strengthen clinical decision-making. However, technological innovation also introduces challenges involving privacy, data security, algorithmic bias, clinical reliability, professional accountability, and the risk of widening existing inequalities. This narrative review examines major innovations transforming mental health care, considers their potential applications across prevention, assessment, treatment, and recovery, and explores the organizational and ethical conditions required for responsible implementation. It argues that innovation should not be understood simply as the introduction of new technologies, but as the development of accessible, effective, equitable, and person-centered systems of care. The future of mental health services will depend on integrating technological capabilities with professional expertise, therapeutic relationships, community participation, and evidence-informed policy.
topics: Psychiatric care and mental health services

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Inquiry-Induced Depletion of Later Examination Capacity, an account of how one inquiry can consume a resource that a later inquiry also needs. The resource may be material, time, attention, or cooperation. A check can answer its immediate question accurately and still leave a later question harder to examine. The cost depends on what that later question requires and how much of the resource remains available to answer it. The paper sets out three requirements for identifying depletion. An assessment must name the shared resource, establish what the earlier inquiry consumed, and identify a later question whose examination depended on what was lost. This requires comparing what was available before and after the inquiry and considering other causes of the loss. A record may preserve enough evidence for a particular later question, attention may recover, and learning from the first inquiry may offset some of its cost. The paper places the mechanism alongside the 1992 Valletta Convention’s provision for archaeological reserves and examines two documented cases. Near Xi’an, excavation exposed the painted terracotta figures of the First Emperor of Qin. Once exposed, the lacquer beneath the pigment could flake away within minutes, taking with it evidence of the figures’ original colors. Apollo 17 sample 73001 illustrates preservation. NASA kept the lunar sample sealed for nearly 50 years. In 2022, researchers used X-ray computed tomography to record the core’s internal arrangement before removing and dividing it for study. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can sequence or stop an examination and who bears the cost when a shared resource runs low. A potential application in human–AI evaluation is the allocation of reviewer time. If an AI assistant requests several routine checks before a deadline, an evaluator could trace how much time those checks consumed and whether the reviewer still had enough time to examine a disputed source on which the final judgment depended.

Modern sociotechnical systems—spanning sovereign signals intelligence, hyperscale semiconductor supply chains, connected automotive infrastructure, and frontier artificial intelligence laboratories—exhibit a recurring divergence between physical system state (C) and institutional representation (I). When architectural shortcuts, default-open perimeters, or circular capital commitments generate structural failures, governing bodies rarely initiate immediate remediation. Instead, they execute a standardized crisis-containment protocol termed The Ba Sing Se Doctrine: an active administrative posture that suppresses internal error signals until an external leak forces public visibility, at which point the institution issues formal decrees reclassifying systemic breaches as routine maintenance, isolated personal errors, or resolved minor friction. Tracing this mechanism from classical imperial theater at the Hellespont and the English Channel to four concurrent November 2026 infrastructure and technology crises, this paper formalizes the structural anatomy of zero-admission governance and demonstrates why narrative equilibrium accelerates physical collapse.

Safety culture, psychosocial safety, work design and worker well-being are increasingly considered together, although they describe different organisational conditions, processes and outcomes. We conducted a safety-culture-anchored conceptual review informed by structured bibliographic searching and purposive source selection to examine these boundaries. Searches of Scopus and Web of Science on 29 June 2026 identified 3129 records. A dated duplicate audit reconciled 2500 report records; 28 verified complete texts from a 44-source conceptual set supported detailed synthesis. Recurrent organisational practices concerned management commitment, enacted priorities, resources, communication, participation, justice and feedback for improvement. Their recurrence did not establish a single higher-order construct. The synthesis compares referents, levels, mechanisms, measurement and outcomes across safety, psychosocial-health and well-being approaches. It provides explicit rules for connecting these entities without treating their measures or outcomes as interchangeable. Three conditional propositions specify future tests of construct discrimination, cross-domain pathways and diagnostic usefulness. Purposive selection, incomplete records of later selection decisions, unequal coverage of adjacent fields and the absence of documented independent duplicate screening limit coverage and reproducibility. The proposed framework is a conceptual interpretation, not a validated causal model.

This study aims to analyze the extent to which current Brazilian labor legislation is sufficient to protect workers subject to algorithmic management through artificial intelligence systems. It seeks to understand the impact of these technologies on labor relations, particularly regarding legal subordination, control mechanisms, and the risks arising from their use. To this end, qualitative bibliographic and documentary research was conducted through the analysis of legislation, legal scholarship, scientific articles, institutional documents, and case law related to artificial intelligence and worker protection. The results demonstrate that Brazilian legislation provides legal instruments capable of protecting workers against algorithmic management, particularly Articles 2, 3, and 6, sole paragraph, of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), as well as provisions concerning non-pecuniary damages and civil liability. The study also found that algorithmic subordination may constitute legal subordination, since computerized systems can perform command, control, and supervision functions. However, challenges were identified regarding the effectiveness of legal protection, judicial interpretation, and liability for damages arising from these technologies. It is concluded that the Brazilian legal system provides an adaptable normative framework for worker protection, but its effectiveness depends on the proper application of existing legal provisions, the development of case law, and the ability to address the challenges posed by technological advancement.

Introduction. Artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for personalized learning in basic education through tools capable of adapting content, providing feedback, and addressing diverse educational needs. The objective of this study was to analyze artificial intelligence applications in personalized learning, identifying pedagogical opportunities, implementation challenges, and research trends. Methodology. A scoping review was developed following the methodological guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute and the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The bibliographic selection exercise covered publications from 2020 to 2026, considering Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and SciELO. Results. The methodological flow included 420 identified records, 90 duplicates removed, and 330 records screened. Following the screening and eligibility stages, a set of 25 studies was established for thematic synthesis. The results were organized into five categories: adaptive systems and intelligent tutoring, generative artificial intelligence, AI literacy and teacher mediation, equity and ethics, and implementation and evaluation. The literature examined revealed opportunities related to content adaptation, individualized support, immediate feedback, and academic progress monitoring. Challenges associated with data protection, algorithmic bias, digital inequalities, and teacher preparation were also identified. Conclusions. It is concluded that artificial intelligence offers relevant possibilities for diversifying learning experiences, although its educational integration requires pedagogical supervision, ethical criteria, and contextualized evaluations to establish its actual contributions.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Disease-outbreak information is spread across surveillance reports, environmental observations and population statistics,and public-health users need it presented in a form they can inspectand question. This paper presents the design and implementationof an SDG 3 health platform that combines a multi-factor outbreak risk-scoring module, a what-if climate-variation analysis, acollaborative multi-agent chatbot, a locally hosted Mistral 7B Instruct model accessed through LM Studio, a retrieval-groundedknowledge module, and a heuristic hallucination detector for usersubmitted outbreak reports. The risk module combines new cases,rainfall, humidity, temperature, population density and hospitaladmissions into a weighted score from 0 to 100, classifies it as Low,Medium or High, and derives four-week and three-month projections. A React front end communicates with a FastAPI back endthat provides JWT authentication, role-based access, an administrator review workflow with audit events, and report generation. Thelanguage model communicates information only; it does not compute risk scores. The platform does not forecast case counts witha time-series model. A Random Forest classifier for risk-categoryclassification (Low, Medium, High) was evaluated on a balancedtest set of 90 samples and reached 88.89% accuracy and a macroF1-score of 88.89%. The worked examples of the scoring rules arenot accuracy measurements, and learned time-series forecasting,such as LSTM, is identified as future work.Keywords—Disease outbreak risk assessment, generative AI, multiagent systems, Mistral, LM Studio, retrieval-augmented generation,hallucination detection, public health, SDG 3.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has emerged as a new source of academic support for university students. However, students' willingness to seek academic help may also be influenced by social evaluation concerns surrounding traditional interpersonal help-seeking. This study examines how academic help-seeking (AHS) stigma relates to interpersonal help-seeking avoidance through academic shame, and whether interpersonal avoidance is associated with GAI help-seeking tendency under different levels of perceived anonymity. Methods Two independent cross-sectional survey studies were conducted among Chinese university students. Study 1 examined the relationships among AHS stigma, academic shame, and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance using data from 183 undergraduate students. Study 2 extended the model with a sample of 401 university students by examining the relationship between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency, as well as the moderating role of perceived anonymity. PLS-SEM was used to test the proposed relationships. Results Across both studies, AHS stigma was positively associated with interpersonal help-seeking avoidance. Academic shame showed significant indirect associations between AHS stigma and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance in both studies. Study 2 further showed that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance was positively associated with GAI help-seeking tendency. Moreover, perceived anonymity positively moderated this relationship, such that the positive association between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency was stronger at higher levels of perceived anonymity. Discussion The findings highlight the social-emotional dimensions of academic help-seeking, showing that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance can coexist with a greater willingness to seek support from GAI tools. Perceived anonymity further conditions this association, suggesting that the perceived social visibility of help-seeking is relevant to students' support preferences. These findings extend the understanding of GAI-assisted academic help-seeking beyond technology-related considerations, while distinguishing help-seeking tendencies from actual changes in support-source use.

The expression of emotions in sculptures is conveyed through structural forms, spatial relationships, material characteristics, and symbolic elements. However, traditional artistic analysis mainly relies on expert interpretation, making emotional expression difficult to quantify. With the development of computer vision and multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI), deep learning approaches provide new opportunities for visual art understanding. Nevertheless, existing methods still face challenges in establishing connections between visual features and abstract emotional semantics, as well as providing interpretable prediction processes. To address these issues, an interpretive model of emotional expression in sculptures based on visual-affective semantic analysis is proposed. A public sculpture image dataset containing 1,800 instances is constructed. A 50-layer Residual Network (ResNet50) is employed to extract morphological and textural features, while Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) is used to establish associations between visual representations and affective semantics. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates visual and semantic features for emotion classification. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and semantic ablation methods are further applied to analyze the decision-making process of the model. Experimental results show that the visual-semantic fusion model achieves an accuracy of 82.59% and a Macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 80.73% on the test set, outperforming the ResNet50 visual model with 76.30% accuracy and 75.67% Macro-F1, as well as the CLIP semantic model with 73.85% accuracy and 72.58% Macro-F1. Interpretation analysis demonstrates that the model mainly focuses on essential artistic elements, including posture, contour, and spatial structure, with strong consistency with expert evaluations. This research provides an effective artificial intelligence framework for sculptural emotion analysis and offers potential applications in digital museums, art education, intelligent retrieval systems, and computational cultural heritage studies.

This conceptual paper introduces Irreducible-Realization Classification Protecting a Settled Model, a mechanism through which calling a surprising result ordinary variation can keep a model or one of its assumptions from being reopened. The mechanism applies when the classification itself prevents diagnostic inquiry and the model’s account of uncertainty gives inadequate grounds for that decision. The paper asks what the model projected, what range or probability distribution supported that projection, and how the observed departure compared with it. A well-supported account of uncertainty can justify leaving a model in place after a surprising result. Possibility alone gives little guidance about whether a departure of this size warrants investigation. Identifying the mechanism also requires evidence that the classification actually stopped inquiry. A public description of a result as bad luck can coexist with an investigation already underway. The paper places the mechanism alongside Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s account of highly improbable events and examines two documented cases. Casino consultant Eliot Jacobson recalled initially attributing a report about the Lucky Lucky blackjack side bet to ordinary variation. Further reports prompted an analysis showing that players could gain an advantage by choosing when to bet. The published accounts provide no casino results from which to estimate the probability of the initial report. The 2011 OPERA neutrino measurement illustrates a different response. The apparent early arrival was large relative to the stated timing uncertainties, and the collaboration invited scrutiny. Subsequent investigation traced the anomaly to a fault in the fiber-optic timing system. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can inspect the uncertainty estimate behind a decision to close an inquiry. A potential application in human–AI evaluation is a transit planner’s review of an unexpectedly long wait. If the planner closes the review because an AI forecast allows occasional delays, an evaluator could ask how often the forecast predicted waits that long under comparable conditions and what evidence supported that estimate.
