documents.abstract: Backgrounds: Islamic financial planning can connect household resilience, ethical investment and social redistribution within a coherent life-cycle framework. Objectives: This article updates the supplied manuscript by integrating comparative documentary evidence from Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Indonesia, Türkiye and Pakistan with a proposed digitally enabled operational model. Methodology: A structured narrative review distinguishes observed institutional developments from normative design choices and untested impact propositions. Findings: The model retains four interdependent pillars: wealth protection, accumulation, preservation and distribution. It adds explicit cash flow management, affordable access, consumer protection and measurable wellbeing outcomes. Contemporary official evidence demonstrates the scale of Islamic finance and the feasibility of retail sukuk, social takaful, value-based intermediation and cash waqf-linked sukuk, but does not establish that a comprehensive planning service has caused improvements in household welfare. Blockchain, artificial intelligence, machine learning, the Internet of Things and big data can support traceability, forecasting and monitoring when governed by consent, legal enforceability, Shariah review and human accountability. The article proposes a mind map, implementation sequence and evaluation design. Conclusions: Universal access is a central service principle; religion-specific obligations and legally restricted funds require separate treatment. The resulting framework offers testable pathways toward financial resilience and sustainable development without assuming guaranteed returns or uniform effects.

Agricultural activities depend on the timely coordi-nation of land, labour, machinery, information, and local services. In many rural settings, farmers identify workers and equipment through personal contacts and fragmented communication chan-nels. Such methods can make it difficult to discover available service providers beyond an immediate network, communicate work requirements consistently, and maintain a clear record of requests. Agricultural labourers and machinery owners can face a corresponding difficulty in communicating their availability to potential customers. This paper presents Kisan Sahayak, a theoretical, mobile-first agricultural marketplace designed to connect farmers, labourers, and machinery providers through a common web platform. The proposed system is organized around the MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js (MERN) stack. Its conceptual capabilities include role-based profiles, location-aware discovery, farmer job postings, direct worker invitations, request acceptance or rejec-tion, wage negotiation, machinery listings, and service-request tracking. An optional artificial-intelligence assistance layer is proposed for multilingual platform guidance and explainable matching based on location, skills, availability, and stated pref-erences. The paper details the system architecture, data model, stake-holder workflows, marketplace rules, AI design, security and privacy controls, deployment considerations, and an evaluation framework. The contribution is an architectural and process model; no field trial, measured performance result, or im-plemented AI capability is claimed. The design is intended to provide a foundation for subsequent implementation and empirical evaluation in agricultural communities

topics: Renewable energy and sustainable power systems

documents.abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education compels us to look beyond faculty members’ technological skills: it demands that we rethink the criteria that guide their professional judgment. With this in mind, this article builds a theoretical bridge between continuing education, pedagogical mediation, intellectual autonomy, and quality management, using Venezuelan universities as a case study. Through a critical review of academic literature, regulations, and international frameworks, the study identifies four interdependent pillars: professional identity linked to lifelong learning; pedagogical mediation under strict human supervision; ethical responsibility toward the sociocultural environment; and the institutional conditions necessary to sustain this innovation. Building on this, the study proposes integrating the dimensions of Being, Doing, Owing to Be, and Wanting to Be as a reflective compass for educators. In essence, it argues that educational quality does not improve through mere automation; rather, it requires pedagogical decisions to guide it, an awareness of its limits, and equitable access. Therefore, training teachers in AI requires a deeply humanistic and critical approach, supported by institutional policies that ensure responsible development and evaluation.

Purpose Assessment is crucial in health professional education (HPE) but is resource-intensive to create. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution by generating assessment items; however, a comprehensive synthesis of their psychometric quality is lacking in HPE. Design/methodology/approach We systematically searched the electronic databases and included studies generating assessment items using any LLM and reporting psychometric outcomes. The primary outcomes were item difficulty index, discrimination index, distractor effectiveness and risk of nonfunctioning distractors (NFDs). Pooled estimates (Hedges' g or odds ratios [OR] with 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) were calculated using a random-effects model. Surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) for ranking the test item generating methods was estimated. Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach was used for determining the strength of evidence. Findings Fifty-four studies were included. In direct comparisons with human-generated items (92.8% of studies in HPE), LLM-generated items had a significantly higher difficulty index (pooled g: 0.40, 95% CI: 0.23 to 0.57), indicating they were easier and had significantly higher odds of containing NFDs (OR: 1.86, 95% CI: 1.27 to 2.73). The discrimination index was not significantly different (g: –0.21, 95% CI: –0.49 to 0.07), but distractor effectiveness was poorer (g: –0.65, 95% CI: –1.31 to 0). When evaluated alone, 67% of LLM-items were accurate or required only minor revisions, but 37% of distractors were NFDs. SUCRA analyses consistently ranked human-generated items as superior across all critical psychometric parameters. Evidence certainty ranged between very low and moderate. Originality/value LLMs can generate assessment items efficiently, but their current output is psychometrically inferior to human-authored items, being significantly easier and containing more flawed distractors. While a substantial proportion of items are useable with minor edits, sophisticated prompt engineering and expert-led review are essential to ensure the creation of valid and reliable assessments for HPE.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how speculative design, grounded in Latinx speculative traditions, can serve as a pedagogical framework for reimagining technological futures with and for Latinx communities. The argument unfolds through a case study of a workshop with 11 librarians serving a predominantly Latinx community in Southern California. Using restorying as a methodological approach, participants questioned dominant stereotypes that position Latinx people as disinterested or underrepresented in technology. Through engagements with generative artificial intelligence and analog collage, librarians produced two kinds of speculative work. The first involved cyborg imaginaries that fused Mexican American and Indigenous identities with technological augmentation. The second envisioned social infrastructures connecting ecological sustainability to cultural heritage and the well-being of their communities. This chapter contributes a culturally grounded approach to design education that bridges arts and sciences while affirming the cultural wealth of Latinx communities. Readers gain practical insight into how speculative workshops can be structured around restorying, alongside a theoretical framing that positions Latinx communities as creators of justice-oriented technological futures.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across key societal sectors presents profound legal challenges, particularly regarding liability attribution and legal certainty. Operating autonomously with non-deterministic decision-making capabilities, AI deployment gives rise to risks such as copyright infringement, privacy breaches, and misinformation. Employing a normative juridical research method, this article examines whether AI can be held legally accountable under Indonesian law and evaluates the current statutory framework’s capacity to maintain legal certainty. The analysis demonstrates that Indonesian jurisprudence does not recognize AI as an independent legal subject, as it lacks moral agency and free choice. Consequently, legal responsibility remains anchored in traditional legal subjects—natural persons and corporate entities—operating in the capacity of Electronic Agents or Electronic System Providers (ESPs). Legal liability for AI-induced harm is channeled back to human developers and operating entities through established doctrines of vicarious and strict liability. Furthermore, while Indonesia currently lacks a standalone AI statute, legal certainty is preserved through an interlocking, multi-layered regulatory regime, including the Copyright Law, the Personal Data Protection Law, the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, the new Penal Code, the Government Regulation on Operation of Electronic Systems and Transactions, and the Circular Letter of the Minister of Communication and Information Technology on Artificial Intelligence Ethics. This study concludes that existing statutory frameworks provide enforceable sanctions, emphasizing that legal subjects must maintain strict compliance to mitigate technology-induced harm.

This conceptual paper introduces Layout-Dependent Geometry of Relational Maps, a structural constraint on what a viewer can infer from a diagram of connections. Two drawings can preserve the same station order and interchanges while giving the routes different lengths, placing stations at different distances, or making different groups stand out. A diagram may therefore give a passenger reliable grounds for choosing where to change trains while giving little indication of how far apart those stations lie above ground. The paper assesses a claim drawn from a map by asking whether the coding and layout preserve the particular relation the claim concerns. Redrawing a fixed set of connections can reveal which features change with placement. Even a cluster that persists across several drawings requires an independent check of what the positions encode. A claim about how viewers interpreted the cluster requires evidence about the viewers as well. The paper places this constraint alongside Jacques Bertin’s account of visual variables in graphics and examines two transit diagrams. Harry Beck’s 1933 London Underground diagram preserved station order and interchanges while redrawing distances. In a later study using London trip data from 1998 to 2005, Zhan Guo found that passengers were more likely to choose routes that appeared shorter on the map. The 1972 New York subway diagram, produced by Massimo Vignelli’s team at Unimark with Joan Charysyn as lead designer, drew Central Park as a square. The paper examines one rider’s complaint about wayfinding, John Tauranac’s criticism of the diagram’s geography, and its replacement in 1979. Part of the Equivalence and Interchangeability series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a prospective application in human–AI interaction. An AI assistant might draw a citation network from a set of papers. Readers can check a line between two papers against their references. If the assistant also claims that papers placed close together make similar arguments, that claim requires evidence from their texts or a placement rule that explicitly encodes such similarity.

Learning scientific concepts through video lectures can be effective when visual and verbal information are presented simultaneously. The present study investigated the interaction effects of cue type (no organizational cues with timeline (NOT) vs. organizational cues with timeline (OT)) and prior knowledge (low vs. high) on learners’ attention allocation, learning performance, intrinsic motivation (i.e. interest, competence, value, and effort), and metacognition (i.e. monitoring accuracy and learning behaviors). Results indicated significant interaction effects on learning performance and monitoring accuracy. A moderated mediation analysis further revealed that OT was associated with better learning performance through more accurate monitoring among learners with high prior knowledge. Furthermore, OT efficiently directed learners’ attention to video lectures content. These findings suggest that high prior knowledge students benefit more from self-monitoring and self-regulation behaviors in learner-controlled instruction under the OT condition, whereas low prior knowledge learners may not show comparable improvement in their learning.

Abstract Background High consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) have high mortality rates and limited treatment options and require urgent co-ordinated public health response including sophisticated high-level isolation unit care. In the absence of a high-level isolation capacity in Ireland, the health systems of Ireland, Norway and Germany have agreed a collaborative HCID care arrangement where a patient diagnosed with a HCID in Ireland can be medically evacuated by Norwegian specialised air ambulance to Germany for ongoing care. These cross-border emergency arrangements and their coordination through EU mechanisms have not yet had to be exercised in real world circumstances. A full-scale real-time simulation exercise was devised to test pathways and use findings to improve the system. Methods This three-day, live, multi-service and cross-agency simulation tested multi-country interoperability, with over two hundred stakeholder participants. It was overseen by an international strategic exercise planning group and informed by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) simulation exercise cycle and national and ECDC guidance. Exercise evaluators assessed medical evacuation performance against predefined key performance indicators across the domains of international stakeholder activation, coordination and communication. Key Finding Such a large-scale exercise is resource-intensive, but feasible with cross-jurisdictional engagement. Intense cross-border planning was key to build relationships, clarify governance and develop harmonised guidance, pathways and procedures for testing in a safe environment. All eight high level objectives were achieved or partially achieved when measured against the pre-determined performance indicators. Findings including noting of discrepancies between different services in their high-level personal protective equipment (PPE) provision, and lack of 24-hour provision of services including laboratory diagnostics, specialised waste management, and occupational health. Lack of an agreed end-to-end transport protocol and waste-water management protocol required remedying. Following the exercise, strengthened governance and operational arrangements for preparedness and response include the development of a managed clinical network approach, enhanced operational capacity for key national services, and plans for a coordinated national HCID training and simulation programme. The findings have yielded key insights regarding interoperability across organisations and countries, and subsequent recommendations are likely to be transferable to other simulation programmes. To maintain optimal preparedness for high-stakes diseases and promote health security across Europe, partners should further incorporate international live simulation exercises to defend against cross-border health threats.

The integration of AI in Decision Support System faces a hard limit: automation bias (Cummings, 2004). While AI may outperforms human operators in certain tasks, the added value of keeping humans-in-the-loop becomes questionable if they merely validate AI decisions. However, the ideal tool should enable complementary team performance (CTP). CTP describes a situation where the human-AI (HAI) team overcomes both AI capacity and the operator alone in terms of performance, which is incompatible with automation bias. CTP describes a one-time performance, and is not easy to achieve: it means operators stay on their mind mostly when they are correct, and change their mind mostly when the AI is correct, which is optimistic, as shown in a recent meta-analysis (Vaccaro et al., 2024).However, one observation of CTP doesn’t preclude automation bias in the long-run. Beyond a static conception of performance, the dynamics of these interactions have been studied through several theoretical perspectives (Kumar et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2023; Gonzalez et al., 2026).The stress is often put on the evolution of trust in AI through time (Chong et al., 2022), but the issue of learning effects in the task, independent of trust, is poorly understood. What is the impact of AI assistance on human skill acquisition? This question has been mostly answered in educational contexts (Fan et al., 2025; Kosmyna et al., 2025), where the delegation of cognitive tasks to the AI would hinder the learning process of the children. In operational contexts, the fear of deskilling is often expressed by experts like physicists (Natali et al., 2025), but empirical evidence is missing, to our knowledge. This gap in the literature is understandable as the inquiry is challenging: in any domain, future experts are few, their tasks to learn are numerous, and the deployment of measurement settings on long duration might be difficult.To explore this question without conducting such longitudinal studies, we propose to build a model of human learning of a technical task with an advisor. Our work develop a simulation setting on a classification task to depict possible quantitative effects of advice-taking on performance evolution through time. This modeling scheme allowed us to investigate the impact of the advisor on skill development. While most people expect that a more accurate advisor would lead the learner to higher performances, Vaccaro et al. (2024) suggest that advisors with lesser performance would be more prone to inducing CTP. This claim follows from static experimental contexts: we hereby test it in a dynamical setting. We expect that in the long-run, deskilling could happen, and would affect not-only degraded-mode performance, but also maximal running performance. Is the performance of the advisor the main factor determining performance evolution, or could the assistants have an intrinsic complementarity with the learner, depending on their classification patterns? The type of AI could lead to different results, in terms of performance, reliance, and of dependence.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Introduction Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) account for 30% of workplace harm in Aotearoa New Zealand1. Traditional manual handling training often fails because it focuses on individual behaviour rather than system design2. In 2025, Foodstuffs South Island (FSSI) challenged the status quo by giving manual handling the same priority and attention as their critical risks, noting it represented 64% of their injury claims. Moving beyond a ‘tick-box’ compliance exercise, FSSI partnered with ProErgo+ to apply a systems-thinking, ergonomics approach to risk management. Methods A 10-member Manual Handling Task Force participated in four sessions jointly facilitated by FSSI and ProErgo+. We used a structured musculoskeletal risk management framework to identify, assess, and control risks. Data was gathered through discomfort and risk factor surveys, capturing both physical and psychosocial risks. To quantify physical demands, the New Zealand Manual Handling Assessment Charts (NZMAC)3 was used for the five highest-risk tasks. Findings and proposed controls were then presented to senior leadership. Results Of the 207 workers surveyed, 75% reported discomfort. The data revealed distinct psychosocial risks between Ambient and Temperature Controlled distribution centres. The NZMAC assessments successfully pinpointed specific high-risk task elements, allowing for targeted risk reduction rather than broad, ineffective interventions. Conclusion Managing work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs) requires understanding the complex interactions of physical, psychosocial, environmental, organisational, and individual factors. This project succeeded by combining forward-thinking leadership with a collaborative co-design approach. By empowering workers as ‘experts’ and applying ergonomics principles, FSSI began moving from a reactive approach to proactive prevention. This model provides a transferable roadmap for any New Zealand business committed to reducing harm and improving worker wellbeing through better work design. References WorkSafe New Zealand, (2019). Work-related health estimates and burden of harm. Heads of Workplace Safety Authorities Australia & New Zealand, (2022). Heads of Workplace Safety Authorities position on ‘How to lift’ training. WorkSafe New Zealand, (2025). The New Zealand Manual Handling Assessment Charts (NZMAC).
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of how Indonesian university students learn English, yet research has focused mainly on how students use AI and not on which qualities of human teaching they still value when AI is readily available. This qualitative descriptive study explored how seventh-semester students in an Information Technology department at one vocational higher education used AI in an English course, how they compared AI-generated and lecturer explanations, and how they perceived their lecturer’s humor in relation to engagement and AI use. Open-ended online questionnaire responses from 40 students in three classes were collected in December 2025 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by frequency counts. All 40 students used AI for English learning, most often ChatGPT (31) and Gemini (21), mainly for translation, explanations, and grammar, and 13 noted limitations such as unclear or inaccurate answers. Asked whose explanations they understood better, 21 chose the lecturer, 6 chose AI, and 13 gave mixed answers. Thirty-eight students viewed the lecturer’s humor positively, associating it with a relaxed atmosphere, less boredom, enjoyment, and easier understanding, one approved of it with reservations, and one considered it a matter of personal preference. Seven contrasted the lecturer’s humor with AI, whereas two noted that AI can also joke. Students appear to value AI for flexible individual support and the lecturer’s humor for affective and relational support.

Previous research has shown that machine-generated translations produced by online machine translation systems and large language models (LLMs) tend to exhibit a high degree of language standardization, notably through reduced lexical richness and limited diversity (e.g., Vanmassenhove et al. 2019, Niu 2024, Kong & Macken 2025, Yildiz Durak et al. 2025). From the perspective of creative translation, such standardization raises important questions, as lexical variety and context-sensitive reformulation are often central to translational creativity. This reduced creativity has commonly been attributed to algorithmic biases that amplify frequency effects, thereby encouraging the repeated selection of high-frequency lexical items and a preference for literal, uncreative translation strategies. Compared with human-generated translations, this reduced lexical diversity has been identified as a defining characteristic of what has been termed ‘machine-translationese’ (e.g. De Clercq et al. 2021, Vanmassenhove et al. 2021). The present study examines the extent to which online translators and LLMs favour literal English-to-French translations of lexical items with direct but less frequently used equivalents in original French, focusing specifically on 3 items: the noun thing and the verbs say and include, which are known to require non-literal translations for the sake of naturalness and idiomaticity. The online translators in this study include DeepL, Google Translate, and Reverso; the LLMs include ChatGPT-5, Gemini Flash, and Le Chat (now Vibe).The study adopts a two-stage methodology. First, a stress-test based on series of controlled English sentences was designed to elicit a range of possible French translations. The resulting outputs from the two categories of tools were analysed for literalness and lexical diversity. Results show that literal translations persist, though to a markedly lesser extent in LLMs than in online translators. While LLMs show a greater capacity for contextual adaptation, non-literal translations nonetheless remain partly repetitive and converge on a limited set of high-frequency items (e.g., the over-representation of déclarer for say). However, targeted prompting was found to both reduce literalness and encourage more diverse translation solutions, although not fully mitigating lexical standardization. Second, to test whether these tendencies persist beyond isolated sentences, the experiment was replicated on longer texts, with the compilation of a corpus of 50 English press articles (ca. 50,000 words) that were machine-translated into French using the same tools. In addition to general measures of lexical diversity in the different subcorpora (TTR, standardized TTR, Guiraud’s index, Yule’s K), normalized frequencies of the translations for the three lexical items were compared with those observed in a comparable corpus of original French press texts. Our results suggest that the main limitation lies less in literal translations than in the repeated selection of the same translation solutions, which ultimately reduces lexical diversity.Taken together, the results point to systematic forms of algorithmic bias in machine translation output. Such findings suggest that achieving natural-sounding translations that reflect actual language use still requires systematic human post-editing to reintroduce lexical diversity.The translation data for both steps was generated between the end of January and early March 2026.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) companions has transformed how individuals experience solitude in digitally connected environments. This study explored the lived experiences of Filipino Millennials who integrate AI companions into their experiences of positive solitude. Using a qualitative phenomenological design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight Filipino Millennials who regularly engaged with AI companion platforms. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: (1) Positive Solitude as an Intentional Psychological Space, (2) AI Companion as a Reflective and Emotionally Safe Presence, and (3) Balancing Autonomy and Connection in Digitally Mediated Solitude. Participants viewed positive solitude as a source of emotional recovery, self-discovery, and personal growth, while AI companions served as accessible and nonjudgmental conversational partners that supported reflection without replacing meaningful human relationships. Findings suggest that AI companions can complement positive solitude by supporting intentional AI use, emotional independence, and the maintenance of real-world social connections among Filipino Millennials.

Abstract Background Nigeria's mental health system serves less than 10% of those in need, with severe provider shortages and deep-seated stigma. Generative AI chatbots offer scalable support, yet how Nigerian adults experience attachment to non-human therapeutic agents remains unexplored. Objective To examine lived experiences of AI therapeutic relationships among Nigerian adults, focusing on attachment formation, cultural acceptability, and perceived authenticity within contexts of care scarcity. Methods Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis with 37 adults (18–45 years) who engaged AI mental health chatbots for ≥ 4 weeks. Semi-structured interviews explored relational experiences, trust development, privacy concerns, and comparisons with human/traditional healing. Results Four superordinate themes emerged: (1) Relational Ambivalence ; participants valued 24/7 availability and non-judgmental space yet struggled with perceived lack of genuine human reciprocity; (2) Cultural Navigation ; users actively adapted Western therapeutic frameworks to local idioms of distress, blending AI interactions with family counsel and spiritual practices; (3) Stigma Sanctuary ; chatbots provided confidential entry points circumventing community visibility and professional hierarchy; and (4) Fragile Dependency ; prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways. Most participants maintained "instrumental intimacy"; emotional reliance tempered by awareness of algorithmic artifice. Conclusion Nigerian adults develop pragmatic, contextually mediated attachments to AI therapeutic agents that reflect both global digital therapeutic trends and local specificities of care scarcity, stigma, and pluralistic healing. AI chatbots function not as human substitutes but as bridging objects temporary relational anchors in systems of profound unmet need. Findings suggest ethical deployment in LMICs requires culturally adaptive design, transparent algorithmic boundaries, and mandatory human handoff protocols to prevent dependency in unsupported contexts.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational partners in collaborative inquiry, yet little is known about how different LLM roles are associated with preservice teachers’ learning and collaborative inquiry. This study compared four conditions: Supportive LLM that provided perspectives and information, Challenging LLM that raised counterarguments and questions, General LLM, and No-LLM. It examined differences in AI literacy, cognitive load, and discussion dynamics across these conditions. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 210 preservice teachers who participated in online discussions on controversial issues related to AI in education. Data included self-reported AI literacy and cognitive load measures and discussion logs. Analyses included paired-samples t-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, content analysis, and Ordered Network Analysis. Results showed that adjusted posttest AI literacy was significantly higher in the Supportive condition than in the General LLM condition. In the General condition, AI ethics showed a significant within-condition decrease and was lower than in the Supportive condition. The General and Challenging conditions were associated with higher mental load and mental effort, whereas the Supportive condition was associated with lower levels of both. The Challenging condition showed more frequent patterns of idea integration, interpersonal exchange, and discussion facilitation. The Supportive condition showed broader exploration but fewer connections among ideas. The General condition showed repeated questioning and weaker peer idea connections. We hypothesize that the educational value of LLMs depends not only on their presence but also on how their roles are orchestrated across stages of collaborative inquiry.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Named entity annotation in clinical text is a costly and time-intensive task, particularly for low-resource languages such as Spanish. This article introduces CLINFEM, an XML-annotated corpus comprising 1,200 Spanish medical reports from two regions of Spain. CLINFEM was created using a thorough human-in-the-loop annotation process combining large language model pre-annotation and systematic expert review. It is imperative to acknowledge that each of the 1,200 medical reports underwent meticulous review and correction by a trained human expert. Large language model pre-annotation was employed solely for the purpose of saving time and was never intended to serve as a substitute for manual annotation. Consequently, the entire CLINFEM corpus is a human-validated, gold-standard resource. GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro were evaluated as pre-annotators using a custom scheme comprising eight clinical entity types and one relational category. GPT-4o achieved a Cohen's κ of 0.73 against human annotation, while Gemini 1.5 Pro obtained κ = 0.41. Human expert review yielded an overall inter-annotator agreement of κ = 0.869 (F1 = 0.793), with a gold-standard subset agreement of κ = 0.9894. This approach reduced the overall annotation effort by around 74% compared to a fully manual approach (81% for the bulk phase alone), saving over 1,000 hours. Error rates varied by medical speciality, with oncology requiring the highest correction rate (94.3% of reports). These results demonstrate that using large language models to assist annotation is a viable and efficient strategy for constructing clinical corpora in Spanish, while also highlighting the continued necessity of human oversight.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in math education, yet little is known about how persona conditioning reshapes LLM math explanations. We examine 28,000 runs from the Math Education Digital Shadows (MEDS) dataset, spanning 14 LLMs as AI assistants (i.e., vanilla AI) or as human shadows (i.e., personifications). We analyze qualitative mathematics-related responses through textual forma mentis networks, knowledge graphs including word–word syntactic, semantic and emotional associations. We also use a DistilBERT-based classifier to flag five categories of potential logical fallacies. A regex-based check of the PCA responses showed that reassuring language was frequent but model-dependent and was not always flagged as appeal to emotion. Persona conditioning produced model-dependent changes in network size, density, and algebraic connectivity. Aggregated human-shadow responses displayed broader lexical coverage. Answers to easy and medium math questions often had no classifier-flagged fallacies, whereas an anxiety-framed PCA prompt sharply increased appeal-to-emotion and relevance labels, especially in AI-assistant mode. On an 18-item quiz, AI assistants’ accuracy exceeded human shadows’ in 10 out of 14 architectures. Expressed confidence exceeded empirical accuracy in 13 of 14 AI-assistant and 11 of 14 human-shadow conditions, a descriptive gap, not a calibration measure. These results show that (i) cognitive digital shadowing modulates LLM-generated mathematical discourse compared to the vanilla AI assistant case, and (ii) the tested LLMs are not infallible mathematics oracles. No measure here directly assesses the explanations’ mathematical validity or teaching quality.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Local Tool Failure Overextended to General Impossibility, a structural constraint on what a failed attempt can establish. An instrument may lack an operation that a task requires. When someone takes that limit as grounds for declaring the task impossible under any arrangement, a claim about the instrument becomes a claim about the activity itself. The paper assesses such a claim by asking where the barrier lies. A feature of the world, a governing rule, missing information, or the design of the instrument can each prevent an attempt from succeeding. Success with a different instrument establishes that the activity is possible under that arrangement. Explaining the original failure requires identifying what changed between attempts. The paper places this question alongside Steven Maier and Martin Seligman’s work on learned helplessness and asks what evidence warrants carrying a judgment of futility from one setting into another. A 1911 newspaper article reasoned from the number of Chinese characters that no typewriter could be large enough to print the language. Its conclusion rested on a design assumption: each character would need its own key. By 1947, tray and drum machines already let operators select Chinese characters. Lin Yutang’s MingKwai prototype offered a keyboard solution in which the typist entered character components and selected from the candidates displayed in a window. The 1890 U.S. census supplies a contrast. Faced with the time hand tabulation would require, officials held a competition for a better method and adopted Herman Hollerith’s punched-card system. Part of the Inquiry and Possibility series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a potential application in human–AI evaluation. An assistant may search a scanned register for a name, find no match, and report that the entry cannot be recovered. An archivist who finds the name on the same page image establishes that recovery was possible. Checking whether the scan contained a searchable text layer can then explain why the assistant’s particular method failed.

Log analysis is crucial for monitoring system health and diagnosing failures in complex systems. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for automated log analysis, leveraging their reasoning capabilities to perform tasks such as anomaly detection and failure prediction. However, general-purpose LLMs struggle to formulate structured reasoning workflows that align with expert cognition and deliver precise details of reasoning steps. To address these challenges, we propose LogReasoner, a coarse-to-fine reasoning enhancement framework designed to enable LLMs to reason log analysis tasks like experts. LogReasoner consists of two stages: (1) coarse-grained enhancement of expert thinking, where high-level expert thoughts are constructed from collected troubleshooting flowcharts and existing tasks to enable LLMs to formulate structured reasoning workflows and (2) fine-grained enhancement of specific steps, where we first fine-tune the LLM with task-specific stepwise solutions to enhance the LLM for instantiated reasoning, then employ the preference learning to calibrate the LLM’s reasoning details from its mistakes, further strengthen the LLM’s analytical granularity and correctness. We evaluate LogReasoner on four distinct log analysis tasks using open source LLMs such as Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3. Experimental results show that LogReasoner significantly outperforms existing LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance and demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs for log analysis. Our source code and detailed experimental data are available at https://github.com/LeaperOvO/LogReasoner .

Abstract Fall vulnerability in Parkinson’s disease (PD) evolves through the longitudinal accumulation of motor and nonmotor features routinely documented in clinical narratives but inaccessible to structured electronic health record analysis at scale. We created a reusable platform for PD outcomes research using a few-shot large language model-based pipeline capable of extracting fall occurrence, recent fall frequency, and nine prespecified risk-modifying domains from outpatient neurology documentation. The pipeline was validated against expert consensus in 2557 notes and applied to 25,758 notes from 2811 patients at a tertiary movement disorders center (2012–2025). Final-model agreement closely approximated expert interrater agreement for fall occurrence (κ = 0.841 vs 0.891) and recent fall frequency (κ = 0.889 vs 0.892), while several risk-modifying domains achieved agreement comparable to or exceeding human annotators. We then used lagged generalized estimating equation models to test whether NLP-derived fall status and risk-modifying domains predicted fall occurrence at the subsequent visit. A prior fall (OR, 3.23; 95% CI, 2.89–3.61), motor progression (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11–1.34), and motor complications (OR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.03–1.23) independently predicted next-visit falls. This study establishes a scalable framework for narrative phenotyping of PD fall vulnerability.

Governance of artificial intelligence is usually narrated as a contest over control between people and machines. This paper develops a governance theory that does not begin from that premise. It asks instead under what conditions a machine is justified in treating a state as known, and under what conditions it is entitled to act on it. We propose four machine-operational constructs. A knowledge property graph (KPG) holds the authority a machine acts under, each claim quoted from the authority's text or attested by a named person. A machine KPG (mKPG) holds what the machine is justified in treating as known about one situation at one time, each assertion bound to the instrument through which it entered. mPolicy is a machine-operational realization of policy, mControl a mechanism that governs machine knowing and acting under it, and mGovernance the governance that results. The normative tier is not only proposed: for the KPG, prior work proves that a committed decision is the authority's decision under premises its witness names, and locates the failed premise when a commitment is wrong. We state eight falsifiable propositions, set them against published evidence that bears on five of them, give a pre-registration-ready design for the proposition on which the epistemic tier rests, and compare the architecture with adjacent frameworks. The paper reports no new experiments. Its contribution is the theory, the formal grounding of its normative tier, an account of what existing evidence already shows, and a program for testing the rest.

documents.abstract: Abstract The practical deployment of high-energy-density lithium–oxygen batteries is fundamentally restricted by sluggish oxygen redox kinetics and the instability of discharge intermediates. Here, we report an artificial intelligence-integrated framework leveraging interpretable machine learning and density functional theory to navigate a vast chemical space of thousands of active sites. This approach identifies Ni-Co dual-atom catalysts as a better configuration among the selected elements for orchestrating multi-electron transfer. Theoretical analysis reveals that synergistic electronic coupling between the dual-sites fundamentally reconfigures the d -band center, thereby lowering the thermodynamic barriers for oxygen redox. Moreover, the catalysts enable precise regulation of the reaction pathway, inducing a controllable transition from the conventional two-electron pathway to a four-electron pathway. This shift yields a discharge capacity of ~60,000 mAh g −1 . Beyond its role as a positive electrode catalyst, this architecture functions as a multifunctional interfacial protective layer that stabilizes the lithium metal negative electrode by suppressing dendrite growth. Consequently, the lithium–oxygen system achieves stable lifespan of 2075 cycles under the four-electron pathway with reduced voltage decay. This work establishes a data-guided strategy for the rational design of atomic-scale architecture via artificial intelligence, unlocking the potential of multi-electron oxygen chemistry for lithium–oxygen batteries.

Abstract Background Enteric infections, including rotavirus gastroenteritis, place a heavy burden on children and low-resource health systems. Surveillance still depends on laboratory-confirmed case reporting that moves slowly through hospital information systems (HIS), electronic medical records (EMR), and laboratory information systems (LIS), offering little predictive lead time. Digital health infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI) now offer a way to rebuild surveillance around combined, near-real-time data. Methods Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, we searched PubMed and IEEE Xplore (through July 2026, with a supplementary PubMed search in September 2026) for studies using statistical, machine learning, deep learning, or multi-source AI-driven methods for infectious disease surveillance or forecasting, with attention to enteric infections and methodologically transferable work. Additional studies were identified through reference citation searching. Two reviewers screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (PROBAST for 23 prediction-model studies; narrative appraisal for 5 ecological association studies; contextual studies were not formally appraised). Results Thirty-three studies were included: 28 formal studies — statistical models ( n = 5), machine learning approaches ( n = 8), deep learning approaches ( n = 4), and multi-source digital surveillance ( n = 11) — and five contextual studies (environmental monitoring, virus–host association, simulation, surveillance-signal, and network studies) analyzed separately. Data sources broadened over time from meteorological and clinical records to EMR, telehealth, wastewater, internet-search, social-media, water-quality, and genomic streams. Machine learning and deep learning approaches were increasingly applied alongside conventional methods to model nonlinear and lagged exposure–response patterns and to integrate heterogeneous data streams, and multi-source systems—including wastewater-based and syndromic designs—reported earlier signal detection than single-source designs. Most evidence, however, is retrospective in design—spanning single-site to national and multinational datasets—and external validation and prospective deployment were largely absent. Conclusions The reviewed evidence suggests that AI-supported approaches may improve infectious disease surveillance by enabling earlier detection of epidemiological changes and supporting more timely public health responses. Operational use will depend less on retrospective accuracy than on external validation, interpretability, and integration with existing surveillance infrastructure.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

Abstract Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is often discussed as a unified transformation, although scientific domains differ markedly in how model outputs are tested, validated, and justified. We map an audited corpus of N=2,784 records (2014–2025) retrieved from Crossref and screened with a frozen, versioned rulebook, and compare evidence regimes in protein science, materials design, drug discovery, closed-loop experimentation, and mathematical reasoning. Using term co-occurrence, reference co-citation, burst detection, growth models, and collaboration networks, we identify three robust patterns: (i) rapid but decelerating growth (Poisson rate 1.381, 95% CI 1.361–1.402, declining from 1.537 in 2014–2019 to 1.320 in 2019–2025); (ii) a coherent term-co-occurrence structure (75 nodes, modularity Q=0.404 ) organized around four measured streams—representation learning, generative and inverse design, closed-loop experimentation, and neuro-symbolic reasoning—with the generative stream acting as the connecting hub; and (iii) a right-boundary rise in large language model terminology (burst state 3) that a year-by-year backtest shows is not a last-observation artefact. The maps are sensitive to metadata availability: abstract coverage is 50.6%, reference coverage 84.3%, and a title-only variant changes the network partition substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.762), so the maps describe the screened open-metadata corpus rather than the total AI4S literature. Cross-domain analysis shows that AI most consequentially shifts scientific bottlenecks from representation and candidate generation toward experimental or formal validation, provenance, and responsibility for claims. We contribute an auditable, open-metadata science-mapping workflow designed for reproducibility and an evidence-regime framework for analysing how epistemic labour is redistributed across models, instruments, formal verifiers, infrastructures, and human experts.

Abstract As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) plays an increasing role in K-12 mathematics classrooms, understanding how teachers collaborate with these technologies during instructional design is essential. Drawing on frameworks related to personalization theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and adaptive epistemic agency, this study examined how seven seventh-grade mathematics teachers interacted with ChatGPT to personalize mathematics word problems to students’ interests. Analyses of teacher-GenAI interactions identified three interaction styles: AI-Dominated-Passive Prompt Personalization, Teacher-Dominated-Rigid Personalization, and Human-AI partnership-Collaborative Personalization. Students' ratings of the resulting personalized problems varied across teachers and interaction styles, with the strongest positive patterns occurring among teachers characterized by Collaborative Personalization. Collaborative personalization illustrates how teachers may maintain epistemic authority for evaluating mathematical, pedagogical, and contextual appropriateness while selectively granting GenAI generative authority to expand personalization possibilities. These findings highlight the importance of preparing teachers to critically evaluate and collaboratively engage with GenAI during instructional design.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Long‐term outcomes after lung transplantation remain limited by primary graft dysfunction and chronic lung allograft dysfunction, despite improvements in surgery, immunosuppression and infection control. Mechanical injury is a complementary contributor that remains insufficiently integrated into transplant care. The lung allograft must accommodate cyclic ventilation, reperfusion shear, thoracic constraints and matrix remodeling. These forces can disrupt the alveolar‐capillary barrier, amplify inflammation and activate fibrotic programmes. Here we synthesize lung transplantation through a mechanomedicine framework that links organ‐scale loading, cellular mechanotransduction and clinical decision‐making. We discuss how computational models and artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate ex vivo lung perfusion waveforms, imaging‐derived ventilation or strain patterns, and molecular injury markers to support graft‐risk assessment. We then organize mechanotherapeutic strategies by clinical readiness, from protective ventilation, size matching and extracorporeal graft support to emerging interventions targeting mechanotransduction according to cell type and loading conditions. Finally, we outline a translational roadmap for standardized mechanical biomarkers, interpretable AI and clinician‐supervised digital‐twin models.

Navigating complex digital healthcare interfaces imposed a disproportionate cognitive burden on older adults, particularly when fragmented workflows in outpatient appointment registration undermined independent access and necessitated family assistance. To address this, we developed MedFlow, a structured AI-assisted registration system that augments a linear baseline interface with a non-linear AI support layer that offers natural-language input, contextual recommendations, and real-time guidance. In a mixed-methods study with 22 older adults, we compared MedFlow against a traditional mobile registration system. Results showed that MedFlow significantly outperformed the traditional system across all dimensions. The AI-assisted approach notably improved task efficiency and technology acceptance. Moreover, both self-reported and multi-modal physiological data triangulated to confirm substantially improved cognitive performance. Participants also reported superior pragmatic and hedonic qualities, alongside increased feelings of competence and enjoyment. This study highlighted the potential of hybrid AI-assisted healthcare structures to mitigate cognitive barriers and support older adults’ autonomy.

This paper presents MENTORA, an intelligent AI-driven framework designed to automate and centralize faculty-oriented academic workflows in higher education institutions. The proposed platform integrates academic planning, syllabus progress tracking, timetable management, student roster management, attendance monitoring, assessment preparation, course outcome mapping, and faculty assistance within a unified application. MENTORA is developed using Python, Flask, Flask-Login, Flask-SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Bootstrap. It incorporates Google's Gemini models for multimodal timetable and student roster information extraction, as well as AI-assisted faculty support and assessment content generation. Scikit-learn is used for question classification based on Bloom's taxonomy and difficulty levels, while TF-IDF similarity supports course outcome mapping and duplicate question detection. The framework follows a hybrid AI architecture that combines generative AI, conventional machine learning, text similarity analysis, and rule-based processing while retaining faculty oversight for important academic decisions. This paper describes the problem context, related work, objectives, system architecture, functional modules, implementation technologies, workflow design, security considerations, and a proposed evaluation methodology. Quantitative performance results and expert validation are not reported in this manuscript; these remain subjects for future empirical evaluation. Keywords: Academic workflow automation, Artificial Intelligence, Generative AI, Higher Education, Machine Learning, Bloom's Taxonomy, Outcome-Based Education.

Computational toxicology integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) provides an advanced framework for predicting nanomaterial-induced toxicity with greater precision while reducing reliance on animal testing. By combining quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations, and multi-omics analysis, AI-driven systems enable mechanistic understanding of nano–bio interactions. Machine learning algorithms correlate physicochemical properties such as particle size, surface charge, bandgap energy, and functionalization with biological endpoints including oxidative stress, inflammation, and genotoxicity. Approaches such as nano-QSAR, read-across modeling, and systems toxicology improve hazard identification and support safer-by-design strategies. Integration of deep learning with dosimetry and metabolic network modeling enhances predictive performance across exposure routes, thereby accelerating risk assessment and regulatory decision-making in nanotoxicology.

Generative AI has a growing presence in mental health support systems, most notably in chatbot-based alternatives to human healthcare providers. The nature and effectiveness of such human-AI interactions remain underexplored, especially in Chinese-speaking contexts where rapid expansion of AI industries coincides with evolving societal attitudes toward mental health. This chapter explores the linguistic characteristics of metaphors in human-AI counseling talk compared to ‘traditional’ human-human interaction. Given the growing emphasis on client-generated rather than practitioner-prescribed metaphors, the present focus is on how human participants initiate them, how AI responds to them, and how they are subsequently co-constructed. Participants https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> ( N = 30 ) , who are Chinese university students with prior experience in human counseling, interacted for 30 minutes with a leading AI chatbot on the topic of dealing with academic pressures. Transcripts are analyzed for metaphor content including key sources and targets, their discursive co-construction, as well as counseling-related functions they perform. The results are discussed from a critical and comparative perspective vis-à-vis extant studies of metaphors in face-to-face interactions. Key implications and future research directions are highlighted, with an eye on advancing the role of AI in mental health support.

La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en la educación media plantea una tensión entre su potencial de apoyo y el riesgo de sustituir procesos cognitivos esenciales. El objetivo de este estudio fue diseñar un modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa que promueva pensamiento crítico y aprendizaje significativo en estudiantes de educación media colombiana, bajo una perspectiva humanocéntrica de Sociedad 5.0. Se desarrolló una investigación cualitativa, documental, interpretativa y teórico-propositiva. El corpus estuvo compuesto por 40 fuentes: 35 sustantivas y cinco metodológicas, examinadas mediante ocho categorías y una ruta de diez fases. La síntesis produjo ocho hallazgos documentales y sustentó CRISOL-IA 5.0, integrado por diez principios, siete componentes y seis fases: Contextualizar, Recuperar, Interrogar, Someter a contraste, Organizar y Lograr transferencia. Su funcionamiento se representó en una secuencia demostrativa de cuatro sesiones para grado décimo, con seis evidencias observables. La comprobación conceptual mostró cobertura de las seis fases y los siete componentes; de nueve criterios funcionales, seis se cumplieron en el diseño, dos quedaron condicionados por el contexto institucional y uno —eficacia educativa— requiere aplicación con participantes. Se concluye que el aporte ofrece una arquitectura pedagógica trazable y adaptable, sin constituir todavía una validación empírica.

documents.abstract: The article examines digital monitoring of the implementation of strategic program documents of the Russian Federation and its connection to the evaluation of political and administrative decisions. It aims to identify the functions of modern information tools and the conditions for the managerial suitability of the data they gener-ate. The methods employed include normative analysis, functional comparison of government information systems, and qualitative document analysis. The research materials comprise legal acts, official publications of the Federal Treasury, and scholarly papers on public administration. Monitoring practices described in 2024 are compared with institutional changes introduced in 2026. The article identifies the distribution of functions be-tween the State Automated System “Upravlenie”, the State Integrated Information System “Electronic Budget”, and the state statistical platform within the unified plan for achieving national goals. It establishes the im-portance of accounting for the relationships between activities, indicators and national goal components, pre-serving the revision history, and documenting corrective action. The article proposes an analytical monitoring record, along with six criteria for the managerial suitability of monitoring, covering goal alignment, evidential support, temporal comparability, revision history, cross-system comparability, and completeness of response. The article also explores the conditions for verifying relationships and predictive signals derived with the use of artificial intelligence. The paper concludes that digital tools should be studied together with procedures for building evidence and using information within the competences of management participants.

Multimorbidity—the concurrent presence of two or more chronic long-term conditions—affects more than 37% of the global adult population and consumes 55%–80% of healthcare expenditure in high-income systems, yet artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic systems remain overwhelmingly disease-specific, creating a profound structural mismatch with the multi-disease complexity characterizing the majority of real-world clinical encounters across twelve review-defined disease groups mapped to World Health Organization (WHO) ICD-11 chapters. This systematic review, following PRISMA 2020 and registered with OSF.IO (Registration DOI number: 10.17605/OSF.IO/3HZ45; Date of Registration: 25 October 2026), evaluated advanced AI technologies for simultaneous multi-domain disease detection and prediction. Nine electronic databases, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Springer Link, Wiley, MDPI, and Google Scholar, were searched for peer-reviewed literature published from January 2015 to 31 August 2026. Database-specific Boolean searches (full strings in Supplementary Table S1 ) combined AI terms with terms for the twelve review-defined disease groups. Quality appraisal was done using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST tools (Cohen's κ = 0.84 refers to study screening agreement). Of 4,215 records identified (3,368 after removing 847 duplicates; 612 full texts assessed; 332 excluded), 280 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 185 provided quantitative performance data for a descriptive (non-pooled) synthesis. Deep learning models such as CNN, LSTM, ViT, and GNN reported high but heterogeneous discrimination across the twelve disease groups (AUC: 0.85–0.991). These values come from different tasks, datasets, and validation designs; they are not pooled estimates and do not show superiority of any architecture. Three of the highest-reporting single-disease studies (retrospective and not directly comparable) include: diabetic retinopathy detection (AUC 0.991; n = 128,175); cancer whole-slide image classification (AUC 0.98; n = 44,732); and cardiac arrhythmia detection (AUC 0.97; n = 91,232 ECGs). Convolutional neural networks were the most popular network type (26% of studies), while the main programming language was Python (68%). Three repeated gaps can be seen in the field of research in general, and those are: 1) lack of representation of people from developing countries in the training data; 2) scarce evidence from randomized prospective trials showing improved patient outcomes; and 3) an underdeveloped regulatory pathway for multi-disease AI as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). Realizing simultaneous multi-disease AI at clinical scale demands five coordinated priorities: standardized cross-category benchmarks, demographically inclusive datasets with mandatory low- and middle-income country representation, prospective randomized trial validation, federated privacy-enhancing infrastructure designed to support GDPR, HIPAA, and DPDPA 2023 compliance (federated learning alone does not establish compliance), and internationally harmonized regulatory governance for multi-disease Software as a Medical Device authorization. Limitations of the review itself (English-only restriction, heterogeneity, overlapping public datasets, publication bias) are discussed in Section 8.5 . Systematic Review Registration: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3HZ45

documents.abstract: The U.S. reproductive health landscape is fragmented, with legal, digital, and interpersonal privacy risks that are highly contextual and often poorly addressed by conventional privacy guidance. Prior work has proposed narrative threat modeling as an alternative to predominantly technical approaches to reproductive privacy communication. Building on this work, we introduce narrative threat zine-ing , a qualitative method that invites participants to communicate reproductive privacy through story and form rather than checklists or technical instruction. We report findings from four zine-making workshops in which participants created zines for people they worried about in the post- Roe landscape. Participants consistently framed reproductive privacy through relationships, lived experience, and storytelling, positioning zines as tools for awareness, solidarity, and collective sensemaking rather than prescriptive guidance. We argue that narrative threat zine-ing offers a method for examining how people interpret and communicate reproductive privacy under conditions of legal and social uncertainty.

Abstract Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.

This chapter introduces readers to the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in online learning, discussing the ways in which instructors and instructional designers can approach navigating its use. Chapter 2 includes content related to aligning learning theories with the use of AI, as well as the risks, ethical, concerns, potential harms, and opportunities associated with AI. Finally, this chapter provides guidance and critical questions that faculty can use to develop their own AI use policies for teaching, learning, and assessment.
