AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

Background/Objectives: Nipple-sparing mastectomy (NSM) is increasingly performed in BRCA1/2 carriers, both for risk reduction and for treatment of breast cancer, but concern remains about glandular tissue left beneath the preserved nipple. We summarised the oncological outcomes of NSM in carriers. Methods: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PubMed Central (Europe PMC) up to 30 September 2026, CENTRAL on 26 September 2026, and Embase on 7 November 2026 and screened the citations of relevant articles for series reporting outcomes of NSM in BRCA1/2 carriers. The outcomes were breast cancer diagnosed after risk-reducing NSM and locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM; cancers found at surgery were not counted. Proportions per woman were pooled with a binomial random-effects model (generalised linear mixed model, no continuity correction) and are reported as marginal (average-risk) and median-type (typical-study) proportions, with crude proportions, a beta-binomial model, follow-up strata, and approximate person-time analyses as checks. Two human reviewers went through all articles, with generative AI used only as an assistant, and the statistics were reviewed by a third author. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Joanna Briggs Institute checklist and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Results: Fifteen studies were included. After risk-reducing NSM, seven breast cancers occurred among 1215 women from eleven studies (crude proportion 0.58% (exact 95% CI 0.23–1.18%); model-based marginal proportion 0.60%, median-type 0.41% (95% CI 0.04–1.07%)); follow-up ranged from 33 to 129 months, and four of the seven cancers came from one international registry. After therapeutic NSM, locoregional recurrence occurred in 16 of 363 women from five studies (crude 4.4% (exact 95% CI 2.5–7.1%); model-based marginal proportion 4.3%, median-type 4.2% (95% CI 1.1–6.9%)); one study contributed 11 of the 16 events. Recurrence within the nipple–areolar complex was reported explicitly by only one study (none in 114 breasts). Sensitivity analyses yielded median-type proportions of 0.30% to 0.74% after risk-reducing NSM and 2.6% to 4.2% after therapeutic NSM. Risk of bias was moderate to high in most studies, and the certainty of the evidence was very low for both outcomes. Conclusions: In BRCA1/2 carriers, about 0.6% of women had breast cancer after risk-reducing NSM and about 4% had locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM, but follow-up was short and heterogeneous and the certainty of the evidence is very low. These data describe observed event frequencies and do not establish oncological safety or equivalence to other mastectomy techniques; longer prospective studies with time-to-event, gene-specific, and comparative reporting are needed.

This study aims to discuss and analyze the use of Languaging as a tool for linguistic construction in the teaching and learning process of Portuguese as a Heritage Language. The Languaging process is examined through Language-Related Episodes (LREs), understood as analytical tools for investigating learners’ linguistic reflection and for supporting pedagogical practices in heritage language education, more specifically in Portuguese. The study is based on the analysis of interactions that occurred in a Portuguese as a Heritage Language classroom context with participants living in South Africa, aged between 10 and 11. The main findings indicate that the LREs identified in the study are predominantly related to grammatical aspects and structural mechanisms of writing, and they highlight the crucial role of teacher mediation in learners’ cognitive engagement. The conclusions suggest that the use of Languaging in collaborative writing activities constitutes a powerful analytical and pedagogical tool for Portuguese as a Heritage Language instruction, as it promotes the articulation between form, meaning, and discourse, fostering interculturality in the classroom, while also underscoring the need for teacher education specifically focused on heritage language instruction and sensitive to the linguistic and sociocultural particularities of heritage speakers.

Abstract Low back pain (LBP) is a common occupational health problem among healthcare workers. While physical demands are known to contribute to LBP, few large-scale studies have investigated the contribution of psychosocial stressors. This study examined the association between occupational LBP and stress-related factors at a university hospital in Japan. In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed responses to the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire administered to 2,450 staff members. Participants were categorized into LBP and non-LBP groups. The prevalence of LBP and high stress was compared by occupation. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with LBP. The overall prevalence of frequent LBP was 29.1%, being highest in nurses (39.3%) and lowest in doctors (11.1%). The odds ratio for LBP in nurses versus doctors was 3.54 (95% confidence interval 2.22–5.63). High stress status was more common in the LBP group than in the non-LBP group (25.1% versus 6.9%). Multivariate analysis showed that subjective physical workload, interpersonal stress in the workplace, physical fatigue, depressive symptoms, support from supervisors, work/life satisfaction, and body mass index were independently associated with LBP. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that both physical and psychosocial stressors are associated with occupational LBP among healthcare workers.

The study focused on the occupational hazards and safety practices among brewery workers in Rivers State. Six specific objectives, research questions and 6 hypotheses were raised and tested at a 0.05 level of significance. The research design adopted for the study was a descriptive survey design using triangulation mixed method. The population of the study was one thousand six hundred (1,600) workers in brewery industry in Rivers state. The sample size for the study was 671 workers and 8 participants for the qualitative study; the sample size was determined using fishers formula for calculating sample size. The instrument for data collection was a structured questionnaire and unstructured interview guide for the qualitative study; a reliability coefficient of 0.84 was obtained. The result showed that workers exposure to physical, biological, ergonomic, mechanical, chemical and psychosocial hazards were low, findings revealed that the grand mean of 2.65 ± 0.34 indicated a high extent of safety practices among brewery workers. The result illustrated a correlation coefficient, r = -0.05 indicating a very low relationship between hazards exposure and safety practices. It was recommended among others that Management of brewery companies should immediately institute and implement safety measures to avoid occupational risks and put in place adequate preparedness against other hazards, Management of brewery companies should always organize workshop aiming at promoting occupational safety and health through appropriate prevention programs and provision of comprehensive occupational health and safety services with the provisions of personal protective devices, and focused interventions for workers.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background Maintaining safe workplace environments in manufacturing industries is important for ensuring employees' health and maintaining effective production performance. Research on environmental safety and occupational health and safety is extensive, but the association between environmental safety and production efficiency and whether employees' safety knowledge supports this relationship, has received limited attention. Methods Data were collected from two independent cross-sectional purposive samples of footwear production workers (Wave 1 and Wave 2; N = 385 each), 3 months apart, and analyzed separately using Hayes PROCESS macro model 7 to investigate the indirect association between environmental safety and production efficiency through occupational health and safety, and the moderating effect of safety knowledge, with a simple slope test used to probe the interaction. Total effects were estimated using model 4. Results Contrary to the hypothesized direction, the association between environmental safety and occupational health and safety was weaker at higher safety knowledge in both waves; the interaction was significant after correction for multiple testing in Wave 1 only. In Wave 1, the interaction was a crossover: environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety only at low safety knowledge, and the indirect effect on production efficiency was significant only at low safety knowledge. The direct and total effects were not significant. In Wave 2, environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety at all levels of safety knowledge, with the association weakening as knowledge increased. The indirect effect was significant at low, mean and high safety knowledge, and the direct and total effects were also significant, indicating partial mediation. Conclusion In both waves, environmental safety was indirectly associated with production efficiency through occupational health and safety, at least among workers with lower safety knowledge, and this indirect association was weaker among workers with higher safety knowledge. These cross-sectional findings suggest that safe working environments may be particularly relevant for workers with lower safety knowledge.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Municipal solid waste workers operate in high-risk environments with limited institutional support, exposing them to diverse occupational hazards. This study explored occupational health and safety knowledge, practices, and experiences among municipal waste workers in Calabar, Nigeria, and examined the perceived impact of a health education intervention using a qualitative approach. A qualitative exploratory design was employed, involving Key Informant Interviews (KII) with 12 managers and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with 36 waste workers. Data were collected using semi-structured interview guides and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings revealed low baseline knowledge of occupational hazards, poor safety practices, and systemic barriers such as inadequate provision of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), weak monitoring, funding constraints, and poor prioritization of worker health. The intervention improved awareness and perceived understanding of occupational hazards and safety practices, although structural barriers persisted. The study concludes that health education enhances knowledge but must be complemented by systemic reforms, including provision of PPE, enforcement of safety policies, and improved worker welfare.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Introduction Occupational health and safety (OHS) knowledge is important for identifying worker training needs and informing workplace injury prevention strategies. However, immigrant workers are often treated as a homogeneous group despite differences in settlement duration, residency status, and previous training experiences that may influence their knowledge of workplace rights, responsibilities, and safe work practices. This exploratory study examined differences in OHS knowledge among immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years, immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years, and Canadian-born construction workers in Ontario, Canada. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 206 construction workers assessed OHS knowledge using scenario-based questions developed with reference to Ontario OHS requirements. Associations between OHS knowledge scores and participant characteristics were examined using univariable analyses and a generalized linear model. Results Immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years had higher OHS knowledge scores than immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years. Knowledge also differed by residency status, with Canadian citizens born outside Canada and permanent residents scoring higher than Canadian-born and temporary-resident participants. In the adjusted model, longer residence in Ontario, residency status, and previous OHS training outside Ontario were significantly associated with higher OHS knowledge scores. Discussion The findings demonstrate that OHS knowledge cannot be adequately characterized through a simple immigrant/non-immigrant distinction. Differences associated with settlement duration, residency status, and previous training highlight important heterogeneity among construction workers and may help identify OHS educational and prevention needs. Future research should evaluate whether targeted interventions addressing these differences improve safety practices and occupational health outcomes.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) plays a crucial role in managing the uncertainty of remanufacturing by enabling the needed flexibility and reconfigurability. However, a systematic evaluation approach of the remanufacturing system design is essential before deploying new HRC workstations. This paper presents a decision-making method, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), to streamline the quantification of process quality metrics. By processing scenario descriptions, the LLM autonomously assigns metric values, enabling efficient, data-driven assessment of workstation configurations. The deployed system’s architecture, data pipeline, and prompt engineering strategy are also detailed. A case study from the household appliance sector is used to validate the approach leading to enhanced robustness, adaptability, and efficiency while also reducing manual engineering effort while supporting optimal workstation design.

Abstract Current diabetic retinopathy management relies primarily on contemporaneous severity grading and does not directly quantify the short-term risk of vision-threatening complications. We developed and internally evaluated image-based artificial intelligence models for one-year prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity, proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and center-involved diabetic macular edema (ci-DME) using retinal imaging acquired during routine care.The prospective multicenter EviRed cohort included 3,183 patients with diabetes, 8,520 visits and 16,509 eye-level observations collected across 14 French hospitals. Device-specific ensembles were developed for ultra-widefield color fundus photography (CLARUS500 and OPTOS) and OCT angiography (CIRRUS5000 and PLEX Elite9000). Predictions from individual images and both eyes were aggregated at the patient-visit level. Participants were partitioned at the patient level into adevelopment set (65\%) and a held-out test set (35\%).For prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity at the subsequent annual visit, OPTOS and CLARUS500 achieved quadratic weighted kappa values of 0.866 (95\% confidence interval, 0.842--0.878) and 0.852 (0.830--0.877), respectively. For incident ci-DME, CIRRUS5000 achieved the highest discrimination (AUC, 0.826; 0.770--0.878), whereas PLEX Elite9000 yielded the highest AUC point estimate for incident PDR (0.877; 0.807--0.950). Late fusion did not consistently outperform the strongest device-specific model. In secondary complete-case analyses, observed ci-DME incidence increased across quartiles of the image-derived risk score, reaching 19.7--30.4\% in the highest-risk quartile. AI models also achieved higher AUC point estimates than unassisted expert risk assessments for both complications, although these comparisons were exploratory.Retinal imaging acquired at a single routine-care visit therefore contains information associated with diabetic retinopathy severity and vision-threatening complications one year later. These findings support image-based short-term risk stratification, while external validation, calibration and prospective clinical utility assessment remain necessary before deployment.

A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights for retailers and platforms to optimize reputation management and system design. Ultimately, our work offers a holistic framework for understanding online review behavior and proposes a rich agenda for future research in the digital marketplace.

Abstract Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering the everyday work of secondary schools. Teachers encounter AI-based tools both in classroom organisation and in feedback or adaptation tasks. As these tools become more visible in school practice, their educational role and practical value need to be examined in relation to the conditions of real classrooms. This is especially relevant in classes with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in pace and readiness to participate. In these settings, AI may help teachers adapt instructional material and provide more individualised support. Its value, however, depends on professional judgement and on how each tool is connected to pedagogical purpose. This paper examines opportunities and challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. The planned study will use teachers’ accounts to examine how AI tools are understood and used in secondary school practice. It is designed as a qualitative inquiry based on semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers, with the interview material examined thematically. Through teachers’ accounts, the study will explore how AI is understood in relation to lesson preparation and student support, while also examining what makes its use difficult in day-to-day teaching. The paper approaches AI as a tool whose usefulness depends on classroom context and teachers’ pedagogical decisions.

documents.abstract: Urban biodiversity loss is increasingly framed as a governance challenge with intertwined ecological and social dimensions, yet little is known about who participates in local biodiversity planning, what authority that participation carries, and whether plans recognize and address disproportionate harms. This study presents the first comparative analysis at this scale of participation in Local Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (LBSAPs), examining 98 plans from 98 municipalities across 26 countries. Using a hybrid methodology combining large language model-assisted verbatim extraction with manual coding (96.4% extraction accuracy), plans were assessed across four dimensions: participant recognition, participatory mechanisms, authorship, and transparency. Of the 98 plans, 71 (72%) documented some participatory mechanism, but only 18 (18%) granted participants any authority over plan content, and only 2 (2%) shared control over resources. Authorship was concentrated in city governments (93 of 98 plans), and 39 cities (40%) provided no transparency about participatory processes. Knowledge-holder positioning was dominated by scientists (M = 0.60 on a 0–1 scale) while Indigenous peoples (M = 0.08), marginalized groups (M = 0.01), and youth (M = 0.03) were systematically excluded. A distributive analysis revealed a marginalized-specific redress gap: 16 plans recognized marginalized groups as bearing environmental harm, but only 4 of those plans offered programmatic response; a 75% recognition-without-remedy rate not seen for any other actor type. These findings indicate that prevailing LBSAP governance architectures may constrain conservation effectiveness, by excluding the situated knowledge of communities most affected by biodiversity loss, and may reproduce environmental injustice, by acknowledging disproportionate harms without acting on them. Governance reforms that meaningfully redistribute participatory authority are needed to advance both biodiversity outcomes and equitable urban conservation.

Plant genomics with a hybrid classical-quantum model Artificial intelligence and quantum computing for the digital design of plant genomes Italian patent application no. 102026000034324, filed on 18 November 2026. Inventor, applicant and sole rights holder: Paolo Ciccolella. This invention proposes combining artificial intelligence and quantum computing to explore possible combinations of plant DNA and identify those worth investigating further. For businesses interested in plant genomics, the idea is to provide early guidance for computational design: turning a vast number of possibilities into selected, evaluated and documented digital candidates. The challenge is easy to picture. If DNA is a large instruction book, studying alternative versions of some passages means comparing many combinations. Three alternatives for each of twenty regions already produce more than three billion possibilities. The method tackles this complexity by dividing the work between a classical computer, two AI models and a quantum search component. HOW THE HYBRID MODEL WORKS The idea is to choose one alternative for each DNA region being studied, put the choices together and evaluate the resulting combination. Everything happens on a computer. The process follows six steps. • Prepare the data. The computer starts with a digital version of the plant’s DNA, called a reference genome. It identifies the regions to study and organises the available alternative sequences for each one, recording where they come from. • Give each alternative an initial score. The first AI model examines each alternative separately. Having learned from other cases, it can provide guidance before any complete combination in the new case has been evaluated. The computer also measures similarity between the ends of sequences that will be placed next to one another. These scores and measurements define the selection problem. [B12] • Search for combinations. The quantum component receives this problem expressed in numbers. It uses QAOA, an algorithm whose role is to propose combinations while seeking to favour those with better scores. Qubits represent the possible choices; the DNA sequences remain on the classical computer, which sets and updates the algorithm’s parameters. [B11] • Evaluate the whole combination. The computer checks that each combination selects exactly one alternative per region and assembles valid choices into a digital candidate. The second AI model evaluates the complete candidate, including relationships between its parts that the first AI model could not observe when examining them separately. • Guide the next search. The system compares the overall evaluation with the score predicted at the start and uses the difference to update the search. When only a few results are available, it limits the correction’s influence to avoid relying too heavily on sparse information. • Return verifiable proposals. For each selected candidate, the system retains the chosen sequences, their provenance and the evaluations performed. It also records a digital fingerprint, a code used to check the content. Researchers can reconstruct the proposal and understand how it was selected. If necessary data are missing, the system flags this. A concrete example: the patent uses the digital reference for Micro-Tom tomato and considers three regions, each with three alternatives created for the test. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible combinations. The search uses a nine-qubit quantum circuit simulated on a classical computer. This tests the computational method without producing plants. [B14] INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS The patent describes the production of verifiable digital representations of candidate genomes. Its industrial role lies in designing and selecting hypotheses, ahead of experimental work. Applications across sectors require data and models suited to the objectives under study. • NGT and assisted evolution techniques. NGTs, or new genomic techniques, include approaches known in Italy as TEA, meaning assisted evolution techniques, which enable targeted changes to genetic material. The proposed method could support research by comparing genomic hypotheses before experimental work. For seed and biotechnology companies, the prospect is to build a reasoned set of digital candidates for further investigation within NGT/TEA programmes. • Seed industry and variety development. For seed companies and research teams, the method could support the preliminary selection of combinations for further study. Research objectives could include drought or salinity tolerance, disease resistance and yield stability. Its contribution would be to establish research priorities while preserving the reasoning behind them. • Fresh produce and food processing. Computational design could focus on commercial characteristics such as product quality, shelf life and processing suitability. Tomato, pepper and aubergine are examples of supply chains that future projects could address, connecting growers’ and processors’ needs with the criteria used to evaluate candidates. • Nutraceuticals and plant ingredients. One possible development concerns plants of interest for functional ingredients, extracts and bioactive compounds. The method could explore genomic combinations in programmes focused, for example, on pigments or plant metabolites, providing documented candidates to guide subsequent analysis. • Plant biotechnology and industrial raw materials. For crops intended for oils, fibres or biomass, the method could help compare genomic hypotheses against supply chain objectives. Reconstructible digital records would support information exchange between teams developing the models and those planning subsequent experimental work. • Bioinformatics and computing centres. The most direct application is within the information systems of laboratories, computing centres and plant genomics businesses. The process could underpin software modules or analytical services that explore combinations and return candidates with scores and execution logs, integrating quantum search into the workflow. Introduction As part of a strategy to increase magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) capacity, the UK government funded the purchase of manufacturer artificial intelligence (AI) MRI image reconstruction software on MRI scanners. It aimed to reduce scan duration without compromising image quality and has been widely installed on clinical MRI scanners across the UK. Methods This is a mixed methods study, using an initial questionnaire to quantify opinions followed by focus groups of responders to further explore their views on technical issues. Patient views on the use of AI in MRI image reconstruction for reducing acquisition times, and more generally in their MRI pathway, were assessed. Results Study participants prefer improved image quality over faster acquisition times. If reducing acquisition times with AI, they feel it should only be used if extremely accurate images can be ascertained. They are uncomfortable with the use of manufacturer AI software for image reconstruction where accuracy is not stated and would like to be told about the use of AI in MRI. Conclusions Many participants felt that manufacturer AI software for MRI image reconstruction may be used only if a high accuracy is demonstrated, and if the training data is representative of the patient population, to not exacerbate health inequalities. This information is not currently given by manufacturers, which made the patient representatives concerned. Implication for practice •Local validation of AI image reconstruction software may make patients more confident about its use. •AI patient information materials should be accessible and discuss accuracy, and radiographers can be trained to help inform and reassure patients. •Engagement with all clinical stakeholders in MRI should be undertaken to understand their views on AI, and how manufacturer AI software should be implemented.

documents.abstract: Over the past decade, the innovative convergence of cloud computing, natural language processing (NLP), and large language models (LLM) has triggered a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction. This study aims to conceptually review and propose a research design to objectively analyze the effect of security and privacy perceptions on the use of AI as a venting medium. The proposed method is a conceptual quantitative research design with a correlational approach, planned for Generation Z respondents. Based on a literature synthesis of referenced studies, the findings indicate a highly significant positive correlation between dispositional shame and self-disclosure to artificial intelligence (r = 0.337, p < 0.001, n = 182). The conceptual review concludes that AI operates effectively as a complementary screening instrument but risks triggering an atrophy of social resilience, thus necessitating juridical protection through the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed businesses aiming at increasing the efficiency of operations. This technological revolution, considered meritorious, is not exempt from limitations. The prime focus is shifted from people to technology. In the fourth industrial revolution, the processes are automated in manufacturing through advanced technologies. Industry 5.0 emerged as a new paradigm where humans are prioritized along with the adoption of technology. Human centeredness is always at the heart of spirituality. Among the various forms of spirituality, Ignatian spirituality is structured and more popular. The challenges posed by Artificial Intelligence and digital transformation can be addressed by imbibing Ignatian spirituality. There are limited studies connecting Ignatian spirituality and Industry 5.0. This prompted the researchers to do this conceptual study. An extensive literature review on the areas of artificial intelligence, Industry 5.0 and Ignatian spirituality was done. An Ignatian framework is proposed to implement human friendly AI practices. This paper will guide business leaders, technology designers, and organizational development experts to design systems that promote human-centric approaches in the AI-driven world.

Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital inclusion with generative AI depends not only on educators’ access to tools but on how they use them. Comparing the benefits educators perceive with the uses they report may reveal gaps between what educators believe AI can do and how they use it in teaching. In this exploratory secondary analysis of survey data from 293 Minnesota PK-12 and higher education educators, we compared endorsement of improved accessibility for diverse learners as a benefit of generative AI with reported use of AI to enhance accessibility for students with disabilities. Because the items differ in scope and target population, the comparison describes response proportions, not a failure to act on a belief. Among 160 AI-using educators who answered both items, 133 (83.1%) endorsed the benefit and 51 (31.9%) reported the use (McNemar exact p < 0.001). Subgroup differences were not detected, though power was limited. Among all AI users, self-rated competence was associated with reported accessibility use (44.0% vs. 27.9%; adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI [1.13, 4.73]); among endorsers, the estimate was imprecise. Keyword-selected open-ended responses more often described general differentiation and language support than disability-specific use. We discuss measurement implications and propose supports as hypotheses for evaluation.

Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction and aims To evaluate the authenticity detection performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using real and AI-generated intraoral photographs and to compare their performance with human evaluators with different levels of dental experience. Methods A dataset of 1,000 intraoral photographs (500 real and 500 AI-generated) across 5 standardised views was constructed from single-institution clinical images and the publicly available AI-Hub dataset. GPT-5.1 (OpenAI), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic), and Gemini 3.0 Pro (Google) evaluated all images through vendor APIs. Human evaluation was conducted using a stratified random subset of 200 images by fourth-year dental students, dentists with ≤5 years, and dentists with ≥6 years of clinical experience (n = 5 per group). Results In the 200-image subset, dentists with ≥6 years showed the highest performance (accuracy: 0.740; F1-score: 0.675), followed by dentists with ≤5 years (accuracy: 0.690; F1-score: 0.557). Across the 1,000-image dataset, GPT-5.1 achieved the highest performance among the MLLMs (accuracy: 0.646; F1-score: 0.452), whereas Claude Opus 4.5 showed the lowest (accuracy: 0.571; F1-score: 0.249). All groups demonstrated substantially higher accuracy for real images than for the curated, visually plausible AI-generated images, with the MLLMs combining near-perfect specificity (0.998-1.000) and low recall (0.142-0.292), whereas human specificity was 0.890-0.990 and recall 0.390-0.540. The mandibular occlusal view showed the lowest accuracy among the MLLM groups. Conclusion Current MLLMs showed lower performance than experienced human evaluator panels, with limited recall for the AI-generated images in this study, suggesting that they are not yet suitable as standalone authenticity detection tools in dentistry. Clinical Relevance The increasing visual realism of generative artificial intelligence-generated intraoral photographs suggests that authenticity cannot be judged from visual inspection alone, and robust validation is needed before such images are used as clinical records, teaching material, or training data for artificial intelligence.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in news production, journalistic credibility can no longer be understood only through audience trust in machine-generated content. This article examines how AI-generated and AI-assisted journalism is made to appear trustworthy through textual, editorial, and institutional cues. Drawing on qualitative comparative content analysis of a 37-text corpus comprising 14 AI-generated or AI-assisted news articles, 14 human-written comparison articles, four newsroom AI policy documents, and five correction or controversy-related texts, the study analyses how credibility is constructed through authorship, disclosure, sourcing, human oversight, correction practice, and institutional framing. The findings show that AI-assisted journalism can reproduce familiar signs of professional news, including factual tone, structured formats, institutional attribution, and data specificity. Yet these cues do not necessarily make editorial responsibility visible. The article develops the concept of algorithmic credibility performance to explain how AI journalism assembles trustworthiness through uneven arrangements of transparency, evidence, and accountability before audiences respond.

documents.abstract: Background: The clinical relevance of routinely available peripheral inflammatory indices in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain, particularly regarding recent suicide attempts, depressive symptom severity, and their discriminative performance. This study investigated these associations using conventional statistical analyses and explainable machine learning. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 86 patients with MDD and 80 healthy controls. Six blood-derived inflammatory indices were examined for between-group differences and associations with recent suicide attempts and depressive symptom severity. Individual-marker discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, while three ensemble machine-learning models were evaluated using nested cross-validation and compared with MHR alone. Explainable artificial intelligence methods were applied to interpret model predictions. Results: Patients with MDD showed higher MHR, NHR, SIRI, and AISI values than controls. Recent suicide attempts were associated with higher SII, SIRI, and AISI, and these associations persisted after adjustment for age and sex; lower LHR was observed only in the unadjusted comparison and was not significant after adjustment. No inflammatory index was significantly associated with depressive symptom severity. MHR demonstrated the strongest individual discrimination. Machine-learning models showed modest discriminative performance without clear improvement over MHR alone, and feature-importance analyses consistently highlighted MHR. Conclusions: Here we show that peripheral inflammatory indices exhibit distinct observational associations with MDD and recent suicidal behavior. However, their diagnostic and predictive clinical utility remains unestablished and requires prospective, adequately controlled, independently validated studies.

This conceptual paper introduces Persistent Records Without Decoding Support, a mechanism by which a record outlasts the conventions, skills, or equipment needed to read it. The paper distinguishes two requirements for practical access. Recoverability concerns whether a reader can extract the marks or data. Intelligibility concerns whether the reader can establish what they mean. Each depends on the support available to a particular reader at a particular time. The documented case is the decipherment of Linear B. Clay tablets from Knossos and Pylos preserved palace accounts for more than 3,000 years. Before decipherment, scholars could copy the signs and recognize some pictured objects while the words beside them remained unreadable. Building on work by Alice Kober and Emmett Bennett, Michael Ventris identified the language as an early form of Greek in 1952. A tablet discovered later at Pylos helped confirm the reading. The words for two tripods appeared beside a tripod sign and the numeral 2. The 1986 BBC Domesday Project provides a contrast. By 2002, few working systems could read its videodiscs. A surviving drive supplied data for the CAMiLEON emulation demonstration, and preservation teams carried material onto newer systems. Access had become precarious while the means of reading still existed. The paper places this case alongside Jeff Rothenberg’s account of digital obsolescence and his proposal to emulate older computers. Part of the Records and Circulation series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a distinction relevant to human–AI interaction. An archive might preserve an AI system’s responses as sequences of token IDs. A later reader could copy every number, yet recovering the wording would depend on finding or reconstructing the mapping from those numbers to text.

Narrative theorising (rather than theorising based on constructs and models) is much called for in qualitative research in management and organisation studies. Despite this, how to emplot, i.e. the process of configuring fragmented events into coherent and meaningful accounts with the objective of sensemaking and understanding remains underexplored. This Perspectives piece showcases recent exemplars illustrating how we can practice narrative theorising using three distinct styles: historical, metaphorical, and discursive narratives. Since narrative theorising is commonly observed in single-case studies, we begin our exploration by drawing on six such articles published in Organization Studies to demonstrate how these styles foreground the temporal evolution of phenomena, bridge between multiple divergent accounts, or highlight conflicts between competing discourses to construct theoretical accounts and understanding. We illustrate each style in terms of its distinctive form, set of paradigmatic assumptions, analytical moves, and intended aims, with the overall aim of advancing the potential of narrative theorising in organisation and management research.

Our goal is to offer proof of concept for the idea that behavioral networks emerging with and beyond assigned treatment networks in experiments can provide a valuable window on agency. We call these often unobserved behavioral structures phantom networks. Most evidence of agency is entangled with audience—what people recall, how others attribute, or who is seen to act. We strip that away to observe agency directly in the ties participants build within and beyond what they are assigned. Their deviation from assignment is not error but structure in action, a behavioral trace of agency. We offer three exhibits of that “behavioral deviation” revealing agency in gendered brokerage, rival brokerage, and structural reproduction. Across the three exhibits, behavioral deviation shows how a team works (sometimes in surprising ways), not how well the team works. Teams perform as expected in theory, but the behavior responsible for their performance is made more apparent by watching behavioral deviation. We close with a summary proof of concept and discussion of next steps for particularly promising future work. Funding: This work was made possible by financial support from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business for data-processing software and financial support from MIT Sloan for transitioning our earlier experiment to the more flexible Empirica platform and funding the experiment trials on which we report here.

Abstract Dynamic Modulus (DM) is a critical characteristic for the design of Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA), which is currently determined through complex empirical models. This study applies advanced explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques to predict DM, enhance the understanding of the factors affecting it, and support design optimization applications. An extensive experimental dataset was used that included a variety of aggregate gradations, different types of bituminous binders, volumetric characteristics, and test conditions in terms of test temperature and loading rate. Eight different predictive models were developed, ranging from simple linear regression to advanced machine learning models, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and ensemble techniques, using a random selection scheme for cross-validation. Comparison of model performance indicated that the best performing model was the Cubic SVM, with an R 2 = 0.96 and RMSE = 2.22 × 10 5 psi, representing an approximate 39% reduction in error compared to the baseline linear regression. Explainable AI analysis revealed that phase angle was the most significant parameter in predicting DM, followed by aggregate gradation and binder characteristics. Overall, the findings show that the DM of HMA is influenced by complex nonlinear interactions among multiple factors. The AI-based models provided higher predictive accuracy and insights into interactions among material properties, supporting the development of optimized asphalt mix design guidelines for durable pavements.

Background Mosquito-borne diseases remain a major global public health challenge, with expanding geographic distribution driven by climate change, urbanization, and environmental modifications. Accurate forecasting of mosquito vector populations is essential for effective surveillance and control. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches have emerged as promising tools for modelling complex, nonlinear relationships in vector ecology. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the predictive performance of AI and ML models applied to mosquito vector surveillance worldwide and to summarize comparative evidence with traditional statistical methods where directly reported. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted up to August 2025. Studies modelling mosquito vectors (Aedes, Culex, Anopheles) using AI/ML techniques were included. Data on study characteristics, modelling approaches, predictors, and performance metrics (e.g., AUC, sensitivity, specificity, RMSE, R 2 ) were extracted. Results were primarily synthesized descriptively because of substantial methodological and clinical/ecological heterogeneity. Exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for commonly reported performance metrics, with pooled estimates interpreted alongside measures of between-study heterogeneity and prediction intervals. Risk of bias was assessed using a PROBAST-informed assessment adapted to the ecological and entomological context. Results Seventy-one studies were included, spanning diverse geographic regions and ecological settings. Random Forest was the most frequently used algorithm. Reported predictive performance varied substantially across studies and prediction tasks, with AUC values ranging from 0.61 to 0.99. Exploratory quantitative syntheses showed exceptionally high between-study heterogeneity, limiting the generalizability of pooled performance estimates. Most studies relied on internal validation, with limited use of external validation, further limiting assessment of model performance across independent surveillance settings. Conclusions AI and ML approaches show potential for supporting mosquito vector surveillance, but reported predictive performance varies substantially across prediction tasks, taxa, ecological settings, and validation frameworks. The extreme heterogeneity observed across studies limits the generalizability of pooled performance estimates and precludes broad conclusions regarding the predictive performance of AI/ML approaches across surveillance settings. Methodological standardization, transparent reporting, external validation across independent settings, and direct comparisons with conventional statistical approaches are needed to establish the reliability and real-world applicability of these models. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251129623 , PROSPERO identifier CRD420251129623.

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Preservation of Reopening Conditions Through Provisional Closure, an account of how inquiry can end for the purposes of action while retaining a planned route for later reopening. The mechanism consists in preserving an unresolved dependency, a condition that would warrant reconsideration, and an accessible route through which relevant evidence can be detected, connected to the closed question, and brought to someone able to act. The paper assesses provisional closure by whether the specified trigger can be detected, linked to the prior issue, and translated into a feasible step of reopening. It distinguishes retaining these conditions from their subsequent use: storage alone does not ensure monitoring, recognition, authority, or action. It also separates preserving a route back from the later conversion of detected discrepancy into effective revision. The account concerns consequential unresolved dependencies and does not require every conclusion to remain provisional. The mechanism is situated alongside Charles S. Peirce’s account of inquiry as the settlement of doubt and examined through two documented cases. Olympic anti-doping sample storage preserves material for later reanalysis when new information or improved detection methods become available. Japan’s conditional, time-limited approval of HeartSheet required follow-up and reapplication with survival evidence; the submitted analysis did not demonstrate superiority on its primary endpoint, and regular approval was refused. These cases are interpreted through published studies and institutional reports, with attention to the retained evidence, review conditions, and authority required to reopen a settled decision. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who retains and monitors reopening conditions, who can authorize reconsideration, and who bears the continuing cost of maintaining a route back. Potential applications in human–AI research include preserving assumption records, specifying review triggers, routing later evidence to responsible decision makers, and designing processes through which decisions can return to active inquiry.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can expand the range of candidate solutions available during design exploration, but it can also obscure whether students have engaged in the iterative design reasoning and evaluative judgement that studio teaching is intended to develop. This article examines how GenAI can be integrated into creative media education without displacing the cognitive processes through which creative expertise is cultivated. It draws on design research, automation literature, and cognitive load theory, alongside illustrative teaching cases spanning undergraduate and postgraduate animation, visual effects, and game design curricula at Auckland University of Technology and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. We argue that the educational value of GenAI depends not on the sophistication of its outputs alone, but on whether students retain responsibility for evaluative judgement throughout the design process. We propose Process Before Prompting, a pedagogical framework intended to preserve this responsibility within human-led cycles of divergence, convergence, and appreciative judgement. Students establish an initial creative intention before engaging with GenAI and remain responsible for interpreting, refining, and selecting among both human- and AI-generated candidates. This framework offers practical guidance for scaffolding independent judgement and assessing evidence of iterative design reasoning within existing studio teaching practices.

Introduction Attribution theory explains how audiences use observable information to infer otherwise unobservable agents and processes behind creative work. This study applied this perspective to examine how production-source disclosures influence source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation. Methods In a randomized experiment, 626 adults were assigned to one of four production-source disclosure conditions—undisclosed, human-made, human–AI collaborative, or AI-led—while viewing the same three animation clips, all of which were actually produced through human–AI collaboration. We examined between-condition differences in source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience-reception outcomes, as well as concurrent associations between higher-order creative attributions and audience reception. Results The disclosures clearly differentiated participants’ perceptions of AI and human involvement. Perceived creative effort was statistically significant before correction but did not meet the α = 0.05 criterion after Holm adjustment ( p = 0.0502); the only corrected contrast indicated lower perceived creative effort in the human–AI collaborative condition than in the human-made condition. No statistically reliable omnibus between-condition differences emerged for perceived authorship, perceived emotional authenticity, artistic evaluation, situational immersion, or viewing and recommendation intention. Higher-order creative attributions were positively associated with all three audience-reception indicators in concurrent analyses, although the strong correlation between perceived emotional authenticity and situational immersion warrants caution about measurement overlap. Discussion The findings indicate that the diagnosticity of a production-source cue depends on the judgment target: the disclosures clearly reorganized perceived production roles but did not yield statistically reliable corresponding differences across most higher-order creative attributions or reception outcomes. The attribution–reception relations represent concurrent covariation rather than causal mediation. Because the three clips were presented in a fixed order, material and order effects cannot be separated, and the equivalence analyses did not establish negligible between-condition differences.

The World Health Organization (WHO) identifies high blood pressure (hypertension) as a major global public health concern and a significant risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Therefore, facial Shiatsu massage can be a good solution to alleviate them. However, most people are not only unfamiliar with the locations of acupressure points for proper massage but also lack motivation to conduct it regularly. In this paper, we propose a facial Shiatsu massage exergame system as an effective approach to solve these conditions together. The system runs on a low-cost PC with a camera, provides a simple quiz on a selective topic, and recognizes an answer gesture of a player to select one choice to each question. A generative AI-based quiz generator is implemented to automatically generate quiz questions across different categories providing flexible and varied educational content for the proposed smart healthcare exergame system. An answer gesture is defined for pressing a proper acupressure point with an index finger, which is recognized by applying a MediaPipe library to a user’s face image taken by a PC camera. In this paper, four gestures are implemented to select one of the four choices in each question. For accuracy evaluation, first, we implemented the answer gesture recognition program and investigated the gesture recognition accuracy. Then, for effectiveness evaluation, we implemented the quiz generator using Ollama, produced quizzes on Japanese History, Simple Arithmetic, Indonesian Words, and Taiwan Geography with 50 questions for each topic, and asked 20 persons to use the system. For each user, we measured health condition-related indices such as blood pressure, body temperature, and facial skin moisture level before and after the system use by each person. In addition, we conducted a questionnaire and calculated the Usability and User Experience score. These results indicate the potential feasibility of the proposed system.

Abstract Background: Prosthesis users report high cognitive workload, or the mental effort needed to achieve task performance. The NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) is the most common subjective workload measure. However, it was developed for general human–machine interfaces and may not capture prosthesis-specific demands. The recently proposed Prosthesis Task Load Index (PROS-TLX) includes additional domains relevant to prosthesis use, yet its psychometric properties have not been established. This study compared the convergent validity, test-retest reliability, and measurement error of the NASA-TLX and PROS-TLX across two groups.Methods: Ten individuals without limb difference performed a timed reach-and-grasp task using a myoelectric prosthetic emulator in both a physical and virtual environment. Additionally, ten individuals with upper limb difference performed an accuracy- and time-based activity of daily living using their customary myoelectric, multi-grip prosthesis. Both groups completed two sessions at least a week apart and rated workload using the NASA-TLX and the PROS-TLX in both sessions. Because the PROS-TLX has more total subscales, we modified the scoring of the PROS-TLX to align it with the NASA-TLX. For both surveys, total workload scores were a weighted average of the subscales, ranging from low (0) to high (100). We compared total workload scores between the surveys using Pearson's correlation and calculated the intraclass correlation coefficients, measurement error, and minimum detectable change for each survey. We also explored the role of session number, survey, and task environment on the survey subscales and the relationships between subscales and task performance outcomes.Results: For emulator users, the PROS-TLX and NASA-TLX total workload scores were moderately correlated in session 1 (r>0.63), suggesting good convergent validity. However, for prosthesis users, the surveys were weakly correlated in session 1 (r=0.13). The PROS-TLX demonstrated higher test–retest reliability point estimates (ICC=0.44–0.83) and lower measurement error (SEM=7.43-10.79) than NASA-TLX (ICC=0.18-0.45, SEM=10.52-17.29), though the confidence intervals were large. The prosthesis-specific subscale of uncertainty varied by task environment and correlated with performance outcomes.Conclusions: The PROS-TLX adds prosthesis-specific contributors to workload to the NASA-TLX with higher reliability and lower measurement error estimates, but wide confidence intervals limit conclusions. Larger studies in prosthesis users are needed.

Accurate marine target detection is essential for maritime situational awareness and safe navigation by unmanned surface vehicles. However, uneven radar returns and uncertain spatial correspondence complicate radar–camera fusion, while input-level integration does not explicitly adapt subsequent feature processing to local radar evidence. We propose QPAFusion, which refines multi-scale features through query-guided local radar sampling and adaptively aggregates feature branches using radar priors. On the WaterScenes dataset, QPAFusion achieves 64.5%mAP50−−95 and 90.9%mAP50, exceeding the reported three-frame REVP fusion baseline by 2.0 and 2.1 percentage points, respectively, with mAP50 gains of 6.4 and 3.1 percentage points on the adverse-lighting and adverse-weather subsets. These results support combining local-radar refinement with adaptive feature aggregation for object detection on the water surface, with larger accuracy gains on the evaluated adverse-condition subsets.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming embedded in higher education systems, influencing teaching, assessment, research, and institutional decision-making. Despite the growing adoption of AI, existing governance approaches remain largely principle-based, emphasizing ethical guidelines such as transparency, accountability, and fairness without providing operational mechanisms for implementation within quality assurance (QA) and accreditation systems. This creates a critical gap between AI governance principles and the procedural structures through which educational quality and institutional accountability are evaluated. This study addresses this gap by developing an operational quality assurance framework to systematically integrate AI governance into a ten-step higher education accreditation lifecycle, with explicitly differentiated AI permission levels and defined boundaries for human evaluative authority. Using a conceptual and policy-synthesis approach, the study integrates global AI governance principles, established QA standards, and accreditation practices into a risk-based, human-centered governance model. The framework operationalizes AI governance and integration through a model that defines the role, boundaries, and permissible levels of AI use across each stage of the accreditation process. A central feature of the model is the explicit preservation of human decision-making authority in evaluative and high-stakes accreditation stages. The study reconceptualizes AI integration in higher education as a quality assurance and governance challenge rather than solely a technological innovation problem. By embedding AI governance and integrating it directly within accreditation processes, the proposed model provides a practical bridge between ethical principles and operational implementation. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for quality assurance agencies, regulators, and higher education institutions to consider risk-based AI governance within accreditation processes, with its feasibility, effectiveness, and transferability requiring further evaluation through implementation and empirical validation.

Abstract Many tabular classification tasks involve imbalanced classes, but synthetic oversampling can produce rows that violate feature constraints or duplicate existing observations. We present QualSynth, a training-free framework that prompts a large language model to make sparse edits to real minority-class rows under data-derived feature constraints and a machine-readable output contract. A deterministic validation layer checks each candidate’s structure, values, and duplication before admitting it to the training set. We evaluated QualSynth on eight benchmark datasets with ten seeds against four synthetic oversamplers, including the widely used SMOTE, and class-weighted learning without augmentation. QualSynth achieved the highest F1 score among the synthetic oversamplers on four datasets, while SMOTE had the best average ranks. In equivalence tests, QualSynth and SMOTE differed by less than prespecified margins of 0.03 in F1 score and 0.02 in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). After correction for multiple comparisons, the only pairwise difference was higher ROC-AUC for QualSynth than for the diffusion model TabDDPM. Class weighting alone had the best overall ranks, and no augmentation strategy improved aggregate ROC-AUC over the unweighted reference. QualSynth is therefore a controlled, inspectable option for minority-class augmentation, with predictive utility comparable to SMOTE’s.

Abstract Raman spectroscopy is one of the most accessible vibrational probes in materials laboratories, but its forward problem (structure to spectrum) is bottlenecked by the cost of density functional perturbation theory, and its inverse problem (spectrum to structure) typically relies on retrieval against curated references. We introduce RamanGPT, a deep-learning framework that addresses both directions for crystalline inorganic materials. The forward model, an Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), is trained on the 5,099-material Computational Raman Database and predicts 200-bin spectra over 50–1000 $$\hbox {cm}^{-1}$$ with 53.8% of the 509 held-out materials reaching an active-region cosine similarity of at least 0.354, capturing qualitative features of the target spectrum. The model also shows qualitative agreement with an experimental measurement of metallic 1T $$\hbox {VSe}_{2}$$ , a system absent from the training set. The inverse model fine-tunes DiffractGPT, a large language model already trained for diffraction-to-structure generation, via Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation on Raman-plus-formula prompts, recovering lattice parameters with mean absolute errors of 1.13–2.14 Å and reduced-formula consistency of 92.1% on 508 held-out materials, compared to 17.1% for a formula-conditioned retrieval baseline given identical inputs. A cosine-similarity matcher and an inverse $$\rightarrow$$ relax $$\rightarrow$$ forward consistency loop are deployed at https://atomgpt.org/raman .
