documents.abstract: The digital-intelligent transformation of traditional calligraphy education is advancing through the integration of artificial intelligence, big data, and immersive technologies. This study proposes a Dual Helix Reconstruction Model that synergistically couples a data chain with a teaching chain, establishing a closed-loop learning ecosystem incorporating intelligent handwriting analysis, contextual immersion, and collaborative feedback. A longitudinal experiment conducted in an authentic calligraphy course demonstrated the model's efficacy through multisource evidence. Results showed significant improvements in writing precision (d = 0.91), fluency (d = 0.85), and learning motivation (d = 0.88), confirming its role in enhancing skill acquisition, engagement, and self-regulation. Furthermore, the model fostered the integrated development of artistic expression and cultural understanding. This research provides a replicable paradigm for the digital-intelligent evolution of calligraphy education and contributes a methodological foundation for interdisciplinary innovation in art pedagogy.

Mountainous linear cultural heritage corridors include both formal-access and restricted-access sections, but recreation perceptions across these settings remain insufficiently understood. Using 17,034 online reviews from 18 Ming Great Wall sections in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region, China, this study compared perception-element prominence, sentiment orientations, and textual co-occurrence through an integrated analytical framework, LLM-assisted labelling, statistical comparisons, section-level sensitivity analyses, and co-occurrence networks. Embodied recreation was prominent in both settings. Section-level comparisons showed greater attention to management and services, particularly entry costs and infrastructure, in formal-access sections, whereas mountain environments and risk and use impacts were more prominent in restricted-access sections, particularly naturalness and heritage preservation. Although sentiment profiles differed descriptively, no section-level sentiment comparisons remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Co-occurrence analysis revealed associations between infrastructure and embodied recreation in formal-access reviews, while restricted-access reviews linked heritage preservation, mountain environments, bodily activity, and safety concerns. By extending recreation-perception analysis beyond formally managed attractions, this study provides comparative evidence of shared recreational interests and differentiated management concerns within a continuous heritage corridor. The findings inform access-sensitive management and corridor-scale heritage conservation, subject to limitations associated with platform coverage and reviewer self-selection.

Today, many educational institutions are incorporating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into their curricula, although skepticism is increasing among younger generations, particularly in Australia and the United States. Some students are organizing opposition to the use of generative AI in coursework. The creative industry continues to experiment with AI-based production methods, and art museums and film festivals are featuring AI-generated works. Countries such as China maintain a highly optimistic perspective on the technology. This panel convenes experts from Australia, China, South Korea, and the United States to examine critical questions regarding the role of AI in education and the arts.

Background: High-potential incidents in construction are often initially understood through the actions of the person closest to the event. This can narrow investigations, obscure the operational and organisational conditions that shaped performance, and weaken both learning and trust. As HEB Construction’s Critical Control Management programme matured, the organisation identified a disconnect between its prevention approach and the way incidents, individual actions and accountability were considered. Aim: This practice case study describes the development and implementation of Responding Fairly, an approach intended to connect Critical Control Management, Incident Cause Analysis Method investigations, Human and Organisational Performance principles, and people processes. Its purpose is to support fair, consistent and evidence-informed decisions while maintaining accountability. Approach: Rather than introducing a separate process, HEB aligned existing investigation, critical control and people practices around a shared sequence of questions. Investigations first consider which controls should have prevented the event, whether those controls were present and effective, how the work was designed and supported, and which conditions influenced decisions at the time. Individual actions are considered after this context has been established. The approach is jointly supported by Operations, Health and Safety, and Human Resources, with leader coaching and practical guidance used to strengthen consistency. Practice example and findings: A service-strike investigation showed how an apparent failure by an operator was better understood when outdated plans, a changed work scope, conflicting site markings, unavailable technical support and time pressure were examined together. This broader analysis led to strengthened service verification requirements, revalidation following scope changes and clearer excavation controls. Early implementation experience indicates richer learning, more targeted corrective actions, greater leader confidence and improved worker perceptions of fairness. Conclusion: Responding Fairly demonstrates how prevention, investigation and accountability can be treated as one connected learning system. Context does not remove accountability; it enables accountability to be located more fairly and supported by fuller evidence. The experience also suggests that a framework alone is insufficient: leaders require capability, support and confidence to pause, tolerate uncertainty and understand the conditions surrounding an event before reaching conclusions.

The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational practices has raised important questions about responsible leadership, knowledge integration, and employee innovation. This study examined the relationship between responsible AI leadership and employee idea implementation, with human–AI knowledge integration as the mediating variable, among employees of corporate organizations and higher education institutions in Metro Manila, Philippines. A quantitative, cross-sectional, explanatory-correlational, and comparative research design was employed, involving 400 respondents equally distributed between the two organizational sectors. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire employing a four-point Likert scale and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), bootstrap mediation analysis, and multi-group SEM. The study investigated the direct relationships among the three variables, determined the mediating role of human–AI knowledge integration, and examined differences in structural relationships between the two sectors. The final findings revealed significant positive relationships among responsible AI leadership, human–AI knowledge integration, and employee idea implementation. Human–AI knowledge integration partially mediated the relationship between responsible AI leadership and employee idea implementation, while no statistically significant differences were established between the two organizational sectors. Anchored in Socio-Technical Systems Theory and the Knowledge-Based View, the study's final framework emphasizes the importance of combining ethical AI leadership practices with employees' professional knowledge and judgment. The findings demonstrate that responsible AI leadership is positively associated with employees' ability to translate AI-supported insights into practical workplace improvements. The study provides empirical evidence to guide responsible AI governance, employee capability development, knowledge-sharing initiatives, and organizational innovation strategies across corporate and higher education environments.

This conceptual paper introduces Responsive Cues Converted Into Reciprocal Obligation, a mechanism through which repeated signs of attention can lead someone to feel that care is owed in either direction. A device that comes when called or asks to be held may come to seem like a companion who depends on its owner. The owner, in turn, may expect someone to keep that companion functioning. The mechanism concerns the point at which such an expectation extends beyond any commitment established by the people or institutions behind the device. The paper places this account alongside Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass’s work on how people apply social conventions to computers and other media. It asks what a particular person came to expect, which words or actions connect that expectation to a responsive cue, and who undertook to honor it. A person’s account of companionship can establish what the relationship meant to them. A provider’s statements and policies supply evidence about what that provider promised. Sony’s AIBO illustrates the distinction. Sony offered repairs for its earlier models for stated periods, and its repair clinic operated beyond the latest deadline in its notice. In 2018, owners of the new aibo asked Sony to extend its policy of providing repairs for seven years after withdrawal from sale. The founder of A FUN, an independent repair firm, argued that Sony bore continuing responsibility for the companion it had brought to market. The paper leaves the merits of that demand open. GROOVE X’s LOVOT provides a contrast through priced care plans whose written terms specify what the maker will cover. Part of the Presence Through Technology series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a way to examine expectations of discretion in human–AI interaction. A conversational assistant might recall a private concern and ask about it weeks later. If the user explains that being remembered led them to expect the exchange to stay private, that account connects a specific cue to a specific expectation. The provider’s confidentiality commitments can then be compared with what the user understood.

Purpose This study aims to systematically examine the core themes and boundaries of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) assurance, identifying prevailing research hotspots and dominant scholarly conversations. Furthermore, this study seeks to uncover emerging areas and critical gaps that offer opportunities for future research to address current and evolving challenges in ESG assurance. Design/methodology/approach Based on 148 peer-reviewed articles (after rigorous screening), the authors use bibliometric techniques, including network analysis, clustering and co-citation analysis, to synthesise the field’s evolution and reveal underexplored areas. Findings The review identifies five priority directions for future inquiry: the professionalism and evolving role of ESG assurers, ESG assurance quality and firm performance, the influence of governance mechanisms and stakeholder pressures, the implications of Audit 4.0 technologies (e.g. artificial intelligence, blockchain and data analytics) for assurance legitimacy and impact of agentic AI on assurance providers and ESG reporting readability and its consequences for assurance outcomes. By highlighting persistent tensions, contradictions and unresolved debates, this study reconceptualises ESG assurance as an evolving, multidisciplinary domain. Research limitations/implications This study may fully rely on Scopus, which limits the scope by potentially excluding relevant studies from other databases. Further, this paper addresses the key challenges found by International Federation of Accountants (IFAC, 2021), in determining the scope of an assurance engagement, exercising professional scepticism and judgment and obtaining the necessary competency and skills. Practical implications This study advances the emerging field of ESG assurance by identifying underexplored research areas, highlighting key research gaps and outlining promising directions for future inquiry. Beyond mapping the existing literature, this study also discusses the possible theoretical contributions that can strengthen the conceptual development of this domain. The review highlights key practical issues, including the role of governance, AI adoption and assurer professionalism in enhancing the credibility and transparency of ESG assurance. This study offers useful insights for researchers, practitioners, standard setters and regulators aiming to strengthen the quality and reliability of ESG assurance. Social implications This study’s insights can enhance transparency and accountability in ESG reporting, fostering trust among stakeholders such as investors and regulators. Improving ESG assurance practices encourages companies to adopt more responsible and sustainable approaches, benefiting society at large. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is among the first multi-disciplinary systematic literature reviews to study potential future avenues in the ESG assurance area with a holistic view. This study introduces diverse significant areas to meet current challenges in ESG assurance practices.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often store document chunks in a vector index together with a copy of their access-control metadata. When a user's permission is revoked in the authoritative permission store, this indexed copy may remain stale, allowing the vector database to keep returning protected content. This paper measures the duration of this revocation window and separates two outcomes: unauthorized index retrieval, in which the vector database returns a protected chunk, and LLM-context exposure, in which that chunk reaches the context assembled for the language model. We built a controlled synthetic testbed with PostgreSQL as the authoritative permission store and Qdrant as the vector index, and evaluated six enforcement configurations: periodic synchronization, event-driven synchronization, a no-worker control, query-time authorization, hybrid authorization, and query-time authorization with a 10-second decision cache. Each configuration retained 27 trials (5 for the control) within a 35-second observation window. The median context-level revocation propagation time was 9.92 s for 20-second periodic synchronization, 14 ms for event-driven synchronization, and 4.98 s for the cached query-time configuration. Under periodic synchronization, 87.7% of relevant queries placed the protected chunk in the context before revocation was enforced. Query-time and hybrid authorization blocked protected content at the first post-revocation probe (0 ms at probe resolution) even though the stale index kept returning it, while the no-worker control never achieved stable enforcement within the window. These findings describe the tested synthetic testbed and are not production guarantees.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often store document chunks in a vector index together with a copy of their access-control metadata. When a user's permission is revoked in the authoritative permission store, this indexed copy may remain stale, allowing the vector database to keep returning protected content. This paper measures the duration of this revocation window and separates two outcomes: unauthorized index retrieval, in which the vector database returns a protected chunk, and LLM-context exposure, in which that chunk reaches the context assembled for the language model. We built a controlled synthetic testbed with PostgreSQL as the authoritative permission store and Qdrant as the vector index, and evaluated six enforcement configurations: periodic synchronization, event-driven synchronization, a no-worker control, query-time authorization, hybrid authorization, and query-time authorization with a 10-second decision cache. Each configuration retained 27 trials (5 for the control) within a 35-second observation window. The median context-level revocation propagation time was 9.92 s for 20-second periodic synchronization, 14 ms for event-driven synchronization, and 4.98 s for the cached query-time configuration. Under periodic synchronization, 87.7% of relevant queries placed the protected chunk in the context before revocation was enforced. Query-time and hybrid authorization blocked protected content at the first post-revocation probe (0 ms at probe resolution) even though the stale index kept returning it, while the no-worker control never achieved stable enforcement within the window. These findings describe the tested synthetic testbed and are not production guarantees.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a technology with tremendous potential to revolutionize healthcare, contributing to progress in medical diagnostics, clinical decision support, personalized medicine, patient monitoring, medical research, and healthcare management. This systematic review covers the current use of AI in healthcare, its clinical effects and hindrances for implementation. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines were followed to conduct a systematic literature search. The search query was conducted in major electronic databases using specific keywords of the studies and results, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and other sources, including studies on artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, large language models, healthcare applications, clinical decision support, medical imaging, drug discovery, digital health, and healthcare data systems. This evidence review identifies evidence of how AI is being used in a variety of healthcare areas such as medical imaging and diagnostics, virtual patient monitoring, drug design, precision medicine, rehabilitation, patient engagement, and operational health care processes. The use of AI has been shown to have the potential to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis, improve clinical decision‐making, personalize care, and optimize healthcare workflows. However, there are substantial hurdles to overcome, such as data privacy and security issues, algorithmic bias, the lack of the clinical validation of AI models, regulatory scrutiny, infrastructure challenges, and the need for effective clinical validation. The key takeaways from this review are the need for a balanced approach to the integration of AI in healthcare, acknowledging both the technological innovations and the ethical, regulatory, and human factors considerations that need to be addressed. More large‐scale clinical validation studies are needed as well as the establishment of reliable AI systems and strategies to ensure responsible and fair use of AI in healthcare.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT To effectively prevent bridge operation and maintenance (O&M) accidents, a hybrid method integrating text mining with Bayesian network theory was adopted to systematically analyze the causal factors of accidents affecting bridge O&M safety and their interrelationships. First, text mining techniques were applied to preprocess data from 226 Chinese bridge O&M accident cases (1999–2025). Using the BERTopic topic modeling approach, 20 safety risk topics were identified, and 20 corresponding causal factors were extracted based on key feature words under these topics. Drawing on the Human‐Machine‐Environment‐Management safety management theory, the safety risk causal factors were classified into four risk categories, namely, bridge self‐factors, O&M environmental factors, human factors, and management defects. The Apriori algorithm was employed to analyze the interrelationships among risk factors, from which a total of 42 strong association rules were extracted; these rules were then taken as the basis for constructing a Bayesian network model. Through Bayesian network reasoning and sensitivity analysis, the key causal factors, sensitive factors, and the maximum‐probability causal chain of bridge O&M safety accidents were clarified. Analysis of the key causal chain revealed that the chain with the highest probability of leading to bridge O&M safety accidents is as follows: inadequate industrial supervision→substandard construction quality→structural construction defects→insufficient structural bearing capacity→bridge accidents. Sensitivity analysis identified vessel collision and floating debris collision as the key sensitive factors influencing bridge O&M safety accidents, whereas insufficient structural bearing capacity and other relevant factors were defined as moderately sensitive factors, thus providing a robust basis for the targeted prevention and control of such accidents. This method avoids the interference of experts' subjective factors, conducts an in‐depth analysis of bridge O&M safety accidents based on objective data, and provides theoretical support and methodological guidance for formulating more scientific accident prevention measures, which endows it with important practical significance in bridge engineering practice.

Abstract Background Early risk stratification after intensive care unit (ICU) admission may inform treatment intensity, goals-of-care discussions, and resource allocation. Developing and maintaining supervised machine learning models requires large labelled cohorts and technical infrastructure that may not be available in all settings. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) can generate risk estimates with human-readable rationales, but their performance and reasoning quality across independent healthcare systems remain uncertain. Methods We analysed three ICU cohorts: eICU-CRD (208 US hospitals), MIMIC-IV (US), and a Korean tertiary-hospital subset of K-MIMIC (Korea). Seven-day mortality after ICU admission was predicted from routinely collected demographic, laboratory, and vital sign variables recorded during the first 24 hours. Six supervised machine learning and deep learning models were developed in eICU-CRD and externally validated in MIMIC-IV and K-MIMIC. GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro were evaluated with four prompting strategies in 2,000-stay samples per cohort, without cohort-specific training or task-specific fine-tuning. Clinical concepts mentioned in GPT-5 rationales were compared with patient-level predictor importance from an XGBoost reference model; two clinicians rated 150 rationales for clinical trustworthiness. Results Analyses included 124,020, 84,926, and 6,673 ICU stays. Among supervised models, the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.936 for XGBoost in the held-out eICU-CRD set, 0.858 for the multilayer perceptron in MIMIC-IV, and 0.957 for XGBoost in K-MIMIC. In the corresponding 2,000-stay LLM evaluation samples, GPT-5 achieved AUROCs of 0.925, 0.822, and 0.926, respectively, but generally had a lower area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) and, at evaluated operating thresholds, lower specificity. Overlap with the five most influential concepts was partial (precision, 0.47; recall, 0.55), but mentioned concepts had greater mean patient-level importance than nonmentioned concepts in 98.1% of patients (P < 0.001). Clinician-rated trustworthiness averaged 4.03 ± 0.63 on a 5-point scale, with ratings within one point in 83% of cases. Conclusions Supervised models generally achieved the highest discrimination for 7-day mortality after ICU admission. GPT-5 achieved high discrimination without cohort-specific training or task-specific fine-tuning, and its patient-specific rationales preferentially referenced influential predictors and received favorable clinician ratings. Prospective evaluation of reasoning faithfulness and clinical utility is required before clinical use.

documents.abstract: Maintaining consistency between source code and its associated comments is essential for software reliability, maintainability, and user experience, particularly in the Rust programming ecosystem, where comments serve as both developer guidance and an authoritative API contract. However, existing automated inconsistency detection approaches are largely tailored for object-oriented languages and fall short of addressing Rust’s unique features, such as explicit panic semantics, trait-based abstraction, and idiomatic use of option and finiteness constraints. In this article, we introduce RustC 4 ++, a novel hybrid framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-driven constraint extraction, static program analysis, and SMT-based bidirectional verification to detect and diagnose code-comment inconsistencies in Rust. RustC 4 ++ extends previous solutions by supporting a richer taxonomy of constraints, including interval, boundary, existence, option, and finiteness constraints, and pioneers a systematic method for propagating comment constraints across trait and implementation boundaries. Leveraging chain-of-thought prompt engineering, RustC 4 ++ robustly interprets natural language comments, maps it to formal specifications, and checks their alignment with code logic through precise static analysis and formal reasoning. We conduct extensive experiments on 17 diverse, real-world Rust projects, demonstrating that RustC 4 ++ substantially outperforms prior tools in both precision and recall, and is capable of uncovering subtle, actionable inconsistencies that have led to confirmed fixes in upstream repositories. By elevating comments to enforceable, verifiable contracts, RustC 4 ++ not only enhances code quality and comment reliability in the Rust ecosystem but also offers generalizable techniques and insights for automated code comment analysis in other modern programming languages.

Problem: Safety-in-design decisions are often made before users, operating environments and manual-handling demands are understood. This risks products valued by customers creating avoidable physical demands for staff who handle them. Air New Zealand is collaborating with Auckland University of Technology (AUT) to embed human factors and ergonomics (HFE) in product development. Method: The collaboration engages students from second year to Masters level in manual-handling risk assessment, the hierarchy of controls and ergonomic principles. Students examine products and processes as systems through site-based problem framing, worker input, task analysis and concept review. Two case studies: adaptation of an airline jug, and redesign of the Business Premier mattress. The mattress project, led with a Bachelor of Industrial Design student, mapped its lifecycle: laundry, supply and amenities placement, transport to the aircraft, cabin-crew interaction, storage, offboarding and return to laundry. Whilst second year students did the same with the coffee jug.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Schools across Asia are experiencing rapid educational change due to technology integration. Teachers increasingly face pressure to use Artificial Intelligence (AI), while also worrying about errors, cheating, ethical concerns, and unclear institutional policies. This study explored school leaders’ perceptions of how teachers experience AI-related anxiety and how leadership practices support teachers’ AI competence in South Asian countries. A phenomenological research design was employed. Using purposive and snowball sampling, 10 high school leaders from Pakistan, Sri Lanka, India, Bangladesh, and Nepal were selected. Data were collected online through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Four themes emerged from the findings. First, school leaders perceived that teachers feared accountability and public criticism when AI-generated outputs were inaccurate or inappropriate. Second, school leaders reported that teachers expressed concerns about cheating, fairness, and loss of professional identity. Third, school leaders described reducing teachers’ anxiety by creating low-risk professional learning environments and encouraging peer support. Fourth, leaders established clear guidance regarding acceptable AI use, transparency, and student data protection. Across the participating schools, leaders consistently viewed teachers’ AI-related anxiety as a major barrier to responsible AI adoption. The findings suggest that leadership practices supporting ethical AI governance, collaborative professional learning, and equitable AI implementation contribute to sustainable teacher professional development and responsible educational transformation.

Pilot readback of Air Traffic Control (ATC) voice instructions is a primary safeguard against miscommunication in air transportation. However, readback anomalies remain implicated in approximately 80% of aviation incidents. This vulnerability is further exacerbated by rising traffic volume and elevated cognitive workload, thereby motivating automated readback monitoring by machine. Traditional rule-based and machine learning approaches struggle to generalize across the highly variable and evolving phraseology of air traffic controller-pilot communications. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened a new avenue through their strong reasoning and generalization capabilities, existing approaches still face deployment and computational barriers in practice. In this work, we propose Semantic reasoning for Communication via Open-set Plug-in with Examples (SCOPE), a novel lightweight-training LLM framework that advances both the efficiency and accuracy of machine-based ATC readback monitoring. The core idea is to couple a plug-in open-set classifier with a carefully designed in-context learning mechanism on top of a frozen LLM. Extensive experiments on the semi-synthetic communication dataset show that SCOPE attains superior accuracy while delivering the low-latency response required for operational environments. Under a few-shot setting, SCOPE achieves 91.05% accuracy in open-set detection and corrects 96.63% of anomalous readbacks, thereby outperforming the strongest available baselines while providing explanations for its decisions. These findings demonstrate the potential of our framework as a practical pathway toward interpretable and controllable ATC readback monitoring.

University timetabling and resource allocation automation has historically relied on rigid operations research models that scale poorly during sudden operational disruptions. While recent advances in multi-agent systems (MASs) and large language models (LLMs) offer dynamic semantic adaptability, these purely probabilistic architectures fail to satisfy strict, NP-hard combinatorial constraints, rendering them unsafe for independent administrative execution. This research introduces a hybrid agentic-symbolic framework that bridges this evaluation gap by decoupling neural reasoning from deterministic execution. The architecture utilizes a network of specialized LLM agents to negotiate institutional demand. Meanwhile, a Z3 formal verification engine acts as an immutable gatekeeper, mathematically blocking any physically impossible schedule from executing. To evaluate hardware feasibility, the framework underwent an 8-semester longitudinal simulation across two distinct institutional topologies (totaling 16 simulated semesters) across heterogeneous computing environments, incorporating stochastic structural and personnel shocks. Empirical telemetry indicates a critical failure mode within constrained 23 Edge CPU infrastructure, which we characterize as autoregressive token explosion, in which 24 generative model’s attention mechanism collapses during the production of large schemas, paralyzing the system. To address this, the architecture substitutes conventional substantial solvers with a sub-millisecond greedy heuristic fallback. The results demonstrate that this deterministic safety mechanism intercepts catastrophic neural failures and resolves the scheduling matrix in under 1.0 millisecond. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that formally verified multi-agent systems can attain zero-violation compliance and uninterrupted institutional continuity when supported by lightweight, hardware-aware heuristic overrides.

This conceptual paper introduces Separation of Diagnostic Revision Depths, a distinction among four ways to investigate a failed expectation. An inquirer can adjust a value within the current model, reopen a condition previously treated as settled, expand the model’s boundary to include an omitted factor, or revise its account of how one quantity or event depends on another. Each operation holds different things fixed. A value that brings a prediction into agreement with an observation establishes that the model can fit that observation at that value. The assumptions retained in making the adjustment still require their own grounds. The paper assesses a diagnosis by asking what evidence supports the chosen revision and what competing revisions would predict. The four operations can overlap or occur in different orders. A small adjustment may have the strongest support. The paper places this distinction alongside Imre Lakatos’s account of research programs, narrowing the question to what a particular response to a single discrepancy can establish. Two historical cases give the distinction concrete form. To explain the anomalous advance of Mercury’s perihelion, Urbain Le Verrier proposed an unseen planet or smaller bodies, Asaph Hall proposed changing the exponent in the law of gravitation, and Albert Einstein accounted for the advance using a new theory of gravitation. In the Mars case, Johannes Kepler adjusted a circular model to fit Tycho Brahe’s observations of planetary positions at opposition. A check against distances exposed a further difficulty. After correction, some predicted positions missed the observations by as much as eight minutes of arc, beyond their estimated precision of two minutes. This gave Kepler grounds to reopen the assumption of circular motion. He subsequently adopted an ellipse. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the distinction has a prospective application in human–AI evaluation. When an AI forecast underestimates a project’s duration, a reviewer might adjust a task estimate, check whether a promised input arrived, include an omitted approval, or revise which tasks the model treats as able to run in parallel. The project record can help the reviewer decide which change the evidence supports.
